lessons.contentMarkdown:
# What Professional Identity Means in the Digital Age

## What You'll Learn
- What "professional identity" actually means (and what it doesn't)
- What "digital reputation" is, and how it's different from professional identity
- How to tell the difference between a *claim* and *evidence*
- How to take a basic, private look at your own current online footprint
- How to name real evidence you already have from projects you've built

## Why It Matters
Right now, you already have skills — things you've built, bugs you've fixed, ideas you've turned into working code. But if a stranger looked you up online today, would they be able to tell? Most people's online presence is accidental: old posts, unfinished profiles, nothing that shows what they can actually do.

This course is about fixing that on purpose. Over the next few lessons you'll turn your real Lumexa projects into a portfolio site, a brand kit, and case studies that actually show your skill. But before you build any of that, you need to understand what you're building *toward* — that's what today is for.

**Where this fits:** this course follows a path — **Identity → Services → Clients → Professional Presence → Opportunities**. Today is Identity, step one. We are not talking about freelancing, getting hired, or job platforms yet. Today is just about understanding yourself and what you've already got.

---

## The Simple Version

**Professional identity** = the answer to: *"If a stranger saw only what I've made, what would they think I'm capable of?"*

It's not about sounding fake, corporate, or "adult." It's about being **clear and backed up by real evidence.** A 16-year-old's professional identity should still sound like a 16-year-old — just one who can back up what they say.

**Digital reputation** = everything that's already out there about you online, whether you built it on purpose or not. Some of it you control (a GitHub profile, a project page). Some of it just happened (an old comment, a forgotten social post, nothing at all).

Think of it like a game profile: your rank and match history show other players what you can actually do — not what you claim you can do. Professional identity works the same way, except your "stats" are your real projects.

### Claim vs. Evidence — the most important idea in this lesson

| This is a **claim** | This is **evidence** |
|---|---|
| "I'm good at JavaScript." | A link to a working project you coded in JavaScript. |
| "I can build websites." | A live site you deployed on Vercel. |
| "I care about clean design." | A Canva brand kit or a well-designed project page. |
| "I helped my team solve a bug." | A specific description of the bug and what you actually did to fix it. |

Anyone can make a claim. Evidence is what makes people believe you — and it's what the rest of this course helps you build.

---

## Worked Example (Fictional Persona)

> **Note: "Jordan R." below is a completely fictional example created for this lesson. Not a real student.**

Jordan R., age 16, has been coding on Lumexa for about eight months. If you searched "Jordan R." online today, here's roughly what you'd find:

- A GitHub profile with two repositories — one has a clear README explaining what it does and why; the other is unfinished with no description.
- A page from a school robotics club listing Jordan as a member.
- An old social media post from two years ago, unrelated to coding.
- A finished Lumexa project: a simple weather app with a working interface.

**What a stranger would conclude:** Jordan has real technical ability (the weather app and the documented repo prove it), but the picture is inconsistent — the undocumented repo and the unrelated old post don't help, and there's no single place that pulls the good evidence together.

**The fix (which is exactly what this course teaches):** Jordan doesn't need to invent new achievements. Jordan needs to (1) finish documenting what already exists, (2) put the best evidence in one place, and (3) decide what story that evidence should tell. That's professional identity — arranging real evidence on purpose instead of leaving it scattered.

---

## In-Class Activity: Digital Identity Audit

You'll fill out the **Digital Identity Audit worksheet** (shared by your instructor). Here's how it works:

### Option A — If you already have some online footprint
1. Privately (not out loud, not in group chat), think through or briefly search what currently exists about you online: social profiles, GitHub, school pages, anything else.
2. Fill in the worksheet's footprint inventory table with what you find — you will **not** be asked to share this list with the class.
3. Note anything that feels like a gap or a risk (e.g., "nothing shows my coding work" or "an old post I wouldn't want a stranger to see first").
4. Complete the rest of the worksheet (see below).

### Option B — If you don't have much or any online footprint yet
This is completely normal, especially if you're newer to Lumexa or don't have social media. Instead:
1. Skip the search step entirely.
2. In the footprint inventory table, write "No significant footprint yet" — that's a valid, honest answer.
3. Focus your energy on the rest of the worksheet: the 3 things you want people to know about you, and the 3 pieces of evidence you already have from your own work (Lumexa projects count!).

Either way, **you will never be asked to read your search results or personal profiles aloud to the class.** This activity is private and self-paced.

---

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Professional identity** | The intentional, evidence-backed picture of your skills and work that others can see. |
| **Digital reputation** | Everything that currently exists about you online, whether you built it on purpose or not. |
| **Personal brand** | The consistent way you present your identity — your voice, visuals, and the story your evidence tells together. |
| **Portfolio** | A collection of your real projects, organized to show your skills clearly. |
| **Credibility** | The degree to which someone can trust that what you say about yourself is true. |
| **Evidence vs. claim** | A claim is a statement about yourself; evidence is proof — something someone else can look at and verify. |

---

## Knowledge Check

1. In your own words, what is the difference between "professional identity" and "digital reputation"?
2. Give one example of a *claim* and rewrite it as *evidence*.
3. True or false: having little to no online footprint at your age is a sign you're behind. Explain your answer.
4. Why does this course avoid the words "fake" or "corporate" when describing professional identity? What should it mean instead?
5. Name one real project or piece of work you've done that could count as evidence of a skill.

## Reflection Prompts

1. If a stranger looked up your name today, what's one thing you'd want them to *not* be the first thing they see — and why?
2. Of the things you've built so far (on Lumexa or elsewhere), which one are you proudest of, and what does it actually prove about your skill?
3. What's one word you want your future professional identity to make people think of when they see your work?

---

## Submission Instructions

- Complete the **Digital Identity Audit worksheet** in full.
- Submit it using the method your instructor shares at the end of class (Google Doc link or LMS upload).
- Do not include anyone else's personal information (friends, classmates, family) in your worksheet.
- Bring your completed worksheet to Lesson 2 — you'll use it directly to start building your portfolio.

### Section 3 Example

2. I write code that other people can actually understand and reuse.

### Section 4 Example

"By the end of this course, I want a simple portfolio site that shows my three best projects clearly, with a short case study for each one explaining what I built and why — so if someone looks me up, they see real proof instead of just a name."

# Instructor Guide — Course 16, Lesson 1

## Lesson Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path |
| Course | 16 — Build Your Professional Identity |
| Lesson | 1 of Course 16 |
| Title | What Professional Identity Means in the Digital Age |
| Age range | 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led, screen-share video class |
| Duration | ~60 minutes |
| Difficulty | Introductory (conceptual, low technical load) |
| Prerequisites | None. Students should have at least one completed Lumexa project (any course) to reference, but it is not required to complete this lesson. |
| Tools used this lesson | A web browser (for the live demo), Google Docs (for the worksheet) |
| Tools used later in Course 16 | HTML, CSS, Vercel, Canva, GitHub, Google Docs |

**Course 16 progression reminder:** this course sits inside the larger Digital Independence Path sequence of **Identity → Services → Clients → Professional Presence → Opportunities**. Lesson 1 is the "Identity" foundation — nothing here is about freelance platforms, job boards, or client acquisition yet. Keep the lesson focused on self-understanding and evidence, not on "getting hired."

### Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Define "professional identity" and "digital reputation" in their own words.
2. Explain the difference between a *claim* ("I'm good at coding") and *evidence* ("here is a working project I built").
3. Audit their own current online footprint at a basic level, safely and privately.
4. Identify at least three pieces of real evidence they already have from Lumexa or other work.
5. Articulate one personal goal for what they want their professional identity to communicate by the end of Course 16.

### Deliverables
- Completed **Digital Identity Audit** worksheet (submitted via Google Docs link or upload, per your classroom's submission method).
- Verbal or chat participation in the discussion segment.

### Skills Practiced
- Self-assessment and reflection
- Basic online research / search literacy
- Distinguishing claims from evidence
- Early-stage personal branding thinking (not design yet — that's a later lesson)

### Portfolio Connection
This lesson does not produce a portfolio artifact directly, but the worksheet output (their "3 things I want people to know" and "3 pieces of evidence") becomes the raw material for Lesson 2+ of this course, where students start building the actual portfolio site, brand kit, and case studies. Tell students explicitly: *"Nothing you write today is throwaway — you'll reuse this worksheet in the next lesson."*

---

## Instructor Prep Checklist

- [ ] Read this guide fully and skim the Student Lesson and Worksheet files before class.
- [ ] Have a browser window ready for the live "search result walkthrough" demo, using the **fictional persona** described below (never search a real student's name live).
- [ ] Have the Worksheet (Google Doc or PDF) ready to share/link with students at the start of class.
- [ ] Prepare your screen share so the demo search results are pre-loaded or bookmarked — do not fumble live searches on stage.
- [ ] Review the "Common Misconceptions" and "Discussion Questions" sections so you're ready to redirect, not lecture.
- [ ] Have at least one real (with permission) or fictional example of a student project from Lumexa to point to as "this counts as evidence."
- [ ] Confirm your classroom's policy for how students submit the worksheet (Google Doc share, LMS upload, etc.) and state it clearly at the end of class.
- [ ] Note which students are new to Lumexa (no prior projects yet) — you'll need the "no footprint yet" alternative activity ready for them.

## Required Files / Links
- `Student_Lesson.md` — share the "what you'll learn" and glossary sections on-screen as needed.
- `Worksheet.md` — convert to your platform's fillable format (Google Doc template, PDF form, or LMS form) before class; students fill this in live during the activity segment.
- A blank/incognito browser tab for the live demo (so autocomplete/history doesn't leak).

---

## Suggested Teaching Sequence (60 minutes)

| Time | Segment | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:05 | Welcome & framing | Greet students, state the goal of the lesson and how it connects to the rest of Course 16 and the Digital Independence Path. |
| 0:05–0:15 | Concept intro: Professional Identity & Digital Reputation | Explain both terms using the analogies below. Check for understanding with a quick poll/thumbs-up. |
| 0:15–0:20 | Claims vs. Evidence | Explain the distinction with concrete examples pulled from coding contexts. |
| 0:20–0:35 | Live Demo: Search Result Walkthrough | Walk through the fictional persona's search results together, narrating what a stranger would conclude. |
| 0:35–0:40 | Discussion Questions | Pose 2–3 discussion questions, take verbal or chat answers. |
| 0:40–0:55 | In-Class Activity: Digital Identity Audit | Students fill in the worksheet privately (self-paced, instructor circulates / monitors chat for questions). |
| 0:55–0:60 | Wrap-up & submission instructions | Recap key terms, preview Lesson 2, confirm how/when to submit the worksheet. |

---

## Instructor Talking Points

### What is "professional identity"?
Say something like:

> "Your professional identity is the answer to the question: *if someone who's never met you looked at what you've made, what would they think you're capable of?* It's not about being fake or 'corporate' — it's about making the real skills you already have visible and easy to trust."

**Analogy for teens:** Compare it to a gaming profile or a Discord server reputation. *"You know how in a game, your rank, your stats, and your match history tell other players what you can actually do — not what you say you can do? Professional identity works the same way, except the 'game' is your coding skill, and the 'stats' are your real projects."*

### What is "digital reputation"?
> "Digital reputation is what's already out there about you online, whether you built it on purpose or not. It's the difference between the identity you're actively building and the scattered, accidental trail you've left without thinking about it — old social posts, a school project on GitHub nobody documented, a comment on a forum from three years ago."

**Analogy:** *"It's like your search history, except it's other people's search history about you."*

Important: for students under 16 or with little to no online presence, reassure them this is completely normal — the point of the lesson is to start building this on purpose, not to judge them for not having one yet.

### Framing "professional" correctly (counter the "fake/corporate" misconception early)
> "Professional doesn't mean stiff, boring, or pretending to be a 40-year-old. It means: clear, honest, and backed by evidence. A 16-year-old's professional identity should still sound like a 16-year-old — just one who can prove what they say."

---

## Live Demo Instructions: The Search Result Walkthrough

**Do not search a real student's name live.** Use a prepared, clearly-labeled **fictional persona** for the demo. Suggested persona:

> **"Jordan R., age 16, fictional example used for teaching only."**

### How to run it
1. Before class, prepare (as slides, a mock browser screenshot, or a doc — not an actual live web search) a fictional search-results mockup for "Jordan R." showing:
   - A results list with 4–5 fictional entries: e.g., a GitHub profile with two projects (one with a good README, one abandoned/empty), a school club webpage mentioning them, an old social post, and a Lumexa project page.
2. Screen-share the mockup and narrate it as a stranger would read it:
   - *"If I'm a stranger looking at this, what do I conclude about Jordan? What looks strong? What looks unfinished or confusing?"*
3. Ask students to call out (chat or voice) which entries build trust and which ones create doubt.
4. Land the point: *"Notice we didn't judge Jordan as a person — we judged the evidence. That's the whole game: making sure the evidence that's visible is the evidence you'd choose."*

**Never** have students search their own names aloud or share personal search results with the class — this protects privacy and avoids putting anyone on the spot for gaps that aren't their fault (many students are simply too young to have a footprint yet).

---

## Discussion Questions

1. "Before today, had you ever thought about what a stranger would find if they looked you up? What's your gut reaction to that idea?"
2. "What's one project you've made — on Lumexa or elsewhere — that you think is genuinely good evidence of a skill, even if nobody's seen it yet?"
3. "Where's the line between 'professional' and 'fake'? Can you think of an example of someone (a creator, a small business, anyone) who seems professional without seeming fake?"

---

## Common Misconceptions (and how to correct them)

| Misconception | Correction |
|---|---|
| "I need real work experience already to have a professional identity." | Not true. A professional identity starts with *evidence of skill*, not a job history. A working project, a solved bug, a documented process — all count as evidence at 15–18. |
| "Professional = fake, corporate, and boring." | Reframe: professional means *clear and backed by evidence*, not stiff or impersonal. Their personality can and should show through. |
| "I don't have anything online yet, so I have no digital reputation." | Having little to no footprint is a neutral starting point, not a failure — it just means today is about starting on purpose instead of by accident. |
| "This is basically just making a resume." | A resume is a claim-based document. This course is about *evidence-based* identity — portfolios, live projects, and case studies, which is a different (and stronger) kind of proof. |
| "Building a professional identity means I'm trying to get a job / freelance right now." | Correct this directly: this course's sequence is Identity → Services → Clients → Professional Presence → Opportunities. Today is only step one — self-understanding, not job-seeking. |

## Likely Student Difficulties

- **Younger students (15) with no online footprint** may feel behind or discouraged. Have the "no footprint yet" alternative activity ready (see Student Lesson) and normalize it verbally before the activity begins.
- **Students who conflate "professional" with "adult/formal"** may write worksheet answers in a stiff, generic voice. Encourage them to write in their real voice — "professional" is about honesty and evidence, not tone.
- **Students who don't yet have 3 pieces of evidence** may struggle with that worksheet section. Prompt them: a half-finished project, a helpful comment/explanation they gave a classmate, a design they made in another class — anything real and specific counts.
- **Oversharing risk:** a few students may want to publicly discuss personal search results (their own name, social media, etc.) in the group. Redirect this to the private worksheet rather than open chat/voice, per the safe-activity design.

## Troubleshooting & Classroom Management Notes

- If the live demo mockup isn't ready, do **not** improvise a real live search on stage — fall back to describing the persona verbally and sketching the "results" on a shared whiteboard/doc instead.
- If a student starts sharing personal identifying details (full name, school, social handles) in open chat during the activity, gently redirect: *"Let's keep that part private on your worksheet — you don't need to share it with the group."*
- If time runs short, the Activity segment (0:40–0:55) can be trimmed to 10 minutes and finished as take-home; the worksheet submission deadline should then be communicated clearly.
- Keep the tone conversational, not lecture-heavy — this lesson is discussion- and reflection-driven, not content-heavy.

## How to Review Student Work

When reviewing submitted worksheets, check for:
1. **Specificity** — did they name real projects/skills, or write vague claims ("I'm good at coding")? Vague answers need a follow-up nudge before Lesson 2.
2. **Honesty** — flag (privately, kindly) anything that reads as exaggerated or unverifiable; this course is built on credibility, so this is worth correcting early and gently.
3. **At least 3 evidence items** — even informal or small ones are fine; the goal is the habit of pointing at evidence, not the scale of it.
4. **A genuine goal statement** — not a copy of the lesson's own language back at you.

Give brief, specific written feedback (1–2 sentences per student) rather than a grade — this is a foundational, reflective lesson, not a graded skills check.

## How to Close the Lesson

1. Recap the three core ideas in one sentence each: *professional identity is what your evidence says about you; digital reputation is what's already out there; this course helps you make both intentional instead of accidental.*
2. Preview Lesson 2: *"Next lesson, we start turning what you wrote today into the beginning of an actual portfolio site."*
3. Confirm the exact submission method and deadline for the worksheet.
4. Thank students for being candid — self-reflection lessons work best when students trust it's a safe space, so acknowledge that explicitly before ending the call.

lessons.title: Define Your Strengths and Direction
lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Lesson 2: Define Your Strengths and Direction

## What You're Doing Today

Last lesson, you found every trace of your work that's already out there — GitHub repos, Lumexa missions, Canva designs, deployed sites. Today you turn that list into something useful: an honest answer to *"what am I actually good at, and what should my portfolio focus on?"*

You are not inventing a personality or picking a job for life. You're reading your own evidence and choosing one honest, provable direction to build your portfolio around for the rest of this course.

## Why This Matters

A portfolio that claims things you can't back up falls apart the moment someone asks a follow-up question. A portfolio built on real evidence — even small evidence — holds up, because you can always show the receipts. This lesson is about finding the receipts you already have.

---

## Three Kinds of "Good At"

It's easy to mix these up. They're not the same thing, and a strong portfolio treats them differently.

| Level | What it means | What counts as evidence | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Interest** | Something you're curious about or enjoy | None required | "I think game design looks cool." |
| **Strength** | Something you're noticeably better at, or improve faster at, than your other work | A pattern across 2+ attempts, or solid feedback | "My CSS layouts always come out cleaner than my other project parts." |
| **Proven skill** | Something you can point to a finished, working thing to demonstrate | One or more completed artifacts | "Here's a Vercel site I built and styled myself." |

**The rule:** your portfolio direction should be led by proven skills, backed up by strengths, and can mention interests only as "what I want to learn next" — never claimed as if they're already true.

---

## Worked Example (Fictional Student)

> **Note:** "Jordan R." is a made-up example used for teaching. Not a real Lumexa student.

Jordan looked at their project list from Lesson 1:

1. Lumexa Mission "Space Weather Dashboard" — HTML/CSS, styled with Canva graphics, deployed to Vercel
2. Lumexa Mission "Simple Platformer Game" — finished, but the jump mechanic is buggy; Jordan's only game project
3. Personal project — redesigned a birthday invitation in Canva for family
4. Lumexa Mission "Personal Portfolio Starter Page" — HTML/CSS, deployed to Vercel, got positive instructor feedback on layout
5. Group project — helped a teammate fix color scheme and spacing in their CSS (not Jordan's own repo)

**Jordan's honest read:**

- Projects 1, 3, 4, and 5 all involve visual layout and styling — that's the *same skill showing up four times*, across different tools and contexts. That's a real strength.
- Project 2 is a genuine finished game, but it's the *only* one, and it has a known bug. That's an interest with a little early proof — not yet a strength.
- Direction: **front-end web development / visual design** — because the evidence repeats and includes outside positive feedback.
- Game dev goes in the "still want to learn" list — real, but not yet backed by enough evidence to lead the portfolio.

Notice what Jordan did **not** do: claim to be a "full-stack game developer" because one buggy platformer sounded impressive. The direction follows the evidence, not the excitement.

---

## Step-by-Step Activity

Open your Worksheet and your Lesson 1 audit notes, then work through these steps in order.

### Step 1: List every project

Every Lumexa mission, every personal project, every time you helped someone else with code or design — even unfinished ones. Put each in the inventory table.

### Step 2: Tag what each one demonstrates

For each project, write down the actual skill it shows — be specific ("CSS layout and spacing," not just "coding").

### Step 3: Set an honest confidence level

For each project, mark your confidence: **High** (I could do this again reliably), **Medium** (I did it once, with help or some struggle), or **Low** (I tried, it's rough, or someone else did most of it).

### Step 4: Cluster into a direction

Look for a skill that shows up in **two or more** projects at Medium or High confidence. That repeat pattern is your strength cluster. Pick one (or at most two, if they're closely related) to be your portfolio direction.

### Step 5: Write your direction statement

Use the template on your Worksheet. Keep it to 1–2 sentences, and make sure you can point to specific projects that back it up.

### Step 6: Park your other interests

List things you're genuinely excited about but can't yet prove. These go in "what I still want to learn" — not deleted, just set aside for now.

---

## Key Terms Glossary

- **Interest** — something you're curious about or enjoy; requires no evidence to claim.
- **Strength** — a skill you're noticeably better at than your other work, shown by a repeating pattern across multiple projects.
- **Proven skill** — a skill backed by at least one finished, working artifact you can show someone.
- **Direction** — the honest focus area you choose to build your portfolio around right now, based on your strongest evidence.
- **Confidence level** — your own honest rating (High/Medium/Low) of how solid your evidence is for a given project.
- **Strength cluster** — a group of two or more projects that all demonstrate the same underlying skill.

---

## Knowledge Check

1. What is the main difference between an "interest" and a "strength"?
2. Why is claiming an interest as a "proven skill" a problem for a portfolio?
3. In the Jordan R. example, why didn't Jordan pick "game developer" as their direction, even though the platformer game was a real finished project?
4. What makes a group of projects count as a genuine "strength cluster" rather than just one lucky project?
5. Where should a real interest go if you don't have enough evidence yet to call it a strength?

---

## Reflection Prompts

1. Was there a project you almost left off your inventory because it felt too small or unfinished to count? What made you decide either way?
2. Did the direction your evidence pointed to match what you expected before you started, or did it surprise you?
3. If someone asked you right now to prove your direction statement using only what you've already built, what would you show them first?

---

## Submission Instructions

Submit your completed Worksheet (Strengths & Direction Map) through the Lumexa classroom portal before the next live session. Make sure it includes: a filled-in project inventory table, at least one clearly identified strength cluster, a completed direction statement, and a "what I still want to learn" section. Bring a digital or printed copy to Lesson 3 — you'll build your portfolio structure directly from your direction statement.

Name: _______________________  Date: _______________________

Use your Lesson 1 audit notes to complete this worksheet. Be honest — a smaller, true picture is more useful than an impressive-sounding false one.

---

## Part 1: Project Inventory

List every project you can think of — Lumexa missions, personal projects, and times you helped someone else. Include unfinished or informal ones. Add rows as needed.

| Project Name | What It Demonstrates (be specific) | Confidence Level (High / Medium / Low) |
|---|---|---|
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |

---

## Part 2: Strengths Clustering

Look at your table above. Group any projects that show the **same underlying skill**, even if they used different tools. A cluster needs **two or more** projects at Medium or High confidence to count as a real strength.

**Example (Fictional — Jordan R.):**

> Cluster: *Visual layout & styling*
> Projects: Space Weather Dashboard (Lumexa), Personal Portfolio Starter Page (Lumexa), Birthday invitation redesign (personal), Group CSS debugging help
> Why it's a real cluster: same skill shows up 4 times, across school missions and personal work, including outside positive feedback.

**Your clusters:**

**Cluster 1:**
- Skill: _______________________________________________
- Projects that support it: _______________________________________________
- Why this counts as a real cluster (not a one-off): _______________________________________________

**Cluster 2 (optional):**
- Skill: _______________________________________________
- Projects that support it: _______________________________________________
- Why this counts as a real cluster (not a one-off): _______________________________________________

---

## Part 3: My Direction for This Portfolio

Use this template to write your direction statement. Keep it to 1–2 honest sentences you can back up with your inventory above.

**Template:**

> My portfolio direction is **[focus area]**, because my projects show a repeated pattern of **[specific skill]** across **[number]** projects, including **[strongest piece of evidence]**.

**Example (Fictional — Jordan R.):**

> My portfolio direction is **front-end web development and visual design**, because my projects show a repeated pattern of **layout, styling, and visual polish** across **four** projects, including my **Personal Portfolio Starter Page**, which got positive feedback from my instructor and is deployed live on Vercel.

**Your direction statement:**

> My portfolio direction is _______________________________________________, because my projects show a repeated pattern of _______________________________________________ across _______ projects, including _______________________________________________.

---

## Part 4: What I Still Want to Learn

List genuine interests you have that aren't backed by enough evidence yet to be part of your direction. These aren't deleted — they're what you might build toward next.

**Example (Fictional — Jordan R.):**

> - Game development — I have one finished platformer, but it's my only game project and the jump mechanic still has bugs. I want to build 2–3 more before I'd call this a strength.
> - Data visualization — haven't tried it yet, but it looks interesting after seeing it in a Lumexa mission preview.

**Yours:**

1. _______________________________________________
2. _______________________________________________
3. _______________________________________________

---

*Keep this worksheet — you'll use your Part 3 direction statement directly at the start of Lesson 3.*
lessons.teacherNotes:
# Instructor Guide

## Lesson Metadata

- **Path:** Digital Independence Path
- **Course:** 16 — Build Your Professional Identity
- **Lesson:** 2 of course — "Define Your Strengths and Direction"
- **Age band:** 15–18
- **Format:** Live, instructor-led, virtual classroom
- **Duration:** 60 minutes
- **Prerequisite:** Lesson 1 — Digital Identity Audit (students must arrive with their audit notes: a list of every public/semi-public trace of their work — GitHub repos, Lumexa project submissions, Canva designs, any deployed Vercel sites)
- **Tools referenced:** GitHub, Google Docs, Vercel, Canva (no new tool setup required this lesson — this is a thinking/writing lesson)
- **Materials students need:** Their Lesson 1 audit notes, the Worksheet (Strengths & Direction Map), a Google Doc or paper to write in

---

## Overview

Lesson 1 helped students see what already exists online about them as a builder. This lesson turns that raw inventory into something usable: an honest read on what they're actually good at and interested in, and a believable focus area (a "direction") to build their portfolio around for the rest of Course 16.

The core danger this lesson guards against is **fabrication** — students claiming expertise they don't have because they think a portfolio needs to look impressive. The core skill this lesson teaches is **honest self-assessment**: separating what excites them, what they're actually decent at, and what they can prove with a finished artifact — and picking a direction from the overlap, not from wishful thinking.

By the end of the lesson, every student leaves with a completed Strengths & Direction Map: a project inventory, a strengths cluster, and a one-to-two-sentence direction statement they will use as the spine of their portfolio for the rest of the course.

---

## Instructor Prep (before class)

- Re-read your own copy of the fictional example (Jordan R., used in the Student Lesson and Worksheet) so you can reference it fluently during the live demo — don't read it cold in front of students.
- Have 2–3 real (anonymized or consented) examples from past cohorts ready as backup illustrations, if your program allows reusing past student work with permission. If not, rely on the Jordan R. example only.
- Skim each student's Lesson 1 audit notes beforehand if your platform gives you visibility into submissions. Flag students who had thin or empty audits — they'll need extra 1:1 support during the activity, since this lesson assumes Lesson 1 material to work from.
- Open a blank Google Doc or slide to run the live demo in front of students (see Live Demo script below).

---

## Teaching Sequence

### 1. Hook and Framing (5 min)

Open with a direct question to the group: *"If someone you'd never met looked at your GitHub and Lumexa projects right now, what would they think you're good at?"* Take 2–3 quick verbal answers. Don't correct them yet — just collect impressions.

Frame the lesson: *"Today we're not inventing a personality. We're reading the evidence you already have — from Lesson 1 — and figuring out, honestly, what it actually shows. Then we're going to pick ONE thing to focus on for your portfolio. Not forever. Just for now."*

### 2. Direct Teach: Interest vs. Strength vs. Proven Skill (10 min)

Introduce the three-tier framework (full definitions are in the Student Lesson glossary — teach them here, don't just assign reading):

- **Interest** — something you enjoy or are curious about. No evidence required. ("I think game design is cool.")
- **Strength** — something you are noticeably better at, or pick up faster, or get better feedback on, compared to other things you've tried. Some evidence, but maybe not a finished product. ("I always finish the CSS/layout parts of group projects faster than teammates.")
- **Proven skill** — something you can point to a *finished, working artifact* to demonstrate. ("Here is a deployed Vercel site I built and styled myself.")

Key talking point: **a portfolio should lead with proven skills, be supported by strengths, and can gesture at interests as "what I want to learn next" — never the reverse.** Claiming an interest as a proven skill is the fabrication trap this lesson exists to prevent.

Say explicitly: *"You can be interested in ten things. You can be honestly strong at three or four. You can only prove what you've actually shipped. Today we sort your own stuff into those three buckets."*

### 3. Live Demo: Reading a Fictional Student's Project List (15 min)

Use the fictional student **"Jordan R."** (clearly narrate to students that this is made up, not a real classmate). Walk through it live in a doc so students see your thinking, not just a finished answer.

**Demo script:**

Display this project list (or recreate it live):

1. Lumexa Mission: "Build a Space Weather Dashboard" — used HTML/CSS, styled with Canva graphics, deployed to Vercel
2. Lumexa Mission: "Simple Platformer Game" — built in a block-based/JS engine, finished but buggy jump mechanic
3. Personal project: redesigned little sister's birthday invitation in Canva, shared with family
4. Lumexa Mission: "Personal Portfolio Starter Page" — HTML/CSS only, deployed to Vercel, got positive instructor feedback on layout
5. Group project: helped a teammate debug their color scheme and spacing in a CSS project (not their own repo)

Narrate the extraction out loud:
- "Project 1 and 4 are both HTML/CSS, both deployed, both got positive feedback. That's a *pattern* — that's strength evidence, not a one-time fluke."
- "Project 2 is a real finished game, but Jordan says the jump mechanic is buggy and this is their only game project. That's an *interest with early proof* — not yet a strength cluster, since there's only one data point and it's incomplete."
- "Project 3 and 5 both involve visual/layout judgment — Canva design and CSS styling help. That's reinforcing the same thread as 1 and 4: visual/front-end layout is a repeating strength, showing up in multiple contexts, not just one lucky project."
- "So what's the honest direction? Not 'game developer' — one buggy game isn't enough evidence, and it would be a stretch to claim it. The evidence points to **front-end web development / visual design**, because it shows up three separate times, across different tools, with outside positive feedback."

Land the point: *"Jordan is genuinely interested in game dev too — that's fine, that's real, and it can go in the 'what I still want to learn' section. But the portfolio direction has to follow the evidence, not the excitement."*

### 4. Guided Activity (20 min)

Students open their Worksheet and Lesson 1 audit notes and work through, in order:

1. **Project inventory table** — list every Lumexa mission and personal project, what it demonstrates, and a confidence level (see Worksheet).
2. **Strengths clustering** — group projects that repeat the same skill or theme.
3. **Direction statement** — write 1–2 honest sentences naming a focus area, using the template.
4. **What I still want to learn** — park genuine interests that aren't yet provable.

Circulate (or use breakout support in a virtual room) during steps 1–2 especially — this is where students either freeze (nothing to list) or overclaim (list projects they didn't really contribute to). See Common Misconceptions and Student Difficulties below for how to intervene.

### 5. Share-Out and Discussion (7 min)

Ask 2–3 volunteers to read their direction statement aloud. After each, ask the group: *"What evidence from their project list backs that up?"* This keeps peer feedback focused on evidence, not enthusiasm.

**Discussion questions:**
- Was there a project on your list you almost left off because it felt "too small" to count? Why did you decide to include or exclude it?
- Did your direction statement match what you expected before you did the inventory, or did the evidence point somewhere different?
- What's one thing on your "still want to learn" list that you're excited about but not ready to claim yet?
- How would you feel if someone asked you to prove your direction statement right now, using only what's already built? What would you show them?

### 6. Lesson Close (3 min)

Recap: *"You now have a direction — not a permanent label, a current focus. Next lesson, we start building the actual portfolio around it. Keep your Worksheet — you'll use your direction statement directly in the next lesson."*

Remind students: a direction can change later as they build more projects. This lesson is about starting from honest evidence, not locking in a life choice.

---

## Common Misconceptions

- **"I have to pick just one thing forever."** Correct this directly: a direction is a *current focus for this portfolio*, not a permanent identity. Students can and will revise it as they build more. Point to the "what I still want to learn" section as proof the door stays open.
- **"I need to be the best at something to claim it as a strength."** Reframe: a strength is relative to *their own* other work and effort, not a competition against other students or professionals. "Noticeably better than your other attempts" is the bar, not "best in class."
- **"If I only have school/Lumexa projects and nothing personal, I don't have a real direction."** Lumexa mission work counts fully as evidence. Reassure students that assigned project work is legitimate proof of skill — professionals build portfolios from work-for-hire and coursework too.
- **"My direction has to be a job title."** Directions like "front-end web dev" are fine, but so are more specific or blended ones ("data visualization," "game UI design," "creative coding"). Don't force students into a narrow set of labels.

---

## Student Difficulties and Troubleshooting

- **Empty or thin project list (thin Lesson 1 audit):** Prompt with specific questions — "Have you ever fixed a bug for a friend? Made anything in Canva, even for fun? Started something you didn't finish?" Unfinished or informal work can still go in the inventory with an honest confidence level; it just can't be the sole basis for a direction.
- **Overclaiming group contributions:** If a student lists a group project as if they built the whole thing, ask "What part did you personally do?" and have them note that specific part in the "what it demonstrates" column, not the whole project.
- **Underclaiming out of modesty:** Some students, especially after Lesson 1's identity audit, become overly cautious and won't claim anything as a strength. Point them back to repeated patterns across 2+ projects as the objective test, not a feeling of confidence.
- **Direction statement too vague ("I like coding"):** Push for the pattern behind it — ask "What part of coding, specifically, keeps showing up in your projects?" and have them revise using the template's sentence structure.
- **Direction statement too broad/fabricated ("I'm a full-stack AI game developer"):** Ask them to point to the specific finished projects backing each part of that claim. If they can't, walk it back together to what the evidence actually supports.

---

## How to Review Student Work

When checking a student's completed Worksheet, confirm:

1. **Inventory table has real entries** pulled from their actual Lesson 1 audit, not invented projects.
2. **Confidence levels are honest** — not everything marked "high confidence."
3. **Strengths cluster is evidence-based** — at least one cluster should reference 2+ projects, not a single one-off.
4. **Direction statement is specific and backed by the inventory** — you should be able to point at 2–3 rows in their table that justify it.
5. **"Still want to learn" section is present and distinct from the direction statement** — shows they understand the interest/strength/proven-skill distinction rather than collapsing everything into one claim.

If a direction statement is unsupported or fabricated-sounding, don't reject it publicly — follow up privately or in the next 1:1 check-in and walk them back through the evidence together.

# Lesson 3: Build Your Portfolio Website

## What You'll Learn
How to structure and build a real, working portfolio website using HTML and CSS — the same
site that will hold your bio, brand, and project case studies by the end of this course.

## Why It Matters
A portfolio site is proof you can point to. A résumé says "I can build websites." A live
site someone can click through is the difference between a claim and evidence.

## The 5 Sections Every Portfolio Needs
1. **Intro / Hero** — your name + one-line tagline about your direction
2. **About** — a short paragraph (your real bio comes in Lesson 4)
3. **Skills** — a simple list or grid of things you can do
4. **Projects** — cards for your case studies (real content comes in Lessons 4 & 6)
5. **Contact** — a safe way to reach you (school email or a contact form — never your home address or phone number)

## Step-by-Step
1. Open the `starter/` project folder in your code editor.
2. Open `index.html` — find the 5 section comments (`<!-- HERO -->`, `<!-- ABOUT -->`, etc.).
3. Replace the placeholder name and tagline in the Hero section with your own.
4. Fill in a short temporary About paragraph (you'll rewrite this properly in Lesson 4).
5. Add 2–3 skills to the Skills grid based on your Lesson 2 worksheet.
6. Leave Projects as placeholder cards for now — real case studies come in Lessons 4 & 6.
7. Preview your page in the browser and check it at different window widths.

## Key Terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Semantic HTML | Using tags that describe meaning (`<header>`, `<section>`) instead of only generic `<div>`s |
| Responsive | A layout that adapts to different screen sizes |
| Local server | A way to preview your site on your own computer before it's live on the internet |
| Skeleton | The basic structure of a page before real content and styling are finished |

## Knowledge Check
1. Name the 5 sections every portfolio site in this course needs.
2. What's the difference between a `<div>` and a `<section>`?
3. Why shouldn't you put your home address in the Contact section?
4. Why do we build the structure before writing the real bio and case studies?
5. What does "responsive" mean?

## Reflection
1. What's one thing about your direction (from Lesson 2) you want your Hero section to communicate immediately?
2. What part of building this felt hardest today?
3. What do you still want your site to include by the end of the course?

## Submission
Save your working `starter/` folder. Next class, bring it back open and ready — you'll be
writing your real bio and first case study directly into it.

# Instructor Guide — Course 16, Lesson 3: Build Your Portfolio Website

## Lesson Metadata
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Course | 16 — Build Your Professional Identity |
| Lesson | 3 of 8 — Build Your Portfolio Website |
| Age | 15–18 |
| Duration | 75–90 min |

| Portfolio connection | This IS the portfolio website deliverable's skeleton — bio, brand, and case studies (L4–L6) get dropped into it |

## Lesson Overview
Students go from "I have a direction" to "I have a real, running website with my name on it."
This lesson uses the provided `Portfolio_Website` starter project (in `Projects/Portfolio_Website/starter/`)
so no student starts from a blank file — they customize a working structure rather than fighting boilerplate.

## Instructor Prep
- Open `Projects/Portfolio_Website/completed/index.html` in a browser beforehand as the reference example to show.
- Have the `starter/` folder ready to distribute (zip, shared drive, or GitHub Classroom — instructor's choice).
- Confirm VS Code (or comparable editor) + Live Server extension (or `python3 -m http.server`) works on your teaching machine for a live-reload demo.

## Required Files
- `Projects/Portfolio_Website/starter/` (given to students)
- `Projects/Portfolio_Website/completed/` (instructor reference only — do not distribute, since it spoils the exercise)

## Teaching Sequence
| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 0–10 min | Show the completed reference site; walk through its 5 sections (Intro, About, Skills, Projects, Contact) |
| 10–20 min | Distribute starter project; tour the file structure (`index.html`, `style.css`, `assets/`) |
| 20–45 min | Guided coding: edit the Intro/Hero section together — name, tagline, direction from Lesson 2 |
| 45–65 min | Guided coding: About + Skills sections; introduce CSS Grid/Flexbox basics used in the starter |
| 65–80 min | Independent work: students personalize colors/spacing (full branding comes in L5) and add placeholder project cards |
| 80–90 min | Live-reload check on each student's site; wrap-up |

## Instructor Talking Points
- "A portfolio site is not a resume — it's a workspace where people can see and click through real things you built."
- "Five sections is enough: Intro, About, Skills, Projects, Contact. Don't over-build before you have content — content comes in Lessons 4–6."
- Explain semantic HTML briefly: `<header>`, `<main>`, `<section>`, `<footer>` vs. a page made entirely of `<div>`s, and why it matters (accessibility, SEO, maintainability).

## Common Misconceptions
- "I need to build this from scratch to make it mine." → Customizing a solid structure is what real developers do; originality comes from content and design choices, not from avoiding starter code.
- "It has to look perfect today." → This is a working skeleton; brand polish happens in Lesson 5, real case studies in Lesson 4/6, and deployment in Lesson 7.

## Likely Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting
| Issue | Fix |
|---|---|
| CSS changes not showing | Hard-refresh (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+R); confirm the `<link>` tag path to `style.css` is correct |
| Layout breaks on resize | Check for a missing `<meta name="viewport">` tag (already in starter — verify it wasn't deleted) |
| Local server won't start | Use VS Code Live Server extension as the simplest fallback; `python3 -m http.server 8000` as a backup |
| Nothing shows at all | Check the browser console (F12) for a typo'd tag or unclosed bracket |

## How to Review Student Work
Check: all 5 sections present, page doesn't visually break at 375px width (phone) and 1440px (laptop), no console errors, student's real name/direction (not the starter's placeholder text) is in place.

## Lesson Close
Preview Lesson 4: "Next class we write your real bio and your first project case study — the words that go inside the structure you just built."

lessons.title: Tell Your Story Professionally
lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Lesson 4: Tell Your Story Professionally

## What You're Doing Today

You've got a portfolio site started (Lesson 3) and a direction for what kind of projects to build (Lesson 2). Today you write the words that go on that site: a short bio that introduces you, and your first project case study — a short write-up that proves you can actually do the thing, not just that you're interested in it.

## Why This Matters

Anyone can write "I love coding and I'm a fast learner." That sentence tells a reader nothing, because it could be true of literally anyone and can't be checked. What actually convinces someone you can build things is specific, honest description of what you've built. This lesson teaches you a formula for both your bio and your case study so you never have to guess what to write — you fill in real facts about real work.

The voice you're aiming for isn't stiff or corporate ("the candidate possesses strong technical acumen") and it isn't hollow cheerleading ("I am SO passionate about tech!!"). It's just clear and true: what you build, in plain language.

## The Bio Formula

A strong short bio has four parts:

1. **Who you are** — your name, and one honest identifier (student, age/grade optional, what you're focused on).
2. **What you build** — the actual kind of things you make, named specifically (not "cool stuff," but "web pages," "small games," "apps that use APIs").
3. **What you're working toward** — a real current goal or skill you're building next.
4. **One proof point** — something a reader can check: a link to your portfolio, a specific project name, a specific tool you've used.

You don't need all four in every version — see the three length variants in your worksheet — but a full bio should hit all four.

## The Case Study Formula

For each project, use this five-part structure:

| Section | What goes here |
|---|---|
| **Project** | Name of the project and one line on what it is. |
| **Problem** | What need, question, or goal started the project. |
| **My Approach** | What you actually did — tools used, decisions made, steps taken. |
| **Result** | What actually happened. Working or partly working — say which. |
| **What I Learned** | One real thing you now know that you didn't before. |

A case study is not a diary entry and not a sales pitch. It's a short, structured, honest account.

## Worked Example (Fictional Student: Jordan R.)

**Bio (paragraph version):**
> I'm Jordan, a high school student who builds small web tools — mostly HTML/CSS sites and simple JavaScript apps. My latest project is a habit tracker that saves data in the browser so it remembers your streaks. Right now I'm learning how to connect my sites to real APIs. You can see my work at jordanbuilds.dev.

**Case Study:**

| Section | Jordan's Answer |
|---|---|
| Project | Habit Tracker — a browser-based app that lets a user log daily habits and see a streak count. |
| Problem | I wanted a simple way to track a daily habit (drinking water) but didn't want to use someone else's app — I wanted to understand how the logic worked. |
| My Approach | Built the interface in HTML/CSS, used JavaScript to store entries in the browser's localStorage so data persists after refresh, and added a streak counter that checks consecutive days. |
| Result | It works and saves data correctly between sessions. It doesn't yet work across devices — it's tied to one browser, which I know is a limitation. |
| What I Learned | I learned how localStorage works and why apps that need to sync across devices need a real backend/database, which I don't have yet. That's my next thing to learn. |

Notice: nothing here is exaggerated, nothing is invented, and the limitation ("doesn't work across devices") makes it more credible, not less.

## Step-by-Step Activity

1. Open your Worksheet (bio + case study templates).
2. Write your 1-sentence bio first. Then expand it into the 2–3 sentence version, then the paragraph version.
3. Pick ONE real, completed Lumexa or personal project.
4. Fill in the case study template for that project, section by section — don't skip any.
5. Read both pieces aloud to yourself. Cross out any word that could apply to literally any student ("passionate," "hardworking," "amazing") unless a specific fact follows it.
6. Save your drafts — you'll wire them into your actual portfolio page in Lesson 6, and you'll reuse this exact case-study template for your next project.

## Key Terms

- **Bio** — a short written introduction of yourself, used on a portfolio, resume, or profile.
- **Case study** — a structured write-up of one project, describing the problem, process, and outcome.
- **Proof point** — a specific, checkable fact (a link, a named project, a named tool) that backs up a claim.
- **Jargon/buzzword** — a vague, often-overused word ("synergy," "passionate," "detail-oriented") that sounds impressive but carries no specific information.
- **Voice** — the tone and style of your writing; this lesson's target voice is clear, honest, and plain.

## Knowledge Checks

1. What are the four parts of the bio formula?
2. What are the five sections of the case study template, in order?
3. Why is "I'm passionate about coding" considered weak writing in this lesson, even though it might be true?
4. If a project didn't fully work, should you leave it out of your case study? Why or why not?
5. Give one example of a buzzword and rewrite it as a specific, factual sentence.

## Reflection Prompts

1. Which was harder to write honestly — your bio or your case study — and why?
2. Read your first draft bio back. What's one sentence you removed or changed because it sounded generic, and what did you replace it with?
3. What's one real thing your case study project taught you that you didn't expect to learn when you started it?

## Submission Instructions

Save your completed Worksheet (bio, all three length versions, and one full case study) to your course folder in Google Docs, named `LastName_Lesson4_Bio_CaseStudy`. Share it with your instructor for feedback before Lesson 6, where you'll refine this case study and add a second one.

## Part 1: Professional Bio Draft

Reminder — the four parts of a bio: **who you are / what you build / what you're working toward / one proof point.**

**Example (Jordan R.):**
> I'm Jordan, a high school student who builds small web tools — mostly HTML/CSS sites and simple JavaScript apps. My latest project is a habit tracker that saves data in the browser so it remembers your streaks. Right now I'm learning how to connect my sites to real APIs.

> _______________________________________________________________

---

### Version C — Full Paragraph

> I'm _______ [name], a _______ [student/grade, optional] who builds _______ [type of thing you build — be specific about tools/languages]. My latest project is _______ [project name + what it does + one honest detail about how it works or what's still incomplete]. Right now I'm working on/learning _______ [current goal or skill], because _______ [real reason]. You can see my work at _______ [portfolio link or "link coming soon"].

**Example (Jordan R.):**
> I'm Jordan, a high school student who builds small web tools — mostly HTML/CSS sites and simple JavaScript apps. My latest project is a habit tracker that saves data in the browser so it remembers your streaks. Right now I'm learning how to connect my sites to real APIs, because I want my next project to pull in real, live information instead of just storing what a user types. You can see my work at jordanbuilds.dev.

**Your version:**
> _______________________________________________________________
> _______________________________________________________________
> _______________________________________________________________
> _______________________________________________________________

**Buzzword check:** Circle any word in your draft that could describe literally any student ("passionate," "hardworking," "team player," "creative," "amazing"). For each one, either delete it or replace it with a specific fact.

---

## Part 2: Project Case Study Template

Pick ONE real, completed project (Lumexa or personal). Fill in every row honestly — a modest or partial result is a completely valid answer.

| Section | Prompt | Your Answer |
|---|---|---|
| **Project Name** | What is it called? One line on what it is. | |
| **Problem / Goal** | What need, question, or goal started this project? | |
| **Tools Used** | What languages, platforms, or tools did you actually use? | |
| **My Approach** | What did you actually do, in order? What decisions did you make? | |
| **Result** | What actually happened? Does it fully work, partly work, or not yet — be specific. | |
| **What I Learned** | What's one real thing you know now that you didn't before this project? | |
| **Link / Screenshot** | *(Placeholder note: paste your live link here, or attach a screenshot image if the project isn't hosted online yet. Do not leave this section blank — write "screenshot attached below" or "link: [url]" or "not yet hosted — see code file attached.")* | |

---

## Filled Example — Jordan R.

| Section | Jordan's Answer |
|---|---|
| **Project Name** | Habit Tracker — a browser-based app for logging a daily habit and seeing a streak count. |
| **Problem / Goal** | I wanted a simple way to track drinking water daily, but wanted to build my own instead of using an existing app, so I could understand the logic myself. |
| **Tools Used** | HTML, CSS, JavaScript (localStorage). |
| **My Approach** | Built the layout in HTML/CSS first. Used JavaScript to save each day's entry in the browser's localStorage so the data survives a page refresh. Added a function that checks for consecutive days logged and displays a streak count. |
| **Result** | It works — data saves correctly and the streak count updates properly. It only works on one browser/device right now; it doesn't sync across devices, which I know is a limitation. |
| **What I Learned** | I learned how localStorage works and why it's fine for a single-device app but not enough for something that needs to sync — that would need a real backend and database, which I want to learn next. |
| **Link / Screenshot** | Link: jordanbuilds.dev/habit-tracker |

---

**Before you submit:** read both your bio and your case study out loud. Cross out any sentence that sounds like it was copied from a generic template. Replace it with something only you could honestly say about your own work.
lessons.teacherNotes:
# Instructor Guide — Lesson 4: Tell Your Story Professionally

## Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path > Course 16: Build Your Professional Identity > Lesson 4 |
| Audience | Teens, ages 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led, virtual classroom |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Tools | Google Docs, portfolio site (HTML/CSS from Lesson 3), Canva (optional, for screenshots) |
| Prerequisite | Lesson 2 (direction/niche defined), Lesson 3 (portfolio site skeleton exists) |
| Feeds into | Lesson 6, which reuses the case-study template for a second, more polished project write-up |

## Overview

Students learn to write two pieces of text that will live on their portfolio: a short professional bio/introduction, and their first project case study. Both must be honest — no invented job titles, no exaggerated impact claims, no borrowed accomplishments. The lesson's core tension to manage: teenagers default to one of two bad extremes when asked to "sound professional" — stiff corporate jargon copied from LinkedIn, or vague enthusiasm ("I love coding!!") that says nothing. The goal is a third voice: clear, specific, true, and confident without being showy.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Write a bio using the four-part formula (who you are / what you build / what you're working toward / one proof point).
2. Draft a project case study using the Problem → Approach → Result → Learned structure.
3. Identify and remove jargon, filler, and unverifiable claims from their own writing.
4. Explain why honest, specific writing is more credible than generic praise of themselves.

## Prep Checklist (before class)

- [ ] Confirm every student has their Lesson 3 portfolio site accessible (local file or Vercel URL).
- [ ] Confirm every student has at least one completed Lumexa project to write about (check roster against project-completion tracker).
- [ ] Open a shared Google Doc or slide with the "bad bio → good bio" demo rewrite (below) ready to screen-share.
- [ ] Have the Worksheet.md templates ready to share/link (Google Doc copy or PDF export).
- [ ] Prepare 2–3 real (anonymized or self-authored) example case studies as backup demo material if a volunteer doesn't want to share on the spot.

## Teaching Sequence

| Time | Segment | Instructor Action |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:05 | Hook | Ask: "If a stranger read only your bio, would they know what you actually build?" Poll the room informally. Frame today's goal: write text that proves skill, not text that performs enthusiasm. |
| 0:05–0:15 | Direct teach: the bio formula | Present the four-part formula. Show the demo rewrite (bad → good). Annotate live what changed and why. |
| 0:15–0:20 | Talking points: voice | Cover "professional ≠ stiff" and "no buzzwords needed" (see Talking Points below). |
| 0:20–0:30 | Guided practice: bio draft | Students draft their 2–3 sentence bio in the worksheet. Instructor circulates (breakout rooms or chat monitoring), gives 1-line feedback per student. |
| 0:30–0:40 | Direct teach: case study formula | Present Project / Problem / My Approach / Result / What I Learned. Walk through the worked example. Emphasize: result can be modest and still be a good case study — "it didn't fully work but I learned X" is an honest, strong result. |
| 0:40–0:50 | Guided practice: case study draft | Students pick one real Lumexa/personal project and fill the template. Instructor spot-checks for fabricated claims or vague filler. |
| 0:50–0:57 | Peer share + discussion | 2–3 volunteers read their bio or case study aloud. Class gives one specific piece of feedback each ("that's clear" / "that sentence could be more specific"). Run 1–2 discussion questions. |
| 0:57–1:00 | Lesson close | Recap formulas, assign remaining draft as homework, preview Lesson 6 (this same template gets reused and refined). |

## Talking Points: Professional-but-Authentic Voice

**"Professional does not mean stiff or formal."**
Professional writing is clear, specific, and respectful of the reader's time. It is not passive voice, not third person ("Jordan is a highly motivated individual..."), and not a thesaurus exercise. A 16-year-old writing plainly about a real project they built sounds more professional than a 16-year-old copying corporate phrasing they don't fully understand.

**"You don't need buzzwords to sound credible — you need specifics."**
Words like "passionate," "synergy," "detail-oriented," "team player," and "results-driven" are filler because they are unverifiable and generic — anyone can claim them. Replace every buzzword with a fact: not "I'm passionate about coding" but "I've built three web pages and I'm currently learning JavaScript to make them interactive."

**"Confidence comes from precision, not adjectives."**
Compare "I'm a hardworking and creative developer" (adjectives, no proof) to "I built a weather app that pulls live data from an API and redesigned it twice after user feedback" (proof, no adjectives needed). The second sentence does the bragging for you.

**"Honest and small beats impressive and false."**
If a project only partly worked, say so. "The site's mobile layout still needs work" is a mark of self-awareness, not a weakness — real developers describe limitations of their own work constantly.

## Demo Rewrite (Screen-Share This)

**Bad, generic bio:**
> Hi! My name is Jordan and I am a passionate, hardworking, and detail-oriented individual who loves coding and technology! I am a team player who is always eager to learn new things and take on exciting new challenges. I hope to one day work at a big tech company and change the world with my innovative ideas!

*What's wrong with it:* every sentence could be copy-pasted onto any student's page with zero changes. No project is named. No skill is named. "Change the world" and "innovative ideas" are unearned claims for someone who hasn't shown any work yet.

**Strong, honest bio (same fictional student):**
> I'm Jordan, a high school student who builds small web tools — mostly HTML/CSS sites and simple JavaScript apps. My latest project is a habit tracker that saves data in the browser so it remembers your streaks. Right now I'm learning how to connect my sites to real APIs. You can see my work at [portfolio link].

*What changed:* names an actual project, names actual tools, names a specific current goal, and ends with a verifiable proof point (a link). No adjectives about the student's personality at all — the work speaks.

Use this pair as the anchor for the whole lesson; refer back to it during the guided practice segments ("is your sentence more like version 1 or version 2?").

## Discussion Questions

1. Why might a stranger trust the second bio more than the first, even though the first one uses "bigger" words?
2. Is it okay for a case study to describe a project that didn't fully succeed? Why might that actually be a stronger thing to show?
3. Where's the line between "confident" and "exaggerated" when describing your own work?

## Common Misconceptions

- **"Professional means formal and stiff, like a business letter."** Correct framing: professional means clear, specific, and respectful — plain language is often more professional than stiff language.
- **"I need impressive buzzwords to sound qualified."** Correct framing: specific facts about real work are more convincing than any adjective. If a sentence works with the buzzword removed, remove it.
- **"My case study needs to show a perfect result or it's not worth including."** Correct framing: an honest account of a partial result plus a real lesson learned is a legitimate, strong case study.
- **"Writing about myself is bragging, so I should stay vague to be humble."** Correct framing: vagueness isn't humility, it's just unclear. Specific facts aren't bragging — they're information a reader needs.

## Anticipated Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | What it looks like | Instructor response |
|---|---|---|
| Defaults to buzzword bio | "I'm a passionate, dedicated learner..." | Ask: "What's one thing you actually built? Start the sentence with that instead." |
| Can't pick a project to write about | "I don't have anything good enough" | Remind them any completed Lumexa project qualifies — the lesson is about honest description, not about having an impressive project. |
| Inflates the result | "My app works perfectly and everyone loved it" (unverifiable) | Ask: "What can you actually point to — a screenshot, a working link, specific feedback someone gave you?" If they can't point to it, soften the claim. |
| Case study reads like a diary, not a case study | Long narrative with no clear sections | Redirect to the template headers explicitly — have them literally copy the five labels into their doc first, then write under each one. |
| Bio too long / rambling | Paragraph turns into a full life story | Enforce the length variants from the worksheet — start with the 1-sentence version, then expand. |
| Fear of sounding boastful | Refuses to state real skills plainly | Reframe: stating a fact ("I built X") is not the same as boasting ("I'm the best at X"). Facts are safe to state. |

## How to Review Student Work

When checking a bio or case study (live, in chat, or async):
1. **Check for at least one concrete project or tool named.** If none appears, it's still in "generic" territory — send it back.
2. **Check for at least one unverifiable claim** (numbers, superlatives, feelings presented as fact) and flag it: "How do you know / can you show this?"
3. **Check the case study has all five sections present**, even briefly. A one-line "Result" is fine; a missing "Result" is not.
4. **Check tone**, not just content — read it aloud. If it sounds like it was copied from a job-posting template, ask the student to say the same idea "like you're explaining it to a friend," then tighten that into writing.
5. **Praise specificity explicitly** when you see it — this reinforces the behavior more than correcting vagueness does.

## Lesson Close

Recap: "Your bio and case study are proof, not performance. A stranger should finish reading them knowing exactly what you can do — not just that you feel enthusiastic about doing it." Assign: finish both drafts as homework using the Worksheet, save them into the portfolio site's content (ready to wire into the actual page in Lesson 6). Preview: "Next time we build on this exact case-study template for your second project, and start polishing the whole portfolio site around it."

# Lesson 5: Create Your Personal Brand

## What You're Doing Today

You already have direction (Lesson 2), a portfolio site skeleton (Lesson 3), and a bio + first case study (Lesson 4). Today you're building a **Brand Kit** — a small, simple set of visual and voice choices that make your portfolio instantly recognizable as *yours*. By the end of class, you'll have colors, fonts, a simple mark, and a tone of voice, all in one Canva board.

## Why It Matters

Recruiters, teachers, and future collaborators look at a lot of portfolios. The ones that stick in someone's memory usually aren't the ones with the most content — they're the ones that feel **consistent**. Same colors, same fonts, same voice, every time they show up. That consistency is a brand, and it's something you can build in one class period without any professional design training.

**Important reframe:** A brand is NOT a logo. A brand is a *system of repeated choices*. A logo (or in your case, a simple mark) is just one small piece of it.

## The Four Brand Elements

### 1. Color Palette (2–3 colors)
Pick:
- **One dominant color** — used the most (backgrounds, headers).
- **One accent color** — used for buttons, links, highlights.
- **(Optional) one neutral** — usually white, black, or gray, for backgrounds/text.

Keep it to 2–3 total. More than that starts to look cluttered and unplanned.

### 2. Font Pairing (2 fonts, max)
- **One heading font** — bolder, more distinctive, used for titles/names.
- **One body font** — clean and easy to read in longer paragraphs.

Pick two fonts that look *different enough* to create contrast (e.g., a bold geometric heading font with a simple readable body font), but not so different they clash in mood.

### 3. A Simple Mark
This is not a professional logo. It's one small, repeatable visual — pick ONE:
- Your initials inside a simple shape (circle, square, hexagon).
- Your name, always typed in your heading font, in your dominant color.
- One simple icon connected to your interest area (e.g., a small compass for someone into exploration/travel tech).

One shape. One or two colors. Done in under 10 minutes.

### 4. Tone of Voice (3 adjectives)
Three words that describe how you sound when you write — in your bio, your case studies, everywhere. Examples: "curious, precise, encouraging" or "bold, direct, playful." Check: does your Lesson 4 bio actually sound like these words? If not, that's useful to notice.

## A Quick Note on Color Contrast (Accessibility)

Not everyone sees color the same way, and some people have low vision. A basic rule that professional designers follow (called WCAG — Web Content Accessibility Guidelines):

> **Text needs to stand out clearly from its background.** Dark text on a light background, or light text on a dark background, usually works. Two "medium brightness" colors together (like a medium orange on white, or light gray on white) are often too hard to read.

You don't need to memorize numbers today — just remember: **if you have to squint to read your own sample text, so will everyone else.** Save your brightest/lightest accent color for small things like buttons or borders, not paragraphs of text.

## Worked Example: Jordan R.'s Brand Kit

Jordan is interested in game design and wants their portfolio to feel focused and calm but still energetic.

- **Colors:** Deep navy `#1B3A4B` (dominant — header, nav bar, footer), warm amber `#F2A93B` (accent — buttons, links, highlights), off-white `#F5F5F0` (background/neutral).
- **Fonts:** Heading — a bold, geometric sans-serif (e.g., Poppins Bold). Body — a clean, readable sans-serif (e.g., Inter Regular).
- **Mark:** A navy circle with "JR" centered in white, in the heading font.
- **Tone of voice:** "curious, precise, encouraging."

Notice: navy text on the off-white background is easy to read. Amber is only ever used for small elements (buttons, small accents) — never for paragraph text — because it's harder to read at small sizes on a light background.

## Step-by-Step Canva Activity

1. Open Canva and start a blank design (any size — 1080×1080 works well).
2. Add three rectangles side by side. Use the color picker's hex code field to enter your 2–3 chosen colors. Label each one with its hex code and where you'll use it.
3. Add a text box with your heading font — type your name or a sample title.
4. Add a second text box with your body font — type one sample sentence.
5. Build your mark: add a circle or shape in your dominant color, then add your initials or icon on top in your accent/neutral color. Keep it centered and simple.
6. Add one line of text with your three tone-of-voice adjectives.
7. Step back and look at the whole board — every piece should feel like it belongs together.
8. Rename your Canva design "[Your Name] — Brand Kit" and set sharing so your instructor can view it.

## Key Terms

- **Brand:** A consistent, recognizable system of visual and verbal choices that represents you.
- **Color palette:** The specific set of colors (with hex codes) you use everywhere.
- **Hex code:** A six-character code (like `#1B3A4B`) that names an exact color so it looks the same everywhere it's used.
- **Font pairing:** Two fonts — one for headings, one for body text — chosen to work well together.
- **Mark:** A simple, repeatable visual symbol (like initials in a shape) — a lightweight stand-in for a logo.
- **Tone of voice:** The specific personality your writing has, described in a few adjectives.
- **Contrast (accessibility):** How clearly text stands out from its background so it's readable for everyone, including people with low vision.

## Knowledge Checks

1. True or False: A brand is the same thing as a logo.
2. Why is it usually better to limit your palette to 2–3 colors instead of 5 or 6?
3. What's the difference between a "heading font" and a "body font," and why do you need both to look somewhat different from each other?
4. Give one reason a bright, light accent color might be a poor choice for paragraph text.
5. What are the three adjectives in your own tone-of-voice descriptor, and how do they connect to your Lesson 2 niche or Lesson 4 bio?

## Reflection Prompts

1. Which of your three brand colors was hardest to choose, and why?
2. Look back at your Lesson 4 bio. Does its wording actually match your tone-of-voice adjectives? What's one sentence you might rewrite later so it matches better?
3. If a stranger saw only your color palette and mark (no words at all), what might they guess about you? Is that the impression you want?

## Submission Instructions

1. In Canva, set your Brand Kit design to shareable (view access) and copy the link.
2. Complete the Worksheet for this lesson (color table, font pairing with reasoning, tone-of-voice line, mark description, and consistency checklist).
3. Submit both the Canva link and the completed Worksheet through your class's submission method by the end of the session.
