# Instructor Guide — Lesson 1: How the Freelance Economy Works

## Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path → Course 17: Skills That Pay |
| Lesson | Lesson 1: How the Freelance Economy Works |
| Age range | 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led class |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Difficulty | Introductory |
| Prerequisites | None from Course 17. Recommended: at least one prior Digital Independence Path course involving personal projects (e.g., a portfolio-building or digital-citizenship course), so students have something to draw on in examples. |
| Tools used | Google Docs, Canva, Notion, Email, Spreadsheets |
| Objectives | 1) Define "freelance economy" and explain how it differs from traditional employment. 2) Trace the value-exchange chain: skill → service → payment. 3) Identify the parts of a freelance transaction (client, scope, deliverable, payment). 4) Describe, at a factual and non-promotional level, how major platforms (Fiverr, Upwork, Etsy, Gumroad) and direct referrals differ, including their age/account rules. |
| Deliverables | Completed in-class pricing activity (Google Docs or Notion); completed Worksheet: Freelance Economy Landscape. |
| Skills built | Economic literacy, service-based thinking, scope definition, basic pricing logic, platform literacy, informed caution around online work. |
| Portfolio connection | The fictional freelancer case study and the student's own labeled example become the seed of a "service description" they will refine into a real portfolio piece in later Course 17 lessons (e.g., a Canva-designed service one-pager). |

---

## Overview

This lesson is the front door to Course 17. Before students touch any platform, they need a mental model: **a skill becomes a service when someone else is willing to pay for the result, not just the skill itself.** The lesson builds that model through a concrete value-exchange chain (skill → service → payment), contrasts freelance/service work with employment, and gives an honest, factual tour of where this kind of work actually happens today — including the real age and account rules of well-known platforms.

This is explicitly **not** a sign-up lesson. No student creates an account, lists a gig, or is told to bypass a platform's age policy. The goal is literacy and judgment, not premature action. Several platforms require a parent/guardian-owned or co-managed account for minors; this lesson teaches that as a fact of the landscape, not an obstacle to route around.

---

## Instructor Prep (before class)

- Read the Student Lesson and Worksheet so you know exactly what students will see.
- Confirm the platform rules table in the Worksheet is still accurate by checking each platform's current terms of service or help center page (rules change; do not rely on memory or on this guide alone). Update the "verified as of" date when you check.
- Have blank Google Docs, a Notion page, and a spreadsheet template ready to share/demo — students should see the actual tools, not just hear about them.
- Prepare to project (or share) a simple spreadsheet with columns: Task, Time Estimate, Rate, Total — this is used in the live demo.
- Decide in advance how you will handle a student who says they already have a marketplace account or has already tried freelancing — validate the experience without turning it into a recruitment moment for other students.

---

## Teaching Sequence (60 minutes)

### 1. Hook and framing (5 min)
Ask: "Has anyone here ever been paid for something they made or did — outside of an allowance or a regular job?" Collect 2–3 quick examples (tutoring a neighbor, selling art online, building a website for a family friend, editing videos for a local team). Point out: these are all small examples of the same economic idea we're studying today.

### 2. What is the freelance economy? (10 min)
Direct instruction using talking points below. Define freelance economy as a system where people offer specific services to clients on a per-project or per-task basis, rather than being hired long-term by one employer.

### 3. The value-exchange chain: skill → service → payment (10 min)
Walk through the three-step chain on the board or shared doc:
- **Skill**: something a person can do (e.g., graphic design, writing, coding, video editing, tutoring).
- **Service**: that skill packaged as something a specific client can buy — a defined, deliverable outcome (e.g., "a 5-slide pitch deck," not just "I know Canva").
- **Payment**: money exchanged for the completed service, agreed on before the work starts.
Emphasize: the jump from skill to service is where most beginners get stuck — they know they can do something but haven't defined what they're selling.

### 4. Employment vs. freelance/service work (8 min)
Use the comparison talking points below. Keep this factual and balanced — neither model is framed as superior.

### 5. Live demo: pricing and delivering a small job (12 min)
Walk through the fictional freelancer case study (script below) using a shared spreadsheet and Google Doc live. Narrate every decision out loud.

### 6. Landscape overview: platforms and models (10 min)
Introduce the five models students will explore on the Worksheet: Fiverr, Upwork, Etsy, Gumroad, and direct referrals. State each platform's general age/account rule factually, and explicitly flag that these rules can change and must be checked at the source before anyone relies on them. Do not demonstrate account creation. Do not encourage sign-up.

### 7. In-class activity + wrap-up (5 min)
Students begin the value-exchange labeling activity from the Student Lesson (finish for homework if needed). Preview that Lesson 2 will go deeper into defining a service and setting scope.

---

## Talking Points

**On what "freelance economy" means:**
"The freelance economy isn't a single company or website — it's a pattern of work happening across the whole economy, where people sell specific skills as services instead of trading their time to one employer for a steady paycheck. A photographer shooting one wedding, a coder building one small app feature, a tutor helping one student prepare for one exam — all freelance."

**On skill vs. service:**
"Having a skill means you *can* do something. Having a service means you've decided *what exactly* you're offering, *to whom*, and *for what result*. 'I'm good at drawing' is a skill. 'I'll design a custom logo, three concepts, one round of revisions, delivered as a PNG and vector file' is a service."

**On employment vs. freelance (comparison points to cover):**
- Employment: one employer, ongoing relationship, regular schedule/paycheck, employer usually provides tools/training, taxes often withheld automatically, legal protections like minimum wage often apply directly.
- Freelance/service work: multiple possible clients, work is project-based and can start and stop, payment is per-project or per-task and agreed in advance, the freelancer usually supplies their own tools, and — importantly for minors — almost all real marketplace platforms require an adult (parent/guardian) to own or co-manage the account, and some require the freelancer to be an adult entirely.
- Say plainly: "Freelance work is not 'easier' or 'a way around getting a job.' It has its own rules, its own risks, and for anyone under 18, it almost always involves a trusted adult in the account and the money."

**On honesty about the landscape:**
"We're going to look at real platforms people use for this kind of work. Some of them work with the involvement of a parent or guardian if you're a teenager; one is 18-and-up only. We are not signing up for anything today, and I am not telling you to get around any age rule anywhere, ever. Age rules on these platforms exist for real legal and safety reasons, and they change over time — always check the platform directly before assuming a rule still applies."

---

## Live Demo Script: Pricing and Delivering a Small Job

Use this narrated walkthrough with a shared spreadsheet and Google Doc. Introduce the fictional freelancer by name so students can reference her later.

**Character:** Mara, a fictional 17-year-old who designs simple logo concepts.

**The request (read aloud, as if it were an email):**
> "Hi Mara, I run a small dog-walking business in my neighborhood and need a simple logo — just a paw print and my business name, 'Riverside Walks,' in a clean font. Can you help? — Denise"

**Step 1 — Clarify scope (in the Google Doc, write it live):**
"Before Mara can price anything, she needs to know what 'help' means. She replies to Denise with three questions: How many design concepts do you want to see? Do you need any revisions? What file formats do you need (just an image? or a file a printer can use)?" Type Denise's fictional answers: "One or two concepts is fine, one round of changes, and I'll need a PNG for my website and a vector file for a t-shirt company."

**Step 2 — Define the service (write in the Doc):**
"Two logo concepts, one revision round, final files delivered as PNG and vector (SVG)."

**Step 3 — Estimate time and set a rate (build live in the spreadsheet):**

| Task | Time estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Two initial concepts | 2 hours | |
| Client feedback + 1 revision | 1 hour | |
| Final file prep (PNG + SVG export) | 0.5 hours | |
| **Total** | **3.5 hours** | |

"Mara decides her time is worth $12/hour for this kind of work — a number she picked by looking at what friends who do similar design work charge, not a random guess. 3.5 hours × $12 = $42. She rounds to an even **$40 flat fee** so Denise knows the total cost upfront instead of worrying about an hourly clock."

**Step 4 — Confirm terms before starting (write the confirmation email):**
> "Hi Denise, here's what I'll deliver: two logo concepts, one round of revisions, and final files as a PNG and an SVG. The total is $40, due when the final files are delivered. Does that work for you?"

Point out: *the price and scope were agreed on before any work started* — this is the single most important habit in freelance work.

**Step 5 — Deliver and get paid:**
"Mara does the work, sends the two concepts, Denise picks one and asks for a small color change, Mara revises it, and delivers the final PNG and SVG files by email along with a note asking Denise to send payment however they'd agreed (in Mara's case, her parent's account received it, since Mara is a minor and the payment method was set up with her parent)."

Close the demo by asking: "Where in this story did skill become a service? Where did service become payment?"

---

## Discussion Questions

1. In Mara's story, what would have gone wrong if she'd skipped Step 1 (clarifying scope) and just started designing?
2. Why do you think Mara set a flat fee instead of just charging by the hour with no cap?
3. What's one skill you have that could become a "service" if you defined it clearly? What would the defined service look like (not just the skill)?
4. Why might a platform require a parent or guardian to be involved in a minor's account, even if the teenager is the one doing the actual work?
5. What's the difference between "I want to make money" and "I have a specific service I could offer"?

---

## Common Misconceptions

**"Freelancing is a get-rich-quick path."**
Correct this directly: freelance income is earned the same way any income is — by delivering something of value, consistently, over time. Mara's $40 job took real hours and real back-and-forth with a client. There is no shortcut version of this that skips the work.

**"I need a marketplace account to start."**
Correct this directly: the *freelance economy* is the pattern of skill-for-payment work itself — it existed before any of these platforms and continues outside them (direct referrals, word of mouth, school or community projects). A marketplace account is one *channel* into that economy, not a requirement for understanding or eventually participating in it. Many teens' first real service work happens through people they already know, with a parent aware of the arrangement — no platform account required at all.

---

## Anticipated Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | What it looks like | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Confusing "skill" with "service" | Student says their service is "I'm good at Photoshop" | Ask: "If I were your client, what exact thing would you hand me at the end?" Push toward a deliverable. |
| Wanting to sign up for a platform right now | Student asks "Can I make a Fiverr account today?" | Affirm the enthusiasm, redirect: "That's exactly what later lessons in this course help you prepare for. Today we're building the thinking, not the account — and any account for someone your age needs a parent or guardian involved anyway." |
| Assuming freelance work is unregulated or risk-free | Student treats age rules as trivia rather than real safeguards | Explain briefly that age rules exist for legal (contract law, payment processing) and safety reasons, and that they differ by platform and country — which is exactly why the Worksheet has a "verify" column. |
| Anchoring on unrealistic prices | Student guesses a price with no reasoning ("$500 for a logo") | Walk them back to the time-estimate method from the demo: hours × a reasonable rate, not a guessed number. |
| Discomfort naming their own skill | Student says "I don't have any skills people would pay for" | Prompt with categories: writing, design, tutoring, tech help, organizing, video/photo editing, translation. Most students have at least one. |

---

## How to Review Student Work

- **In-class activity (value-exchange labeling):** Check that each student correctly identifies which part of their example is the skill, the service, and the payment — and that the "service" is a specific deliverable, not a restated skill.
- **Worksheet (Freelance Economy Landscape):** Check that the age/account rules column reflects what was taught in class (not a guess), and that the "verified as of" field is filled in with an actual date rather than left blank. The reflection questions should show the student reasoning about their *own* current situation (age, access to a parent/guardian's involvement, etc.) rather than giving a generic answer.
- Look for signs a student thinks they should sign up for a platform immediately — if so, follow up individually and reinforce the misconception correction above.

---

## Lesson Close

Summarize in one sentence: "Today we learned that a skill becomes valuable when it's turned into a clearly defined service someone else will pay for — and that there are many real ways this happens, some requiring a parent or guardian's involvement if you're under 18, and some not requiring a platform at all." Preview Lesson 2: defining a service and setting a scope of work in detail. Remind students the Worksheet is due before the next class.

lessons.title: Turn a Skill Into a Service
lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Lesson 2: Turn a Skill Into a Service

**Course 17: Skills That Pay — Digital Independence Path**

## What This Lesson Is About

In Course 16, you built a portfolio. In Lesson 1 of this course, you learned how the freelance world works — the platforms, the client types, the basics of pricing.

Now it's time to answer a harder question: **what, exactly, would you offer someone?**

"I know coding" or "I'm good at design" is true, but it's not something a client can say yes to. Today you'll turn one skill you already have proof of into a **service** — a specific, describable thing someone could actually hire you for.

## Why This Matters

Nobody hires "a person who knows HTML." They hire someone who can say: "I'll build you a 4-page website for your tutoring business by next Friday." That sentence is clear enough to trust. Vague skills don't get hired — clear services do.

This lesson is the bridge between "I can do things" and "here is a thing you can pay me to do." Everything after this — pricing, finding clients, proposals — depends on getting this part right first.

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Service** | A specific, packaged version of a skill that someone can hire you to do — it has a clear output, a clear audience, and clear limits. |
| **Niche** | A focused slice of a broader skill area — instead of "design," a niche might be "social media graphics for student clubs." |
| **Scope** | The boundaries of what's included in your service (and what isn't) — how much, how long, how many revisions. |
| **Target client** | The specific type of person or group your service is built for — not "everyone," but a named group you understand. |

## The Skill → Service Formula

```
SERVICE = SKILL + SPECIFIC OUTPUT + SPECIFIC AUDIENCE + SCOPE BOUNDARY
```

- **Skill** — something from your Course 16 portfolio you have real evidence of.
- **Specific output** — the actual thing the client receives (a website, a document, a set of graphics, a cleaned spreadsheet).
- **Specific audience** — who actually needs this and might realistically hire a teen for it (student clubs, tutors, small local groups, other students, family-adjacent contacts).
- **Scope boundary** — a limit: how many pages/items, how long it takes, or what's *not* included.

## Worked Example: Jordan R.

Jordan's Course 16 portfolio includes three proven pieces:
1. A personal website built with HTML/CSS
2. A set of presentation slide designs made in Canva for a school debate team
3. A spreadsheet Jordan built to track and chart a class fundraiser's donations

Applying the formula to each:

| Skill | Service Idea |
|---|---|
| HTML/CSS | "I build simple 3-page websites for school clubs, delivered in one week, with one round of revisions." |
| Canva slide design | "I design a matching 10-slide presentation deck for a student team's competition or pitch, turned around in 3 days." |
| Spreadsheet tracking | "I set up a spreadsheet that tracks and charts a club's fundraiser or event signups automatically, so organizers don't have to update it by hand." |

Notice: each one names an output, an audience, and a limit. None of them say "I do design" or "I'm good with spreadsheets."

## Step-by-Step Activity

You'll complete this in the **Skill-to-Service Builder Worksheet** (Notion or Google Docs — whichever your instructor assigned).

**Step 1 — List your skills.**
Open your Course 16 portfolio. Pick 2–3 skills you have real, finished work to back up. Write them in the skills inventory table.

**Step 2 — Draft 2–3 possible services.**
For each skill, use the formula to draft at least one possible service. Aim for 2–3 total service ideas across your skills. Don't worry about picking the "best" one yet — get options down first.

**Step 3 — Pick your strongest one.**
Look at your options. Ask yourself:
- Which one can I describe in one sentence without hesitating?
- Which one is closest to something I could actually start doing soon?
- Which one has the clearest audience — do I know where to even find these people?

Write your final choice into the "My Chosen Service" statement using the template in the worksheet.

## Two Mistakes to Avoid

**"My service has to work for everyone."**
Wrong. A service for "everyone" is actually a service for no one — it's too vague to say yes to. Naming a specific audience (a club, a type of student, a small local group) makes your service *easier* to sell, not smaller.

**"My service has to be completely unique."**
Also wrong. Plenty of people build websites or design graphics. What makes a beginner service work isn't originality — it's being specific, reliable, and easy to understand. You can develop your own style over time; you don't need it to start.

## Knowledge Checks

1. What are the three qualities a service needs that a skill alone doesn't have?
2. Fill in the blank: Service = Skill + ______ + Specific Audience + ______.
3. Why is "I design graphics for businesses" weaker than "I design a 5-template Instagram graphic set for student clubs"?
4. True or False: If another student already offers a similar service, you shouldn't offer yours. Explain your answer.
5. Give one reason a scope boundary (like "one round of revisions" or "3-page limit") actually helps you, the person offering the service.

## Reflection Prompts

1. Which of your Course 16 skills surprised you by turning into a real service idea? Why?
2. Look at your final service statement — what's one specific audience member (a real club, group, or person type) who might actually need it?
3. What's one thing about your chosen service that still feels unclear or unfinished to you, and what would help you clarify it?

## Submission Instructions

Before class ends (or by the deadline your instructor sets):
1. Complete all sections of your Skill-to-Service Builder Worksheet.
2. Make sure your final "My Chosen Service" statement includes a specific output, a specific audience, and a scope boundary.
3. Save your worksheet in your Lumexa portfolio/planning folder (Notion or Google Docs) — the same one holding your Course 16 work.
4. Share the document link with your instructor by end of class or via email if working asynchronously.

You'll need this service statement for the next lesson, where you start figuring out what to actually charge for it.

# Instructor Guide

## Lesson Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path |
| Course | Course 17: Skills That Pay |
| Lesson | Lesson 2: Turn a Skill Into a Service |
| Age range | 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led (video classroom) |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Tools used | Google Docs, Canva, Notion, Email, Spreadsheets |
| Prerequisites | Course 16 (student has a completed portfolio with at least 2–3 documented skills/projects); Course 17 Lesson 1 (understands the freelance landscape: platforms, client types, basic pricing concepts) |
| Lesson goal | Each student converts one skill from their Course 16 portfolio into a specific, scoped, repeatable service they could realistically offer |

## Overview

Lesson 1 gave students the map of the freelance/service landscape — what kinds of paid work exist, who buys them, and roughly how pricing works. This lesson narrows the focus: students take one skill they already have evidence of (from their Course 16 portfolio) and shape it into a **service** — something specific enough that a stranger reading it would immediately understand what they'd get, from whom, and for what.

This is the conceptual hinge of Course 17: "I know Python" is not sellable. "I build a working scoreboard/timer web app for a school club's tournament, delivered in 3 days" is. The lesson does not ask students to set a price yet (that's a later lesson) — it asks them to get the *offer* right first.

All example businesses, clients, and prices used in this lesson are fictional teaching illustrations. No real transaction, business registration, or payment processing is implied or required to complete this lesson.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Explain the difference between a "skill" and a "service" in their own words.
2. Identify at least two possible services hidden inside one of their existing Course 16 skills.
3. Draft one clear service statement using the skill → service formula (skill + specific output + specific audience + scope boundary).
4. Recognize and avoid two common beginner mistakes: trying to serve "everyone," and believing a service must be totally unique to be valid.

## Materials & Prep (before class)

- Open a fresh **Google Doc** titled "Skill → Service Demo" for the live demo (see Teaching Sequence, Step 2).
- Have the **Course 16 portfolio template** on hand (Notion or Docs, whichever the cohort used) — you will pull real skill entries from a student's portfolio during discussion, with their permission, or use the fictional "Jordan R." example from the Worksheet if no student volunteers.
- Pre-load the **Worksheet** ("Skill-to-Service Builder") in Notion or as a Google Doc/Sheet so students can duplicate it individually.
- Have a blank **Spreadsheet** tab ready if you want to log service ideas from the class as a shared brainstorm list (optional, good for larger cohorts).
- Review the fictional Jordan R. example in the Student Lesson and Worksheet so you can reference it fluently without reading it cold.
- Confirm every student can access their own Course 16 portfolio document before class starts — send a reminder email or chat message 24 hours prior if needed.

## Teaching Sequence (60 minutes)

### 1. Open & Frame (5 min)
- Quick recap question: "Last lesson, we mapped out the freelance landscape. Today: who here could tell me, in one sentence, what work you'd actually offer someone?" Take 1–2 quick verbal answers — expect vague ones ("coding stuff," "design"). Don't correct yet, just note them; you'll return to them at the end.
- State the goal plainly: "By the end of today, you will have one sentence that describes an actual service you could offer — specific enough that if I read it, I'd know exactly what I'm getting."

### 2. Skill vs. Service — Direct Teaching + Live Demo (15 min)
- **Core distinction (write on shared screen / Google Doc):**
  - A **skill** is something you can do. ("I know HTML/CSS.")
  - A **service** is a packaged version of that skill that is:
    - **Specific** — a defined output, not an open-ended ability
    - **Scoped** — has a clear boundary on what's included and what isn't
    - **Repeatable** — you could do it again for a different client without reinventing it each time
  - Formula to display: **Service = Skill + Specific Output + Specific Audience + Scope Boundary**
- **Live demo** — in the prepared Google Doc, work through a fictional student profile out loud:
  - Present: "Maya, from her Course 16 portfolio, has: (1) a personal portfolio site built with HTML/CSS/basic JS, (2) a Canva-designed Instagram template pack she made for her robotics club, (3) a short project where she cleaned and charted data in Spreadsheets for a school survey."
  - Think aloud, applying the formula to skill (1): "Skill: HTML/CSS. Output: a small website. Audience: who actually needs a small website and can't easily get one? Not big companies — small student clubs, a tutor, a local youth sports team. Scope: how many pages, how long, what's NOT included (no e-commerce, no ongoing hosting management)." Land on: **Service Idea A — "I build simple 3–5 page websites for student clubs and small community groups, delivered in one week, with one round of revisions included."**
  - Repeat quickly for skill (2): **Service Idea B — "I design a matching set of 5 Instagram graphic templates (Canva) for a school club or small student group, so they can post consistent content without redesigning each one."**
  - Point out: same student, two different services, from two different skills — and neither claims to serve "everyone."

### 3. Guided Discussion (10 min)
Ask and take answers from several students (cold-call gently if needed):
- "What's different between 'I know graphic design' and Maya's Service Idea B?"
- "Why did we say 'student clubs and small community groups' instead of just 'businesses'?"
- "What would happen if Maya's website service had no scope boundary — no page limit, no revision limit?"
- "Could two students both offer 'websites for clubs' and still both be doing something valid? Why?"

### 4. Common Misconceptions — Address Directly (5 min)
Call these out explicitly, even if no student says them aloud — they are near-universal at this age:

- **"My service has to work for everyone, or I'm limiting myself."**
  Correction: The opposite is true. A service aimed at "everyone" reads as aimed at no one — it's what makes "I do graphic design" impossible to say yes to. Naming a specific audience (small clubs, tutors, local shops, other students) makes it *easier* to get a first client, not harder. You can always expand later once you have proof it works.

- **"My service has to be totally unique or no one will notice me."**
  Correction: Almost no beginner service is unique — website-building and graphic design services already exist everywhere. What makes it work isn't novelty, it's specificity and reliability: a clear, scoped offer that's easy to say yes to, delivered well. Uniqueness can come later, from your style or your track record — it's not a requirement to start.

### 5. Independent Activity (20 min)
Students work in the Worksheet (Notion or Docs) individually:
- **Step 1:** List 2–3 skills from their Course 16 portfolio in the skills inventory table.
- **Step 2:** For each skill, brainstorm 1–2 possible services in the brainstorm table (skill / possible service / who needs this).
- **Step 3:** Pick their strongest option and write it as a single service statement using the formula, filling in the "my chosen service" template.
- Circulate (or monitor chat/breakout rooms) while students work — this is where most 1:1 coaching happens. See Troubleshooting below.

### 6. Share & Close (5 min)
- Ask 2–3 volunteers to read their service statement aloud (or paste in chat).
- For each, do a 10-second gut check as a class: "Is it specific? Is it scoped? Could they do it again for someone else?"
- Close: "You now have one sentence that says what you'd actually offer. Next lesson, we start figuring out what to charge for it — but you can't price something fuzzy, so today's work is the foundation."
- Remind students their service statement will be needed for the next lesson and should be saved in their portfolio/planning doc.

## Discussion Questions (use during Step 3 or as backup/extension)

1. Why is "I'm good with computers" not a service, even though it's true for a lot of students?
2. If two students at Lumexa both decide to build websites for clubs, has either of them made a mistake? Why or why not?
3. What's one skill from your own portfolio that could become more than one service, like Maya's HTML/CSS skill did?
4. Why do we include a scope boundary ("what's NOT included") in a service statement instead of just describing what IS included?

## Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| What you'll see | Likely cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Student writes a service statement that's just their skill restated ("I do web design for people") | Hasn't applied output/audience/scope yet | Ask: "If I said yes right now, what exactly would I receive, and by when?" Have them answer that out loud, then write down their own answer. |
| Student picks an audience that's too broad ("small businesses") | Defaulting to landscape-lesson language instead of narrowing further | Ask: "Of all small businesses, who would actually say yes to a 16-year-old? Who do you already have some connection to or credibility with?" Push toward clubs, peers, family-adjacent contacts, local micro-organizations. |
| Student freezes because they think their idea has "been done before" | Uniqueness misconception | Point back to the Canva/website example — remind them two students can offer similar services and both succeed. Redirect focus to specificity, not originality. |
| Student can't decide between two service ideas | Both are genuinely reasonable | Ask which one they could describe in one sentence *right now* without hesitating — that's usually the stronger, clearer one to start with. Reassure them the other idea isn't lost, just parked. |
| Student's scope has no boundary at all ("as many revisions as needed") | Hasn't yet connected scope to sustainability | Ask: "If you had 5 clients at once, could you actually do 'unlimited revisions' for all of them?" Have them add a concrete number or limit. |
| Student wants to list a skill they don't actually have portfolio evidence for | Reaching beyond Course 16 material | Redirect: "Let's build from what you've already proven you can do — that's what makes this believable to a client." Keep them anchored to their real portfolio. |

## How to Review Student Work

Check each student's final service statement for:
- [ ] **Specific output** — names a concrete deliverable (a website, a template set, a document, a chart), not an open-ended ability
- [ ] **Named audience** — a defined type of person or group, not "anyone" or "everyone"
- [ ] **Scope boundary** — states a limit (number of pages/items, timeframe, or what's excluded)
- [ ] **Traceable to Course 16** — the underlying skill is one they have actual portfolio evidence for
- [ ] **Plausible for their age/context** — a real service a teen could credibly deliver without needing adult business infrastructure they don't have

If a statement is missing 2 or more of these, have the student revise it before the next lesson using written feedback (email or a comment in their doc) rather than requiring an in-class redo.

## Lesson Close / Transition

Restate the thread across the course: Lesson 1 = landscape, Lesson 2 = your specific offer, next lesson = what it's worth. Confirm every student leaves with a saved, written service statement — this is the required input for Lesson 3 and should not be treated as optional homework.

lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Lesson 3: Build a Service Package

## What You'll Do Today

In Lesson 2, you chose one service you could offer — something like designing graphics, tutoring a subject, editing videos, building a simple website, writing resumes, or organizing photos. Today you're going to turn that idea into a real, written **service package**: a short document that says exactly what a customer gets when they hire you, and exactly what they don't.

By the end of class, you'll have a one-page package for your own service, ready to actually use.

## Why This Matters

Imagine you hired someone to paint your bedroom, and they finished — but didn't paint the closet, because "you didn't say the closet." Were they wrong? Maybe not, technically. But you're still annoyed, because you assumed it was included.

That's the exact problem a service package solves. It's not about sounding fancy or professional-sounding — it's about making sure you and your customer agree, in writing, on what's being delivered *before* any money or work changes hands. Almost every argument between a freelancer and a customer comes down to one thing: something was assumed but never actually agreed on.

A clear package protects **you** too. If a customer asks for something outside what you listed, you're not being difficult by saying "that's not part of this package" — you already told them what was included, in writing, before they paid.

## The Parts of a Service Package

A simple, first service package has five parts:

| Part | What it answers |
|---|---|
| **Deliverable** | What exact thing will the customer receive? (Format, quantity, detail) |
| **What's Included** | Everything the customer gets for the agreed price |
| **What's Not Included** | Things customers might assume are included, but aren't |
| **Turnaround Time** | How long it will take, and starting from when |
| **Revision Policy** | How many changes/edits are included after the first delivery |

### Deliverable
This is the actual "thing" you hand over. Be specific — not "a logo," but "1 logo design, delivered as a PNG file and a PDF file, by email." Vague deliverables cause more disagreements than almost anything else in this package.

### What's Included
A bulleted list of everything covered by the price. Be generous but realistic — only list what you can actually deliver reliably, every time.

### What's Not Included
This is not rude — it's protective. It tells the customer what's outside this package, so they're not surprised later, and so you're not pressured into free extra work. Example: a tutoring package might exclude "grading homework" even though it includes "reviewing homework together during the session."

### Turnaround Time
How long the work will take — and importantly, starting from *what*. "3 days" is incomplete. "3 business days from when I receive your logo files" is complete, because it protects you from delays that are the customer's fault (like them being slow to send you what you need).

### Revision Policy
How many rounds of changes are included after you deliver the first version. This should be a specific number — never "unlimited." Unlimited revisions sound generous but actually hurt everyone: they remove the customer's reason to give clear feedback the first time, and they can eat unlimited amounts of your unpaid time.

## Key Terms

- **Scope** — the exact boundary of what a service does and doesn't cover.
- **Deliverable** — the actual file, product, or result the customer receives.
- **Turnaround** — how long the work takes to complete, from an agreed starting point.
- **Revision policy** — the rules for how many changes are included after the first delivery.
- **Tier** — a version of a service at a different price/scope level (e.g. Basic vs. Standard). Not used in this lesson — we're building one simple package first.

## Worked Example: Maya's Post Graphics Package

Here's a complete, filled-out example for a fictional student, Maya, who offers Instagram post graphics for small local businesses.

**Service Name:** Maya's Post Graphics

**What's Included:**
- 3 custom Instagram post graphics using the business's logo and colors
- Business name and short text added to each graphic
- Files sized correctly for Instagram feed posts (1080x1080px)

**What's Not Included:**
- Posting the graphics to Instagram
- Video or Reels content
- Additional graphics beyond the 3 included (available as a new order)

**Deliverable Format:** 3 PNG files, delivered by email

**Turnaround Time:** 3 business days from when the business sends their logo and color preferences

**Revision Policy:** Up to 1 round of revisions included (e.g. text or color changes). Additional revision rounds are a small added fee.

Notice: every line answers a question a real customer would have. Nothing is left for either side to guess.

## Step-by-Step Activity

1. Open the Worksheet (Google Docs, Canva, or Notion — your choice).
2. Write your **Service Name** — short and specific to what you actually do.
3. Write your **Deliverable Format** first. Ask yourself: "If I couldn't answer any follow-up questions, would someone know exactly what they're getting — format, quantity, and how it's delivered?"
4. List 3–5 things **Included**.
5. List at least 2 things **Not Included** — think about what a customer might assume, but that would actually take extra time or a different skill.
6. Write your **Turnaround Time**, and make sure you state what it starts counting from.
7. Write your **Revision Policy** with a specific number of rounds — not zero, not unlimited.
8. Read the whole thing back as if you were the customer. Does every line make sense on its own?
9. Save your document — you'll build on it in the next lesson.

## Knowledge Checks

1. What are the two biggest problems with saying "unlimited revisions" in a service package?
2. Why does listing "what's not included" protect both the customer and the freelancer, not just the freelancer?
3. What's wrong with a turnaround time that just says "3 days" with no starting point?
4. Give an example of a vague deliverable and rewrite it to be specific.
5. True or false: a good service package should include as many extras as possible to seem like a better deal. Explain your answer.

## Reflection Prompts

1. Which part of your package (Included, Not Included, Turnaround, or Revision Policy) was hardest to write, and why do you think that one was harder?
2. Think of a time you were a customer somewhere and something wasn't what you expected. What could have been written down ahead of time to prevent that?
3. If a customer asked you for something outside your "Not Included" list, how would you respond in a way that's clear but still friendly?

## Submission Instructions

- Save your completed Service Package worksheet in Google Docs, Canva, or Notion (whichever tool you used).
- Name your file: `[Your Name] - Service Package - [Your Service]`
- Share the link or file with your instructor by the end of class, using the class submission method (Notion page, email, or shared folder as directed by your instructor).
- Bring this document to Lesson 4 — you'll build directly on it.

# Instructor Guide: Build a Service Package

## Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path |
| Course | 17 — Skills That Pay |
| Lesson | 3 of course — Build a Service Package |
| Age range | 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Tools | Google Docs, Canva, Notion, Email, Spreadsheets |
| Prerequisite | Lesson 2: student has already chosen one service to offer (e.g. logo design, tutoring, social media graphics, simple websites, video editing, pet sitting flyers, resume formatting) |
| Lesson output | A one-page "Service Package" document for the student's chosen service, built in Google Docs or Canva |

## Overview

In Lesson 2, students picked one service they could realistically offer. Today they turn that idea into something a real customer could say yes to: a clear, written package. The core skill is **scope clarity** — spelling out exactly what is included, what is not, how the work will be delivered, how long it will take, and what happens if the customer wants changes. This is the single most common gap between beginner freelancers and people who get repeat clients: beginners either promise too much (leading to burnout and resentment) or say too little (leading to disputes about what was "supposed" to happen).

This lesson deliberately keeps things simple: **one tier only**. Multi-tier pricing (basic/standard/premium) is a Course 17 topic for a later lesson, once students already know how to define a single clean scope. Introducing tiers here would let students dodge the harder skill of drawing a firm line around one offer.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Explain why "included" and "not included" lists prevent conflict with customers.
2. Write a specific, non-vague deliverable description (format, quantity, and detail).
3. Set a realistic turnaround time.
4. Write a bounded revision policy that protects their time without sounding unfriendly.
5. Produce a complete one-page service package document for their own chosen service.

## Prep (Before Class)

- Confirm each student's Lesson 2 service choice; have the list ready to reference by name during the demo and check-ins.
- Open a blank Google Doc (or Canva doc template) to demo live. Do not pre-fill it — students should watch it get built from a blank page, including the messy first draft.
- Have the Worksheet.md printed or shared digitally (Notion or Google Docs) for every student.
- Test screen share and confirm all students can access Docs/Canva/Notion/Spreadsheets/Email as needed.
- Optional: have one real-world example (a screenshot of an Etsy or Fiverr service listing) ready to show as a "what a package looks like in the wild" reference — anonymize or use a generic public listing, not a specific person's business.

## Materials Checklist

- [ ] Slide or whiteboard: the four package components (Included / Not Included / Deliverable Format / Turnaround / Revision Policy — five, matching the worksheet)
- [ ] Blank Google Doc for live demo
- [ ] Worksheet.md shared with each student
- [ ] List of student service choices from Lesson 2

## Teaching Sequence

### 1. Opening hook (5 min)
Ask: "Has anyone ever ordered food and it came without something you assumed was included — like fries, or a drink?" Take one or two answers. Point out: the restaurant didn't lie, but the menu wasn't clear enough, and now someone's annoyed. That mismatch between what a customer *expects* and what they *actually get* is exactly what a service package prevents. Today's job: write down, in plain words, exactly what a customer gets when they hire you.

### 2. Why scope clarity matters (10 min)
Direct instruction + discussion. Cover:
- A **service package** is a short written description of exactly what someone gets when they pay for your service.
- The two most common beginner mistakes are (a) being vague ("I'll make you a nice website") and (b) promising too much ("unlimited revisions until you're happy").
- Walk through the "included / not included" idea: listing what's *not* included isn't rude — it's protective, for both sides. Example: a tutoring package might include "one 45-minute session, practice worksheet emailed after" but *not* include "homework grading" or "sessions on weekends." Neither side gets surprised later.
- Emphasize: **the package is a promise you can actually keep.** If it's unclear, disagreements happen after the work is already done — which is the worst time, because trust is already broken and no one wants to redo it for free.

Talking point script (use close to verbatim if helpful):
> "The goal of a service package is not to sound impressive. It's to make sure that if you and your customer never spoke again after this document, you'd both agree on what was owed. That's the test: could a stranger read this and know exactly what they get, and exactly what they don't?"

### 3. Live demo — building a fictional package (15 min)
Build this live in the shared Google Doc, narrating each decision out loud, including the ones you cross out or revise.

**Fictional student: "Maya," service: Instagram post graphics for small local businesses.**

Narrate the build in this order:
1. **Service Name** — "Maya's Post Graphics" — short and specific, not "social media services" (too vague).
2. **Deliverable Format** — decide out loud: "3 finished Instagram post graphics (1080x1080px), delivered as PNG files by email." Point out: file format and dimensions matter — a customer who expected a Canva template link and got a flat PNG will be unhappy, even though Maya technically delivered "graphics."
3. **What's Included** — bullet it live:
 - 3 custom graphics based on the business's colors/logo
 - Text and business name added to each graphic
 - Files delivered as PNG, sized for Instagram feed posts
4. **What's Not Included** — bullet it live, and explain each choice:
 - Posting the graphics to Instagram (Maya isn't managing their account)
 - Video or Reels content (different skill, different service)
 - Additional graphics beyond the 3 (that's a new order)
5. **Turnaround Time** — "3 business days from when I receive the business's logo and color preferences." Point out: turnaround should start from when the customer gives Maya what she needs, not from the moment they pay — otherwise Maya is on the hook for delays that aren't her fault.
6. **Revision Policy** — "Up to 1 round of revisions included (example: adjusting text or colors). Additional rounds are a new small fee." Contrast this with "unlimited revisions" and ask the group why that phrase is a trap (see misconceptions below) before writing the bounded version.

End the demo by reading the whole one-pager aloud as if you were the customer, checking: "Does this answer every question I'd have before paying?"

### 4. Discussion questions (5 min)
Pose to the group, cold-call or thumbs-up/down first:
- "If Maya's package didn't mention turnaround time, what could go wrong?"
- "Why might listing 'what's not included' actually help Maya get *more* repeat customers, not fewer?"
- "What's the risk if Maya offers unlimited revisions?"
- "Could two different customers read this package and expect two different things? If yes, what's still unclear?"

### 5. Guided student activity (20 min)
Students open the Worksheet and build their own package for their Lesson 2 service, using Google Docs, Canva, or Notion (whichever the student prefers or was assigned).
- First 3 minutes: students silently draft their Deliverable Format and Included list only — don't let them fill the whole sheet at once.
- Circulate (or use breakout rooms) and check every student's Deliverable Format line before they move on — this is the field most likely to be too vague.
- Remaining time: students complete Not Included, Turnaround, and Revision Policy.
- Early finishers: have them trade documents with a partner and try to find one sentence that's still vague enough to cause a misunderstanding.

### 6. Lesson close (5 min)
- Cold-call 2–3 students to read just their "Not Included" list aloud — this is usually the most revealing field and a good gauge of understanding.
- Recap the core rule: **a good package answers every question a customer would have, before they ask it.**
- State submission instructions (see Student_Lesson.md) and preview Lesson 4 (which will build on this package, e.g. pricing or the customer-facing offer message).

## Common Misconceptions to Address

- **"More included = a better deal."** Push back directly: a package that includes too much is a package the student can't actually deliver reliably, and it trains customers to expect endless extras for free. A tight, honest package that's delivered well beats an overloaded one that burns the student out or gets delivered late.
- **"I should offer unlimited revisions to seem generous."** This is the single most common trap. Unlimited revisions means unlimited unpaid time, and it removes the customer's incentive to give clear feedback the first time. Bounded revisions (e.g. "1 round included") protect the student's time and, ironically, usually produce *faster* results for the customer because it forces clearer communication upfront.
- **"If I write down what's not included, it sounds negative or unfriendly."** Reframe: it reads as professional and protects the relationship — it's the same reason a syllabus lists what's not on a test.
- **"The deliverable format doesn't matter much — the customer will figure it out."** Push back: format (file type, size, quantity, delivery method) is often exactly where mismatches happen.

## Anticipated Student Difficulties

- **Vague deliverables.** Students often write things like "a good website" instead of "a 1-page website with 3 sections (About, Services, Contact), delivered as a link to a live page." Prompt with: "If I couldn't ask you a single follow-up question, would I know exactly what I'm getting?"
- **Copying the demo too literally.** Some students may just swap in their service name without adjusting content. Ask each student one specific question about their own service to check real understanding (e.g., "What's the biggest thing that could go wrong if a customer assumed X was included?").
- **Turnaround time with no starting point.** Students may write "3 days" without saying 3 days from what. Prompt: "3 days starting when?"
- **Revision policy that's either 0 or unlimited.** Guide students toward a small, defined number (0–2 rounds) rather than either extreme.

## Troubleshooting

- **Student can't decide what to exclude:** Ask, "What would take you the most extra time or skill that isn't part of the core service?" That's usually the exclusion.
- **Student's package is too long/complicated:** Remind them this is a first, single-tier package — simpler is better; multi-tier options come in a later lesson.
- **Tool trouble (Docs/Canva access):** Have a Notion or plain-email fallback ready — the content matters more than the tool.
- **Student finishes early and has spare time:** Have them read their package aloud to a partner and ask the partner to try to "misunderstand" it on purpose — a good stress test.

## How to Review Student Work

Check each submitted package against this quick rubric:
1. Deliverable format is specific (quantity, file type/format, and how it's delivered are all named).
2. At least 2 items are listed as "not included," and they are plausible exclusions for that service (not random).
3. Turnaround time includes a clear starting point.
4. Revision policy is bounded (a specific number of rounds), not "unlimited" and not "none mentioned."
5. Overall: could a stranger read it and know exactly what they get?

Give specific feedback on the field that's weakest rather than general praise — most students will need feedback on exactly one field (usually deliverable format or revision policy).

## Lesson Close / Bridge to Next Lesson

End by naming what comes next: this package is the foundation for how the student will describe their service to a real customer (Lesson 4). Remind students to save their document somewhere they can find it again — they'll build directly on top of it.

lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Lesson 4: Pricing, Scope, and Agreements

## What You're Learning Today

You already have a service package from Lesson 3 — something you could offer to a client. Today you'll learn how to put a fair price on it, how to write down exactly what's included (that's called "scope"), and how to draft a simple agreement so everyone's on the same page.

You'll also learn something important that a lot of people get wrong: **writing something down and signing it does not automatically make it a legal contract.** More on that below — it matters.

## Why This Matters

Freelancers, contractors, and small business owners price their own work every single day. Nobody hands them a price list — they figure it out using simple, honest methods. Learning to do this now, at a small scale with simulated clients, means you'll already know how when it counts for real.

## Pricing, Explained Simply

There are two beginner-friendly ways to price a service:

### Flat Rate
One total price for the whole job, agreed before you start.
- **Best for:** small jobs where you know exactly what's involved.
- **Example:** "$35 for one logo design with two rounds of revisions."

### Hourly Rate
A price for each hour you work, added up at the end.
- **Best for:** jobs where the amount of work is uncertain.
- **Example:** "$12 per hour for tutoring help, however many hours it takes."

**A common beginner method:** estimate how many hours a job will realistically take, multiply by a reasonable reference hourly rate, and use that number to set (or check) your flat-rate price. You'll practice this in the activity below.

## Scope and Price Are Linked

**Scope** = exactly what is included in the job (and what isn't).

If your scope is vague ("I'll design your logo"), a client might expect unlimited revisions and extra requests for the same price. That's called **scope creep** — when the job quietly grows bigger than what was agreed, without the price or timeline changing.

A clear scope protects both you and the client. It's not about being difficult — it's about being clear from the start, so nobody feels surprised or taken advantage of later.

**Vague scope:** "I'll design your logo."
**Clear scope:** "One logo design, two revision rounds, delivered as a PNG and JPG file, within 5 days."

## Worked Example: Pricing Priya's Package

Priya offers Instagram graphic design for small school clubs. Here's how she prices one project:

1. **Scope:** 3 social media graphics, 1 revision round each, delivered as PNG files, within 5 days.
2. **Estimated time:** about 1 hour per graphic (including the revision) = **3 hours total**.
3. **Reference hourly rate:** $12/hour (a reasonable beginner starting point — not a fixed rule).
4. **Math:** 3 hours × $12/hour = $36.
5. **Quoted price:** Priya rounds this to a clean flat rate of **$35** for the whole package.

Notice: Priya used hourly math to *reason her way* to a fair flat-rate quote. This is completely normal — and your price can always shift based on your experience, your local market, and what feels fair.

## The Most Important Part of This Lesson: Agreements vs. Legal Contracts

Read this section slowly. It's the part we spend the most time on in class, for good reason.

When you and a client (even a simulated one) write down what you agreed on — the scope, the price, the deadline — that's a **written agreement**. It's genuinely useful because it:

- Makes sure you both understand the same thing.
- Creates a paper trail you can look back at if there's ever confusion.
- Builds a real skill that adults use in freelance work and business every day.

**But here's the critical part: a written agreement between two people — especially a generic template — is NOT automatically a legally binding contract.** Just because something is written down, and even signed, does not by itself make it enforceable by law.

What actually makes something a real, legally binding contract involves things like:

- **Capacity to contract** — in most places, there are legal rules (often tied to age of majority) about who is legally able to enter into a binding contract. This can specifically affect people under 18.
- **Consideration** — a legal term for something of value being exchanged in a legally recognized way.
- Other legal requirements that are different depending on the country, state, or province you're in.

That's a whole area of law on its own — way beyond this lesson, and not something you need to master to do great beginner client work. What you *do* need is a clear, honest agreement that keeps everyone on the same page. That's what we're practicing.

**One more essential point: if you ever do real client work for real money, a parent or guardian should know about it and be involved** — helping with things like handling payment, communicating with a client if something goes wrong, and making sure the whole arrangement is safe and appropriate for your age. This isn't optional caution — it's simply how paid work should go for someone your age.

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Flat rate** | One total price for an entire job, agreed before starting. |
| **Hourly rate** | A price charged per hour of work. |
| **Scope** | Exactly what is (and isn't) included in a job. |
| **Scope creep** | When a job grows beyond what was agreed, without the price or timeline changing. |
| **Agreement** | A written record of what two people understood and agreed to — useful for clarity, not automatically legal. |
| **Legal contract** | A legally enforceable agreement that requires specific legal conditions (like capacity and consideration) which vary by jurisdiction. |
| **Capacity (to contract)** | The legal ability to enter into a binding contract — often tied to age of majority and other rules. |

## Activity: Price Your Package & Draft Your Agreement

1. Open your Worksheet for this lesson.
2. Re-read your Lesson 3 service package.
3. Fill in the pricing calculator: estimate your hours, apply a reference hourly rate, and calculate a suggested price.
4. Write a clear, specific scope line — not vague.
5. Complete the agreement template for a fictional simulated client (make up a name — do not use a real transaction).
6. Read the disclaimer at the top of the agreement out loud to yourself before filling it in. Do not delete it.

## Knowledge Check

1. What's the difference between a flat rate and an hourly rate?
2. What is "scope creep," and why is a clear scope important?
3. Is a written agreement between two students automatically a legal contract? Why or why not?
4. Name two things (besides being written down) that are generally needed for something to be a real legal contract.
5. If you were going to do real paid client work, who should know about it, and why?

## Reflection Prompts

1. Which pricing method (flat or hourly) fits your Lesson 3 service package best, and why?
2. In your own words, explain the difference between "a clear agreement" and "a legally binding contract."
3. How would you explain the parent/guardian point to a friend who thought it was unnecessary?

## Submission Instructions

Submit your completed Worksheet (pricing calculator, scope checklist, and agreement template) through your Notion workspace by the end of class. Make sure the disclaimer text at the top of your agreement section is present and unedited — this is checked as part of review.

# Pricing & Agreement Worksheet

Name: _______________________ Date: _______________________

Service package (from Lesson 3): _______________________________________________

---

## Part 1: Pricing Calculator

Fill in your own estimate below. This is a **starting estimate to help you think, not a fixed rule** — your real price can change based on experience, your local market, and what feels fair to you and the client.

| Step | Your Entry |
|---|---|
| Estimated hours to complete the job | _____ hours |
| Reference hourly rate (a reasonable beginner starting point, e.g. $10–$20/hour) | $_____ /hour |
| Calculation (hours × rate) | _____ × $_____ = $_____ |
| Suggested price (rounded to a clean number) | $_____ |
| Pricing method you'll actually quote the client (circle one) | Flat Rate / Hourly Rate |

**Filled Example — Jordan R.**

| Step | Jordan's Entry |
|---|---|
| Estimated hours to complete the job | 4 hours |
| Reference hourly rate | $12/hour |
| Calculation | 4 × $12 = $48 |
| Suggested price (rounded) | $50 |
| Pricing method to quote | Flat Rate |

*Note: This is a starting estimate, not a fixed rule — Jordan could quote more or less depending on experience and the client.*

---

## Part 2: Scope Boundary Checklist

Check off each item once you've clearly defined it. If you can't check a box, your scope isn't specific enough yet.

- [ ] I've listed exactly what deliverables the client will receive (e.g., number of files, file types).
- [ ] I've stated how many revision rounds are included.
- [ ] I've stated a delivery timeframe (a specific number of days).
- [ ] I've stated what is **NOT** included (e.g., "does not include printing" or "does not include more than 2 revisions").
- [ ] I've stated how the client should ask for changes if something is unclear.
- [ ] My scope line avoids vague words like "etc.," "and more," or "whatever you need."

**Filled Example — Jordan R.'s Scope Checklist**

- [x] Deliverables listed: 2 flyer designs, delivered as PNG and PDF files.
- [x] Revision rounds included: 1 round of revisions per flyer.
- [x] Delivery timeframe: within 6 days of starting.
- [x] Not included: does not include printing, does not include a 3rd flyer design.
- [x] How to request changes: client sends notes by email within 2 days of receiving drafts.
- [x] No vague language used.

---

## Part 3: Simple Written Agreement (Educational Template)

> **IMPORTANT — READ FIRST:**
> **This is an educational agreement template for practicing clear scope communication. It is NOT a legally binding contract.**
> Writing this down and signing it does not create legal obligations. A real legal contract depends on separate legal requirements (such as legal capacity/age of majority, consideration, and other rules that vary by country, state, or province) that are beyond the scope of this lesson. If you ever do real paid client work, involve a parent or guardian.

### Blank Template

**Project Agreement (Educational Use Only)**

- Service provider (student): ___________________________
- Client (fictional/simulated for this activity): ___________________________
- Date: ___________________________

**1. What's included (scope):**
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

**2. What's NOT included:**
_______________________________________________________________

**3. Price and pricing method:**
$_______ ( Flat Rate / Hourly Rate — circle one )

**4. Timeline:**
Work will be delivered by: _______________________

**5. How changes/extra requests will be handled:**
_______________________________________________________________

**6. How communication will happen (e.g., email, messages):**
_______________________________________________________________

**Signatures (for practice purposes only — not a legal signature):**

Student: ___________________________ Date: _______
Client (simulated): ___________________________ Date: _______

*Reminder: This document helps both sides stay clear and organized. It is not a legally binding contract.*

---

### Filled Example — Jordan R.

**Project Agreement (Educational Use Only)**

- Service provider (student): Jordan R.
- Client (fictional/simulated for this activity): "Maya's Bake Club" (fictional school club)
- Date: September 14, 2026

**1. What's included (scope):**
Two (2) flyer designs advertising the Bake Club's fall event, delivered as PNG and PDF files, each with one round of revisions included.

**2. What's NOT included:**
Printing of physical flyers; a third flyer design; unlimited revisions.

**3. Price and pricing method:**
$50 (Flat Rate)

**4. Timeline:**
Work will be delivered within 6 days of the start date.

**5. How changes/extra requests will be handled:**
The client will send all revision notes by email within 2 days of receiving the drafts. Requests beyond the one included revision round will be discussed as a separate, additional price.

**6. How communication will happen:**
Email, checked once per day by Jordan.

**Signatures (for practice purposes only — not a legal signature):**

Student: Jordan R. Date: 9/14/2026
Client (simulated): Maya's Bake Club (simulated) Date: 9/14/2026

*Reminder: This document helps both sides stay clear and organized. It is not a legally binding contract.*

---

## Final Check Before You Submit

- [ ] The disclaimer at the top of Part 3 is present and unedited.
- [ ] My scope line is specific, not vague.
- [ ] I can explain, in my own words, why this agreement is not the same as a legal contract.
- [ ] I understand that real paid client work should involve a parent or guardian.

# Instructor Guide

## Lesson Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path |
| Course | 17 — Skills That Pay |
| Lesson | 4 — Pricing, Scope, and Agreements |
| Age Range | 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led (video classroom) |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Tools Used | Google Docs, Canva, Notion, Email, Spreadsheets |
| Prerequisite | Lesson 3 — student has a defined service package (service description, deliverables, and target client) |
| Class Size | Best for 4–12 students; works one-to-one |

## Overview

By Lesson 3, each student has a service package — something like "I design simple logos for small local businesses" or "I build basic websites for school clubs." This lesson answers the two questions every student asks next: **"What do I charge?"** and **"How do we agree on what I'm doing?"**

Students learn two beginner pricing methods (flat rate and hourly), why price and scope are two sides of the same coin, and how to write a clear, simple agreement. Woven through the whole lesson — and stated outright, more than once — is a distinction students must leave with:

> A written agreement between two people is a great tool for clarity. It is **not automatically a legally binding contract.** Real legal contracts depend on things like legal capacity (age of majority in most places), consideration, and other jurisdiction-specific rules — topics for a law class, not this one. If a student is going to do **real, paid** client work, a parent or guardian should know about it and be involved.

This is not a footnote. It is a core learning objective of this lesson.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Explain the difference between flat-rate and hourly pricing, and pick one for their own service package.
2. Explain why scope (what's included) and price must be decided together — and what "scope creep" means.
3. Estimate a simple, reasonable price for a small project using a basic calculation.
4. Explain, in their own words, why a written agreement between students is useful but is **not** the same thing as a legally binding contract.
5. Explain why real paid work should involve a parent/guardian.
6. Draft a simple, clearly-labeled educational agreement for a simulated client project.

## Prep (Before Class)

- Review each student's Lesson 3 service package (pulled from their Notion workspace) so you can reference it by name during the live demo.
- Open a blank Google Doc to model the live pricing demo.
- Open Canva only if you plan to show the worksheet's checklist as a visual reference — optional, not required.
- Have the Worksheet and Student Lesson files ready to share/screen-share.
- Reread the "Common Misconceptions" section below — this lesson runs on getting ahead of two specific wrong ideas.
- Decide on one "reference hourly rate" range you'll use in the live demo (suggested: $10–$20/hour equivalent value, framed as "a reasonable beginner reference point," not a rule).

## Materials Needed

- Student's Lesson 3 service package (Notion)
- Instructor demo doc (Google Docs)
- Spreadsheet template with a simple formula (hours × rate = suggested price)
- Worksheet (this lesson's companion file)
- Email — only referenced conceptually today (used more in Lesson 5); no live send required

## Teaching Sequence (60 minutes)

### 1. Warm-Up & Hook (5 min)
Ask: "If a friend asked you to help them for an afternoon, would you charge them the same as a stranger paying you for a full week of work?" Let 2–3 students answer. Land on: price depends on time, effort, and what's included — that's what today is about.

### 2. Flat Rate vs. Hourly, Explained Simply (10 min)
- **Flat rate**: one total price for the whole job, agreed before starting. Good when the job is small and well-defined (e.g., "design one logo" = $40 flat).
- **Hourly rate**: a price per hour worked, tracked and totaled at the end. Good when the job's length is uncertain (e.g., "help me practice my website" = $12/hour).
- Talking point: "Flat rate is simpler for small, clear jobs. Hourly is fairer when nobody knows exactly how long something will take."
- Ask: "Which fits your Lesson 3 service package better, and why?" Cold-call 2 students.

### 3. Scope and Price Are Linked (8 min)
- Define **scope**: exactly what is included in the job — and, just as important, what is *not* included.
- Define **scope creep**: when a client keeps asking for "just one more thing" without adjusting the price or timeline.
- Talking point: "If you don't write down what's included, you can't say no to extra requests without feeling awkward. A clear scope protects both people — it's not about being difficult, it's about being clear."
- Quick example: "I'll design one logo with two revision rounds" is scoped. "I'll design your logo" is not — what if they ask for 10 versions?

### 4. Live Demo — Pricing a Fictional Student's Package (12 min)
Model this out loud in the Google Doc, using a fictional student, **"Priya," who offers Instagram graphic design for small clubs**:

1. Write the scoped job: "3 social media graphics, 1 revision round each, delivered as PNG files, done within 5 days."
2. Estimate time honestly: "Designing one graphic + one revision realistically takes about 1 hour for a beginner. Three graphics = about 3 hours."
3. Introduce the reference hourly rate: "Let's use $12/hour as a reasonable beginner reference point — not a rule, just a starting point to reason from."
4. Do the math out loud in the spreadsheet: 3 hours × $12/hour = **$36**, then round to a clean flat-rate quote of **$35 flat** for the whole package.
5. Talking point: "Notice I did the hourly math *first*, then turned it into a flat rate to quote. That's a completely normal and common beginner method — estimate hours, multiply by a reference rate, then decide how to present the number to the client."
6. Explicitly say: "This number is a starting estimate, not a fixed rule. Your price can depend on your experience, your local market, and what feels fair to you and the client."

### 5. CRITICAL SEGMENT — Agreements vs. Legal Contracts (15 min)
This is the anchor of the lesson. Do not rush it.

- Start plainly: **"We are about to write something down with a client. I need to be very clear about what that piece of paper actually is — and isn't."**
- Explain what a simple written agreement (or template) *is good for*:
  - Making sure both people understand the same thing (scope, price, deadline).
  - Creating a paper trail — something to point back to if there's confusion later ("didn't we agree on 3 graphics, not 5?").
  - Practicing a real professional skill used by adults in every freelance and business relationship.
- State explicitly, slowly, and more than once: **"A generic template, or a simple agreement two students write and sign, is NOT automatically a legally binding contract. Just because something is written down and signed does not make it legally enforceable."**
- Explain — simply, without legal jargon — what actually makes something a real, legally binding contract, and that this varies by location:
  - **Capacity to contract**: in most places, there are rules about the age (often the age of majority) and legal ability required to enter into a binding contract — this can affect minors specifically.
  - **Consideration**: something of value has to be exchanged in a legally recognized way.
  - Other legal requirements exist too, and they differ by country and state/province. **"That's a whole area of law — it's beyond what we're covering today, and it's not something you need to master to do great beginner client work."**
- Land the key contrast clearly:
  - *Meaningful agreement (what we're practicing today)* = clarity + mutual understanding + a paper trail.
  - *Real legal contract* = a separate, more serious legal category with requirements that vary by jurisdiction.
- **Parent/guardian point, stated directly**: "If you're going to do real client work and get paid actual money, a parent or guardian should know about it and be involved — helping you handle payment, communicating with the client if needed, and making sure everything is safe and appropriate. That's not us being overly cautious — that's just how real paid work should work for someone your age."
- Ask the class directly: "Why might it matter that a parent or guardian is aware, even if you're the one doing the work?" Take 2–3 answers before moving on.

### 6. Guided Activity — Draft the Worksheet Agreement (8 min)
Students open the Worksheet and fill in the pricing calculator and the agreement template for their own Lesson 3 service package, using a simulated client (a made-up name, not a real transaction). Circulate (or use breakout awareness on video) to check that:
- The disclaimer at the top of their agreement is intact, not deleted.
- Their scope line is specific, not vague ("logo design" → "one logo, two revisions, PNG + JPG files").

### 7. Wrap-Up & Lesson Close (2 min)
Recap in one line each:
- "Price and scope go together."
- "A written agreement helps everyone stay clear — it is not a legal contract."
- "Real paid work involves a parent or guardian."
Preview Lesson 5: sending a professional first message to a (simulated) client.

## Discussion Questions

1. Why might a flat rate feel riskier for you as the service provider than an hourly rate?
2. What's one way a vague scope could lead to a disagreement later?
3. If a written agreement isn't a legal contract, why bother writing one at all?
4. What's the difference between "this document helps us stay clear" and "this document is legally enforceable"?
5. Who is one adult you'd want to loop in if you actually got paid for a project like this?

## Common Misconceptions (Address Directly)

- **"If we both sign a written agreement, it's a legal contract."** — False. Signing and writing something down makes it clear and organized; it does not by itself make it legally binding. Legal enforceability depends on separate rules (capacity, consideration, jurisdiction) not covered in this lesson.
- **"I should charge as little as possible to get any client."** — Address directly: charging too little undervalues real time and effort, can attract clients who don't respect the work, and makes it harder to raise prices later. A fair, honestly-estimated price is a professional skill, not something to feel guilty about.
- **"Since it's not a real contract, the agreement doesn't matter."** — False. The agreement still matters a great deal for clarity and avoiding misunderstandings — it's just not a legal document.
- **"Hourly is always fairer than flat rate."** — Not necessarily; each fits different job types, which is why students are taught to choose based on scope certainty, not by default.

## Anticipated Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | What to do |
|---|---|
| Student estimates unrealistic time (e.g., "5 minutes" for a multi-part job) | Walk through the task's actual steps out loud with them to build a more honest time estimate. |
| Student wants to skip the disclaimer text in the worksheet template | Do not allow this — explain the disclaimer is a required, non-negotiable part of the document, not optional flavor text. |
| Student conflates "agreement" and "contract" during discussion | Gently redirect with the lesson's key phrase: "clear and organized ≠ legally binding." Repeat as many times as needed. |
| Student asks "so is this fake, then?" about the agreement | Clarify: it's real in the sense that it captures a real, meaningful understanding between two people — it's just not a law-enforceable legal contract. Both things can be true. |
| Student pushes back on the parent/guardian point ("but it's my project") | Validate ownership of the work, then reframe: guardian involvement is about safety and support for the money/communication side, not about taking over the creative work. |

## How to Review Student Work

Check each student's completed Worksheet for:
- [ ] Pricing table filled in with a realistic hour estimate and a stated reference rate (not left blank or copied verbatim from the demo).
- [ ] A clear, specific scope line (not vague).
- [ ] The non-binding disclaimer at the top of the agreement section left fully intact and unedited.
- [ ] A completed agreement referencing their own Lesson 3 service package and a fictional client.
- [ ] Verbal or written confirmation (in the reflection prompts) that the student can explain the agreement-vs-contract distinction in their own words.

If a student cannot restate the agreement-vs-contract distinction in their own words, revisit Section 5 with them one-on-one before moving to Lesson 5.

## Lesson Close Script (Read Aloud or Paraphrase)

"Today you priced your first project and wrote your first client agreement — both real professional skills. Remember: that agreement is a great tool for staying clear with a client, but it's not a legal contract, and if you ever do real paid work, bring a parent or guardian into the loop. Next lesson, we'll write the message that gets this whole project started."
