# Student Lesson — Your Professional Presence

**Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building — Lesson 1 of 8**

## What & Why

Every project you've built, every skill you've practiced, every problem you've solved in Lumexa is worth something beyond the classroom — but only if other people can find it and understand it. That's what a **professional presence** is: the picture of you that exists when someone looks you up online.

Why does this matter now, at 15–18? Because opportunities — mentorships, competitions, internships, scholarships, freelance projects, even your first job — increasingly start with someone searching your name or clicking a link you shared. A strong presence doesn't happen overnight. It's built lesson by lesson, project by project, across this whole course — and it **compounds**: each addition makes the next person's impression of you faster and stronger to form.

This lesson does not assume everyone will use the same tool. It introduces the concept broadly, then splits into two paths so every student — no matter their age — leaves with an equally credible plan.

## The LinkedIn Age Rule — Stated Plainly

**LinkedIn requires account holders to be at least 16 years old.** This is a floor, not a guarantee — some countries or regions require an even higher age, or require a parent/guardian's consent in addition to meeting the age minimum. (This policy can change, so your instructor has verified the current rule before this lesson.)

**If you do not meet the applicable age or consent requirement, you do NOT create a LinkedIn account for this class — no exceptions, and no working around the age check.** This is not a smaller or lesser path. Instead, you will use the **portfolio-first path**: building a professional "presence page" on the portfolio website you already created in Course 16. It shows the same substance — who you are, what you've built, what you can do — without needing any third-party account at all.

Both paths are treated as fully equal in this course. Your instructor will tell you, or confirm with you, which path applies to you before this lesson.

## Two Paths, One Goal

| | Path A: LinkedIn-eligible | Path B: Portfolio-first |
|---|---|---|
| Who | Students who meet LinkedIn's current age/consent requirement | Students who don't yet meet it, or who prefer not to use LinkedIn |
| Where | A LinkedIn profile, kept alongside your portfolio site | A "Presence" page added to your existing Course 16 portfolio site |
| What it includes | Headline, About, Featured projects, Skills, connections | Headline, About, Project gallery, Skills & Growth, contact method |
| Owned by | You, but hosted on LinkedIn's platform | You, fully, on your own site |
| Credibility in this course | Equal | Equal |

## Worked Example: Two Presences for the Same Fictional Student

Meet **Sam K.**, a fictional Lumexa student, age unspecified — used here purely to show what good content looks like on both paths.

**If Sam were on Path A (LinkedIn):**
- Headline: "Aspiring Software Developer | Python & Web Projects | Lumexa Student"
- About: "I'm a student developer who loves building small tools that solve real problems. Currently exploring Python automation and web design."
- Featured: link to a Python quiz-game project, link to a personal portfolio site
- Skills listed: Python, HTML/CSS, teamwork, problem-solving

**If Sam were on Path B (portfolio-first presence page):**
- Same headline, styled as the page's title
- Same About paragraph
- A project gallery showing the same two projects — with screenshots and live demo links (something LinkedIn's Featured section can't always show as richly)
- A "Skills & Growth" section tracking skills over time
- A simple "Contact me" section with an email link — no account required for anyone to reach Sam

Notice: the *content* is almost identical. The only real difference is the venue. That's the point — presence is about substance, not which platform you're on.

## Step-by-Step Activity: Which Path Applies to You?

1. Confirm with your instructor which path applies to you (Path A or Path B) — this has already been determined before class based on age/consent information on file.
2. If you're Path A: note that you'll set up your LinkedIn profile in a later lesson, once your account eligibility is confirmed by you and your family.
3. If you're Path B: open your Course 16 portfolio site and locate (or plan) where a new "Presence" page will live.
4. Either way, open Worksheet.md and complete **Part 1: Eligibility Self-Check** now.
5. Move to **Part 2: Reflection** and **Part 3: Goals for the Course** — these apply to every student regardless of path.

## Key Terms

- **Professional presence** — the full, discoverable picture of your skills, projects, and reliability that exists online, across whatever platforms and pages you use.
- **Reputation** — the pattern of trust and credibility that builds up over time from consistent, honest, quality presence — it compounds rather than resets each time.
- **Discoverability** — how easily someone can find accurate, relevant information about you when they search or click through from something you shared.
- **Portfolio-first** — the approach of building your professional presence entirely on a site you own (your Course 16 portfolio), rather than on a third-party platform account.

## Knowledge Checks

1. What is the minimum age LinkedIn currently requires for an account, and what else might raise that requirement?
2. True or False: A professional presence is the same thing as having one social media profile.
3. Name two things a portfolio-first presence page includes that a LinkedIn profile also includes.
4. If a student doesn't meet the LinkedIn age/consent requirement, what should they do instead?
5. Why does professional presence "compound" over time rather than being a one-time task?

## Reflection Prompts

1. If someone searched your name right now, what would they actually find — and is it a fair picture of you?
2. Which of your existing Lumexa projects would you most want a stranger to see first, and why?
3. What is one thing you want your professional presence to communicate about you by the end of this course?

## Submission Instructions

Complete all three parts of Worksheet.md (Eligibility Self-Check, Reflection, Goals for the Course) and submit it through your Lumexa class dashboard before Lesson 2. If you're on Path B, also come to Lesson 2 with access to edit your Course 16 portfolio site.

# Instructor Guide — Lesson 1: Your Professional Presence

## Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path |
| Course | Course 18 — Professional Presence & Opportunity Building |
| Lesson | Lesson 1 of 8 — Your Professional Presence |
| Format | Live, instructor-led (video conference) |
| Age range | 15–18 |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Group size | Up to 16 students recommended |
| Prerequisite | Course 16 (Portfolio Website) completed — every student must already have a working personal portfolio site |
| Tools referenced | LinkedIn (age-eligible students only), Canva, Google Docs, a content-planning tool (e.g., a simple spreadsheet or planner template) |
| Student materials | Student_Lesson.md, Worksheet.md |

## Overview

This lesson introduces "professional presence" as a broad concept — the sum of what a stranger, recruiter, mentor, or collaborator can find and conclude about a student when they look them up online. It is deliberately platform-agnostic: LinkedIn is one possible venue, not the definition. Students leave this lesson understanding two equally valid paths forward in this course:

- **Path A — LinkedIn-eligible path**: for students who meet LinkedIn's minimum age (currently 16) and any stricter local/consent requirement, and who choose to create a profile.
- **Path B — Portfolio-first path**: for students under the applicable age threshold, or who simply prefer not to use LinkedIn. This path builds a "presence page" on their existing Course 16 portfolio site, extended with the same substance a strong LinkedIn profile would have (bio, skills, projects, contact path) — without an account on a third-party platform.

Both paths are treated as equally credible in this course. No student is disadvantaged, and no student is ever told to misstate their age or work around a platform's age gate.

## CRITICAL Compliance Note — Read Before Teaching

**LinkedIn requires account holders to be at least 16 years old.** This is LinkedIn's current stated minimum, and it is a floor, not a ceiling: some countries and regions set a higher minimum age, and some may require parental/guardian consent even above the platform minimum. Policies like this change, so:

- **Before class**, the instructor must independently verify LinkedIn's current age policy and any applicable local/regional age or consent requirements for the class roster's locations. Do not rely solely on this document or on prior cohorts' information — check LinkedIn's current terms/help center and any local guidance as of the day you teach this lesson.
- **In class**, state the rule plainly: LinkedIn is 16+, subject to local law that may set a higher age or require consent. Never present this as a suggestion — it is a hard eligibility rule.
- **Students below the applicable age must NOT create a LinkedIn account.** There is no workaround, no "just put a different birthdate," no exception. This must be said explicitly and without hedging.
- **The portfolio-first path is not a consolation prize.** Frame it as an equally credible, in some ways more flexible, professional presence — fully owned by the student, with no platform account required at all.

## Prep (Before Class)

1. **Verify current LinkedIn age policy** (see above) and note today's date of verification in your lesson log.
2. **Determine eligibility per student** before class starts, using whatever age/consent information the program already holds on file (do not ask students to disclose age live in class beyond confirming their own path). Prepare a simple two-column roster: Path A (LinkedIn-eligible) / Path B (portfolio-first) so you can address each group directly.
3. Confirm every student's Course 16 portfolio site is live and reachable — this lesson depends on it for Path B and for the demo.
4. Prepare the live demo materials: a fictional student profile mockup (see Demo section) — do NOT use a real LinkedIn account or a real person's profile on screen.
5. Have Canva, Google Docs, and the content-planning template ready to screen-share.
6. Load Student_Lesson.md and Worksheet.md for reference during discussion.

## Teaching Sequence

| Time | Segment |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:05 | Welcome, agenda, why this course exists (opportunity-building, not just "getting a job") |
| 0:05–0:15 | What is "professional presence"? Concept talking points |
| 0:15–0:22 | The LinkedIn age rule — stated plainly, no ambiguity |
| 0:22–0:30 | Two-path structure explained; students identify which path applies to them |
| 0:30–0:45 | Live demo: comparing a LinkedIn profile view vs. a portfolio-first presence page (fictional student) |
| 0:45–0:52 | Discussion questions |
| 0:52–0:57 | Activity: self-assessment (Worksheet Part 1) started in class |
| 0:57–1:00 | Recap, common misconceptions correction, close, submission instructions |

## Talking Points: What "Professional Presence" Means

- Professional presence is **everything a person can discover about you that speaks to your skills, interests, and reliability** — not one profile, one post, or one platform.
- It includes: how your work is described, what projects you can show, how easy you are to find, how consistent your story is across places, and whether what's public represents you accurately and positively.
- It is built through **repetition and consistency over time**, not a single setup session. A presence made once and abandoned decays; one updated after each project or milestone compounds.
- Key framing: **"Presence compounds like a reputation does."** Every project you add, every skill you document, every clear explanation you write makes the next person's first impression better and faster to form — the effect stacks.
- It matters for far more than job-hunting: mentorship requests, competition team invitations, scholarship applications, and collaborators finding you all depend on discoverability.
- Two paths, one goal: by the end of Course 18, every student — regardless of path — will have a professional presence that credibly shows their skills, projects, and growth.

## Talking Points: The Two-Path Structure

- **Path A (LinkedIn-eligible):** For students who meet LinkedIn's current minimum age (16+) and any stricter local/consent rule. They will build and maintain a LinkedIn profile across this course, in addition to keeping their portfolio site current.
- **Path B (portfolio-first):** For students who don't yet meet the applicable age/consent threshold, or who choose not to use LinkedIn. They will build a dedicated "presence page" on their existing portfolio site that does everything a strong LinkedIn profile does — headline, bio, skills, project showcase, and a way for people to reach them — without requiring any third-party account.
- State directly: **"If you're not old enough, or your family hasn't approved it, you do not create a LinkedIn account for this class. You will build an equally strong presence using your portfolio instead, and that is not a lesser option — it's a different, fully-owned option."**
- Every subsequent lesson in Course 18 will offer parallel instructions for both paths.

## Live Demo: Comparing Two Presences (Fictional Student)

Use a fictional student, "Sam K.," for both mock-ups. Never use a real profile.

**Mock-up 1 — LinkedIn profile view (built in Canva/slides, not a live account):**
- Headline: "Aspiring Software Developer | Python & Web Projects | Lumexa Student"
- About section: 2–3 sentences on interests and current focus
- Featured section: 2 project links with one-line descriptions
- Skills: Python, HTML/CSS, teamwork, problem-solving

**Mock-up 2 — Portfolio-first presence page (Sam's Course 16 site, new "Presence" page added):**
- Same headline styled as a page title
- Same About text
- A projects gallery with the same 2 projects, richer (screenshots, live links)
- A "Skills & Growth" section
- A simple contact form or email link — no third-party account needed

**Talking point during demo:** point out that the *content* is nearly identical — the difference is only the venue. This proves presence is about substance, not platform. Ask students: "What's actually different between these two? What's the same?" (Answer: contact mechanism and platform reach are different; substance, credibility, and effort are the same.)

## Discussion Questions

1. If someone searched your name today, what would they find — and is that an accurate picture of you?
2. Why might a portfolio-first presence actually give you *more* control than a LinkedIn profile?
3. What's one project you've already done that deserves to be part of your professional presence?
4. How might your presence need to look different in two years vs. today? What stays constant?
5. Why do platforms set age minimums like LinkedIn's 16+, and why is it important to respect them rather than work around them?

## Common Misconceptions to Correct

- **"I need LinkedIn to have a professional presence."** False — correct firmly: a portfolio-first presence is equally valid and, for this course, equally credited. LinkedIn is one venue among several, not a requirement.
- **"Presence just means being on one platform."** False — presence is the sum of everything discoverable about you (portfolio, projects, any profile, how you're described by others), not a single account.
- **"If I'm not old enough for LinkedIn, I'm behind."** False — reframe: portfolio-first students often build richer, more customized presences because they aren't constrained by a template.
- **"I'll just lie about my age to get an account."** Address directly and firmly: this is not permitted, not supported by the program, and not necessary — the portfolio-first path achieves the same goal without it.

## Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | Response |
|---|---|
| Student unsure which path applies to them | Instructor confirms using pre-class roster; never debate age eligibility live in front of the group — handle privately if needed |
| Student on Path B feels their option is "worse" | Reinforce equal-credibility framing; show the demo comparison again |
| Portfolio site from Course 16 is broken/offline | Pair with a buddy or flag for a quick fix before Lesson 2; do not let this block today's conceptual work |
| Student wants to sign up for LinkedIn "just to see" during class | Redirect: no account creation happens live in class; eligibility must be confirmed first, and today is about concepts, not sign-ups |
| Student confuses "presence" with "having a resume" | Clarify: presence is broader and ongoing; a resume is one static document, presence is a living, discoverable footprint |

## How to Review Student Work

- Confirm each student completed Worksheet Part 1 (eligibility self-check) accurately and chose a path.
- Confirm the path chosen matches the instructor's pre-verified roster (flag any mismatch privately, never publicly).
- Check that the reflection response describes professional presence in the student's own words, not a copy of the lesson text.
- Check that the goals section names a concrete, specific goal for what their presence should look like by Lesson 8 (not a vague "look professional").

## Lesson Close

- Recap: professional presence is broad, ongoing, and compounding — not one profile.
- Recap the age rule one more time, plainly: **LinkedIn is 16+, subject to stricter local/consent rules; below that, use portfolio-first — no exceptions.**
- Remind students both paths are graded and supported equally for the rest of Course 18.
- Assign: finish Worksheet.md (all three sections) before Lesson 2, and bring their portfolio site login/access.

## Lumexa — Digital Independence Path
### Course 18, Lesson 2: Build Your Professional Profile

---

## What You're Doing Today (and Why)

Last lesson, you figured out your values, goals, and a short brand statement. Today you're turning that into an actual professional profile — the thing a teacher, mentor, future employer, or collaborator sees when they look you up.

You'll be in one of two paths today:

- **Path A — LinkedIn:** You'll write a LinkedIn headline, About section, and one Experience/Education entry.
- **Path B — Portfolio-First:** You'll write the same content as a "presence page" — an About/intro section added to your Course 16 portfolio site.

**Both paths matter equally.** LinkedIn has a minimum age requirement, so not everyone in class will use it today — that's completely normal and not a downgrade. A well-written personal site does the exact same job: it tells people, clearly and honestly, what you can do.

The one rule for both paths: **everything you write has to be true.** No invented job titles, no made-up years of experience, no skills you can't actually demonstrate. Specific and true beats impressive and vague — every single time.

---

## Key Terms

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Headline** | A one-line summary (under a LinkedIn photo, or at the top of a portfolio page) that says what you do and where you're headed — in about 8 seconds of reading. |
| **About section** | A short, 4-part written introduction that explains who you are, what you can actually do, what you're working toward, and how someone can connect with you. |
| **Presence page** | The portfolio-site equivalent of a LinkedIn profile — usually your homepage or "About" page, combining an intro/About section with your existing project gallery from Course 16. |

---

## The Headline Formula

```
[What you do / are learning] + [specific tool, skill, or focus area] + [what you're curious about or working toward]
```

This works exactly the same whether it's a LinkedIn headline or the top line of your portfolio site.

**Weak example:** "10th grade student"
**Strong example:** "Aspiring web developer building projects in JavaScript — currently exploring how design and code work together."

Notice the strong version names a real skill and a real direction. It doesn't rely on your grade, age, or title to sound credible — it relies on specifics.

---

## The About-Section Formula

Four short paragraphs, in this order:

1. **Who you are** — 1–2 grounded sentences.
2. **What you can actually do** — 2–3 sentences about real things: a project you built, a class you took, a skill you've practiced. Nothing invented.
3. **What you're curious about or working toward** — shows direction, doesn't overclaim.
4. **How to connect / what you're open to** — an invitation, or a link to your portfolio.

---

## Worked Example — Both Paths (Fictional Student: Sam Okafor, 17)

Sam has completed Lumexa Courses 1–17, built a weather-tracking app (Course 12), has a live portfolio site (Course 16), and volunteers teaching Scratch to younger kids.

### Path A — LinkedIn Version

**Headline:**
> Aspiring software developer building real projects in Python and JavaScript — currently exploring data visualization and teaching coding basics to younger students.

**About section:**
> I'm a high school student who's spent the last year learning to build software that actually works, not just tutorials I follow along with.
>
> I've built a weather-tracking web app that pulls live data and displays it with custom charts, and a personal portfolio site to showcase my projects. I'm comfortable with Python and JavaScript fundamentals, and I'm learning how to write cleaner, more readable code as my projects get bigger.
>
> Right now I'm curious about data visualization and how software can make information easier to understand at a glance. I'd like to keep building projects that solve small, real problems.
>
> I also volunteer teaching basic coding (Scratch) to younger kids at my community center, which has taught me a lot about explaining ideas clearly. Open to connecting with other student developers and mentors in software.

**Experience entry:**
> **Volunteer Coding Instructor — [Community Center Name]**
> Teach introductory Scratch programming concepts to students ages 8–11 in weekly small-group sessions; developed simplified explanations of loops and conditionals for a younger audience.

### Path B — Portfolio Presence-Page Version

Same headline. Same About section, word for word — pasted as the intro/About section of the portfolio homepage, sitting just above the project gallery. Optionally, a simple Canva-designed header (photo or graphic + name + headline) sits above the text as a visual banner. The volunteer teaching role is added as a short line either inside the About text or as its own small "Experience" card on the site, using the exact same honest wording as the LinkedIn version above.

**The takeaway:** the writing doesn't change based on the platform. Only the container does.

---

## Step-by-Step Activity

1. Open your Google Doc worksheet (shared by your instructor).
2. **Draft your headline** using the formula above. Read it out loud — does it sound like you, or like a template?
3. **Draft your About section**, paragraph by paragraph, using the 4-part formula. For paragraph 2, only include things you could explain live if someone asked you about them right now.
4. **Path A:** Draft one Experience or Education entry describing a real project, class, or volunteer role. Use an accurate title — don't invent a position that doesn't exist.
   **Path B:** Confirm (or add) one project/experience entry on your site that uses the same honest, specific language.
5. Compare your draft to your Course 16 bio/brand statement. Does the tone and focus match? If not, decide which version is more accurate and adjust.
6. Raise your hand (or flag in chat) for an instructor check before you publish or save live.
7. **Path A:** Paste your reviewed headline and About section into LinkedIn.
   **Path B:** Add your reviewed About section to your portfolio site, optionally with a Canva header graphic.

---

## Knowledge Checks

1. What are the four parts of the About-section formula, in order?
2. True or False: A strong headline should just state your job title or grade level.
3. Why does the headline formula ask for a *specific* skill or tool instead of a general subject area (like "technology")?
4. A student writes: "I'm an expert in five programming languages." What's wrong with this claim, and how could it be rewritten honestly?
5. What is a "presence page," and how is it similar to a LinkedIn profile?

---

## Reflection Prompts

1. Which part of your About section was hardest to write honestly — the "what you can do" part, or the "what you're working toward" part? Why?
2. Read your headline out loud to yourself. Does it sound like something you'd actually say about yourself to a stranger? What would you change?
3. If you're in the Portfolio-First path: how did it feel to build this presence page instead of a LinkedIn profile? If you're in the LinkedIn path: what surprised you about writing for a professional platform?

---

## Submission Instructions

- Save your completed Google Doc worksheet (headline + About section + Experience/Education draft) — this is your record even after you publish.
- **Path A:** Once your instructor approves your draft, publish it to your LinkedIn headline and About fields, and add your Experience/Education entry.
- **Path B:** Once your instructor approves your draft, add it to your live portfolio site as your About/intro section.
- Submit the link to your finished profile (LinkedIn URL or portfolio URL) through your Lumexa student dashboard before the next class session.

## Lumexa — Digital Independence Path

### Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building
### Lesson 2: Build Your Professional Profile — Instructor Guide

---

## Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Course | 18 — Professional Presence & Opportunity Building |
| Lesson | 2 of course — "Build Your Professional Profile" |
| Age band | 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led (video classroom), synchronous |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Group size | Up to 12 students (recommended max for 1:1 feedback time) |
| Prerequisite | Course 18, Lesson 1 (values, goals, and personal brand statement drafted); Course 16 portfolio site live and bio/brand statement finalized |
| Tools used | LinkedIn (student-eligibility dependent), Canva, Google Docs |
| Student output | A live/drafted LinkedIn profile section (headline + About + one Experience/Education entry) OR a completed "presence page" section added to their Course 16 portfolio site |
| Instructor materials | This guide, shared Google Doc template (headline/about worksheet), Canva template link, sample fictional profiles (below) |

---

## Before You Teach This Lesson: LinkedIn Eligibility Check (Mandatory Prep)

LinkedIn's Terms of Service set a **minimum age of 16** to create an account. Policy details (minimum age, regional variation, and any account requirements) can change, so **verify current LinkedIn eligibility requirements before every cohort run** by checking LinkedIn's official Help Center / User Agreement — do not rely on prior-run notes. As of this lesson's last verification, the global minimum is 16, with some countries setting a higher local minimum.

This means every cohort will likely have a **split classroom**:

- **Path A — LinkedIn-eligible students** (16+ where LinkedIn permits, and who already have or are ready to create an account, with parent/guardian awareness per Lumexa's under-18 platform policy): build directly inside LinkedIn.
- **Path B — Portfolio-First students** (under LinkedIn's minimum age, in a region with a higher local minimum, or who simply prefer not to create a LinkedIn account yet): build an equivalent "presence page" on their existing Course 16 portfolio site. This is not a consolation prize — frame it explicitly as an equally professional, equally credible option. Many working adults are discovered through personal sites, not LinkedIn.

**You must confirm eligibility status per student before class**, ideally via the enrollment form or a pre-class Google Form. Do not ask students to self-report age live in front of the class. Have your student roster pre-tagged into Path A / Path B before the session starts.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

1. Write a headline that communicates *specific value*, not just a job title or grade level.
2. Write an About/intro section using a repeatable formula (who you are, what you can do, what you're looking for/curious about).
3. Translate one real, undramatized experience (school project, class, volunteer role, self-taught skill) into a credible profile entry — with zero fabrication.
4. Apply the same writing formulas to either a LinkedIn profile or a portfolio "presence page," recognizing they serve the same function.

---

## Materials Prep (Do Before Class)

- [ ] Confirm current LinkedIn minimum-age policy via LinkedIn's official Help Center page (do this fresh each term — do not assume last term's answer still holds).
- [ ] Confirm each student's Path A/B assignment from intake data.
- [ ] Duplicate the shared Google Doc "Headline + About Formula Worksheet" — one copy per student, or one shared doc with student-named sections.
- [ ] Have the Canva "Presence Page Header" template link ready for Path B students who want a visual banner/photo card for their portfolio.
- [ ] Pull up each student's Course 16 bio/brand statement (Path B needs this to check consistency; Path A benefits from it too).
- [ ] Have the two fictional worked examples (below) ready to screen-share.
- [ ] If demonstrating live LinkedIn, use a demo/instructor account — never demo inside a real student's account, and never require a student to make a LinkedIn account on the spot during class.

---

## Teaching Sequence (60 minutes)

### 1. Open & Frame (5 min) — Whole class together

Talking points:
- "Today we're not designing anymore — we're writing. Your profile's job is to make a stranger understand, in about 8 seconds, what you're capable of and what you're curious about."
- State plainly to the whole class: "Some of you will build this on LinkedIn today, and some of you will build it on your own portfolio site from Course 16. Both are real, professional, and valid — you're building the same thing, just on a different foundation. I'll tell you which group you're in."
- Announce path assignments (privately reference your pre-tagged roster; avoid saying *why* a student is in Path B out loud — just state the group).

### 2. The Two Formulas (10 min) — Whole class together

Teach both formulas once, since both paths use them identically.

**Headline formula:**
`[What you do / are learning] + [specific tool, skill, or focus area] + [what you're curious about or working toward]`

Example shape: *"Aspiring [field] student building [specific type of project] — currently exploring [specific skill/tool]."*

**About-section formula (4 short paragraphs):**
1. **Who you are** — 1–2 sentences, grounded and specific (age/grade optional, context helpful).
2. **What you can actually do** — 2–3 sentences citing *real* things: a project you built, a class you took, a skill you practiced. No invented job titles or years of "experience."
3. **What you're curious about / working toward** — shows direction without overclaiming.
4. **How to reach you or what you're open to** — e.g., "Open to connecting with other student developers" or a link to your portfolio.

Talking point: "Notice the formula never asks you to inflate anything. Specific and true beats impressive and vague, every time."

### 3. Live Demo — Write One Fictional Profile, Both Ways (12 min) — Whole class together

Screen-share and write live, thinking aloud, using the fictional student below (do not use a real student's identity). Write it once for LinkedIn (Path A shape) and once for a portfolio presence page (Path B shape), so both groups see their version modeled.

**Fictional student: Sam Okafor, age 17, has completed Lumexa Courses 1–17, built a weather-tracking app in Course 12 and a personal portfolio site in Course 16, volunteers teaching younger kids basic Scratch coding at a community center.**

*Path A — LinkedIn headline:*
> "Aspiring software developer building real projects in Python and JavaScript — currently exploring data visualization and teaching coding basics to younger students."

*Path A — LinkedIn About section:*
> I'm a high school student who's spent the last year learning to build software that actually works, not just tutorials I follow along with.
>
> I've built a weather-tracking web app that pulls live data and displays it with custom charts, and a personal portfolio site to showcase my projects. I'm comfortable with Python and JavaScript fundamentals, and I'm learning how to write cleaner, more readable code as my projects get bigger.
>
> Right now I'm curious about data visualization and how software can make information easier to understand at a glance. I'd like to keep building projects that solve small, real problems.
>
> I also volunteer teaching basic coding (Scratch) to younger kids at my community center, which has taught me a lot about explaining ideas clearly. Open to connecting with other student developers and mentors in software.

*Path A — one Experience/Education-style entry (LinkedIn "Experience" section):*
> **Volunteer Coding Instructor — [Community Center Name]**
> Teach introductory Scratch programming concepts to students ages 8–11 in weekly small-group sessions; developed simplified explanations of loops and conditionals for a younger audience.

Talking point: "Notice: 'volunteer,' not 'coding instructor at a company.' True title, true scope, no inflation."

*Path B — Portfolio presence-page intro (same student, no LinkedIn):*
> Screen-share how the *same content* becomes the opening section of a portfolio site — usually titled "About" or "Hi, I'm Sam" — sitting above the project gallery from Course 16.
> Reuse the identical 4-paragraph About text above, formatted as prose on the portfolio homepage, with a photo or Canva-designed header graphic and a line linking to the weather-tracking app project already on the site.

Key talking point to underline for the whole class: "The paragraph doesn't change based on which platform it lives on. What changes is the container. That's the whole lesson."

### 4. Guided Build Time — Split by Path (25 min)

Break students into two breakout groups (or two tabs if solo-paced with instructor rotating).

**Path A group (LinkedIn):**
1. Open LinkedIn (existing account or, if the family has already set one up outside class per Lumexa policy, that account — do not create new accounts live in class).
2. Draft headline using the formula, in the Google Doc worksheet first, then paste into LinkedIn.
3. Draft About section in the worksheet first (draft-then-paste avoids losing work and lets the instructor review before it's public).
4. Add one Experience or Education entry describing a real project, class, or volunteer role — exact title, no invented company or role.
5. Instructor rotates through breakout rooms for 1:1 spot checks (see "How to Review" below).

**Path B group (Portfolio-First):**
1. Open Course 16 portfolio site (published or draft).
2. Draft the "presence page" About/intro section in the worksheet, using the identical 4-part formula.
3. Decide placement: usually the homepage top section or a dedicated "About" page.
4. Optional: use Canva to design a simple header graphic or intro card (photo + name + one-line headline) to sit above the About text — this is the visual equivalent of a LinkedIn banner + headline.
5. Add or confirm one "project" or "experience" entry already on the site reads with the same specific, true language (cross-check against Course 16 project write-ups).
6. Instructor rotates through this group as well.

Instructor circulates between both groups throughout — do not leave one group unsupervised for the full 25 minutes.

### 5. Discussion (5 min) — Whole class together

Discussion questions:
- "What's one word you almost used in your About section that sounded impressive but wasn't quite true? What did you replace it with?"
- "If a stranger read only your headline, what's the one thing you'd want them to walk away knowing?"
- "Path A students: how is a LinkedIn profile different from a resume? Path B students: how is a presence page different from just a project gallery?"
- "Why do you think 'specific and true' works better than 'impressive and vague' — even for a recruiter skimming quickly?"

### 6. Lesson Close (3 min)

- Recap: "Every one of you now has a professional headline and About section written — whether it lives on LinkedIn or on your own site, it does the same job: telling the truth about what you can do, clearly."
- Preview next lesson: extending this presence with a recommendations/references or a "featured work" section.
- Reminder: nothing goes live/public without the instructor's review pass (see below) — worksheet drafts are saved for review before publishing.

---

## Common Misconceptions to Address Directly

1. **"My headline should just be my job title or grade level."**
   Correction: A title alone ("Student" or "10th Grader") tells a stranger nothing about what you can do. The headline's job is to communicate value and direction, not status.

2. **"My About section should list every skill I have."**
   Correction: A skill dump reads as generic and is hard to remember. Two or three concrete, demonstrated skills beat a list of twelve. Depth and specificity build more credibility than breadth.

3. **"If I don't have a 'real job,' I don't have anything to put here."**
   Correction: Class projects, self-taught skills, and volunteer work are real and legitimate. The formula is built specifically so non-employment experience fits naturally and honestly.

4. **"Portfolio-First is the fallback for people who couldn't get LinkedIn."**
   Correction (say this explicitly in class): Both paths produce a professional presence. Neither is lesser. Some adults deliberately choose a personal site over LinkedIn for their whole career.

---

## Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | What you'll see | Instructor response |
|---|---|---|
| Blank-page freeze on About section | Student stares at formula, writes nothing | Have them talk it out loud first — "just tell me what you built" — then transcribe their spoken words into paragraph 2 |
| Over-inflation ("I'm an expert in...") | Language claims mastery not yet demonstrated | Ask "Could you explain that to me right now, live?" — if not, soften language to "learning," "building," "exploring" |
| Under-selling ("I don't really know much") | Headline/About reads apologetic or empty | Point to a specific artifact (their Course 12 or 16 project) and ask them to describe *that thing* concretely — specificity replaces false modesty |
| Path B student feels "less than" Path A | Comments like "I wish I could just use LinkedIn" | Reiterate the presence-page framing from the demo; show that the same paragraph works in both containers |
| Path A student unsure what counts as an "Experience" entry | Leaves the section blank or invents a title | Confirm real activities (volunteering, tutoring, class project team lead) qualify; help them title it accurately (e.g., "Volunteer," not a fabricated job title) |
| Inconsistency with Course 16 brand statement | About section contradicts tone/focus set earlier | Pull up their Course 16 bio side-by-side; ask which version is more accurate and adjust the newer one to match |
| Technical friction inside LinkedIn's editor | Student can't find headline/About fields | Have a quick-reference screenshot ready (captured ahead of class, since LinkedIn's UI changes) rather than live-searching menus mid-lesson |

---

## How to Review Student Work (Instructor Checklist)

Before any student publishes to LinkedIn or their live portfolio site, check:

- [ ] Headline is specific (names a real skill/focus), not just a title or grade level.
- [ ] About section follows all 4 parts and contains no invented job titles, employers, years of experience, or credentials.
- [ ] Every claim in the About section maps to something the student can point to (a project, a class, a volunteer role) — ask the student to show you if unsure.
- [ ] Tone is consistent with the Course 16 bio/brand statement (not contradictory in focus area or voice).
- [ ] No personal contact information beyond what Lumexa's under-18 online-safety guidance permits is included (defer to platform safety policy on this — do not approve personal phone numbers, home addresses, or school names if policy restricts them).
- [ ] Path A only: Experience/Education entry uses an accurate real-world title (e.g., "Volunteer," "Student Project Lead") — not a fabricated position.
- [ ] Path B only: presence-page section is clearly placed and visually distinct (via Canva header or formatting) so it reads as an intentional "About" section, not buried text.

Only after this checklist passes should a student hit publish/save-live. Encourage students to keep the Google Doc draft as a backup record of what they wrote.

# Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building

## Lesson 3: Showcase Your Work

---

### What You're Doing Today

You already did the hard part back in Course 16 — you built real projects and wrote case studies about them. Today you make that work *visible*. You'll pick your 2–3 strongest projects and add them to your LinkedIn Featured section (or your portfolio page's Projects section, if you're using the portfolio-first path). Then you'll run the Portfolio Review Checklist on your own profile/page as a final polish before anyone else sees it.

### Why This Matters

A recruiter, mentor, or program reviewer looking at your profile decides whether to keep reading in the first few seconds. If your best work is buried, invisible, or unexplained, it doesn't count — it might as well not exist. A **showcase entry** is how you make sure your best work is the first thing a stranger sees, and that they understand it without needing to ask you a single question.

---

### How to Present a Project as a Showcase Entry

Every showcase entry has exactly three parts. Skipping any one of them weakens the whole entry.

| Part | What it does | How to write it |
|---|---|---|
| **Title** | Names the project and what kind of thing it is | Short — project name plus a 2–4 word type tag, e.g. "(App Concept)" or "(Website Build)" |
| **Result-focused description** | Tells a stranger what happened because of this project, not just what you did | 1–2 sentences. Include a real number or outcome if you have one (users, testers, time saved, a problem solved) |
| **Link** | Sends the viewer to real proof | A working, publicly viewable link to your case study doc, deck, image, or live project |

**Result-focused vs. task-focused — the key difference:**

- Task-focused (weak): *"I made a budgeting app using Canva for my class project."*
- Result-focused (strong): *"Designed a budgeting app prototype that 8 beta testers used for two weeks; 6 said it helped them track spending more consistently."*

The second version answers "so what?" The first one doesn't.

---

### Worked Example

**Fictional student:** Jordan R., 16, completed a Course 16 case study called "MoodBoard: A Daily Mood Tracker for Teens" — a mobile app mockup, tested with 10 classmates over one week.

**Showcase entry:**

- **Title:** MoodBoard — Daily Mood Tracker (App Concept)
- **Description:** Designed and mocked up a mood-tracking app aimed at teens; tested with 10 classmates over one week, with 8 saying it helped them notice mood patterns they hadn't before.
- **Link:** `https://docs.google.com/[Jordan's shared case study link]`

Notice: the title is short and specific, the description has a real number and a real outcome, and the link points straight at evidence — not just a claim.

---

### Step-by-Step Activity

1. **Open your Course 16 case study/project docs.** Reread them and rank your projects — which 2–3 have the clearest outcome or result attached?
2. **Draft your showcase entries on the Worksheet** for this lesson (title, description, link) before you touch your live profile. Drafting first means you won't publish a weak entry by accident.
3. **Check your link's sharing settings.** In Google Docs or Canva, set sharing to "Anyone with the link can view," then test the link in a private/incognito browser window to confirm a stranger could actually open it.
4. **Add the entry to your profile/page:**
   - *LinkedIn (16+):* Add profile section → Recommended → Add featured → Add a link → paste your case study link → edit the title and description fields to match your worksheet draft → Save.
   - *Portfolio-first (under 16):* Open your portfolio page → go to the Projects section → add a new entry block with title, description, and a "View Project" link → confirm the link is publicly viewable.
5. **View your profile/page as a stranger would.** On LinkedIn, use "View as public." On a portfolio page, open the link in an incognito window. Confirm the entry looks right and the link works.
6. **Run the Portfolio Review Checklist** (`Shared_Resources/Checklists/Portfolio_Review_Checklist.md`) against your whole profile/page. Make at least two edits based on what it turns up.

---

### Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Featured section** | The part of a LinkedIn profile built to highlight a small number of hand-picked posts, links, or media — not a full archive of everything you've done |
| **Showcase (entry)** | A single title + result-focused description + link, presenting one project as proof of a skill or outcome |
| **Result-focused description** | A description that states what changed or who was affected because of the project, rather than only listing the steps taken to build it |

---

### Knowledge Checks

1. What are the three required parts of a showcase entry?
2. Rewrite this task-focused sentence into a result-focused one: *"I built a website in Google Docs for my final project."*
3. True or False: The Featured section should include every project you've ever completed, so viewers see your full range.
4. Why is checking a link in an incognito/private window an important step before publishing a showcase entry?
5. Name one difference between the portfolio-first path and the LinkedIn path for adding a showcase entry.

---

### Reflection Prompts

1. Which of your Course 16 projects did you choose to feature, and what made it stand out from your other work?
2. What is one edit the Portfolio Review Checklist made you notice that you wouldn't have caught on your own?
3. If a stranger looked at your profile/page for 30 seconds, what do you want them to walk away thinking about you?

---

### Submission Instructions

Submit the following to your instructor by the end of class (or before the next session, per your instructor's deadline):

1. A link to your live LinkedIn profile (Featured section visible) or your portfolio page, showing at least one completed showcase entry.
2. Your completed Worksheet with all showcase-entry drafts and the final polish checklist section filled in.
3. One sentence naming the two edits you made after running the Portfolio Review Checklist.

# Instructor Guide — Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building

## Lesson 3: Showcase Your Work

### Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path → Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building |
| Lesson | 3 of course |
| Lesson Title | Showcase Your Work |
| Age Range | 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led (virtual classroom) |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Tools | LinkedIn (16+; students under 16 use the portfolio-first alternative), Canva, Google Docs |
| Prerequisite | Course 16 case studies/projects completed and saved (Google Docs or Canva); Course 18 Lesson 1 (profile setup) and Lesson 2 (headline/about section) completed |
| Reusable Resource | `Shared_Resources/Checklists/Portfolio_Review_Checklist.md` |

---

### Overview

By this point, students have a working LinkedIn profile or portfolio-first presence page and have written at least one strong case study back in Course 16. This lesson is about connecting the two: taking their best project work and presenting it publicly in a way that a stranger — a recruiter, a mentor, a program reviewer — could understand and be impressed by in under 30 seconds.

The core skill is **curation**: choosing 2–3 strongest pieces of work rather than dumping everything, and writing a short, result-focused description for each. Students will add these as entries to the LinkedIn "Featured" section (or the "Projects" section of their portfolio page for under-16 students), then run the full lesson closer: the **Portfolio Review Checklist**, applied to their own profile/page as a final polish pass.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Select their strongest 2–3 projects from their Course 16 case studies to feature publicly.
2. Write a title and a 1–2 sentence, result-focused description for each showcase entry.
3. Add showcase entries to the LinkedIn Featured section or their portfolio Projects section, each linked to supporting evidence (a doc, deck, image, or live link).
4. Run the Portfolio Review Checklist against their own profile/page and make at least two concrete edits based on it.

---

### Materials & Prep (do before class)

- [ ] Confirm each student's Course 16 case study doc/deck is accessible (Google Drive share settings, Canva "anyone with link can view").
- [ ] Have your own demo LinkedIn profile (or a portfolio page mockup) ready with a fictional student's info loaded — see "Live Demo" below. Do not use a real student's account for the demo.
- [ ] Open `Shared_Resources/Checklists/Portfolio_Review_Checklist.md` and have it visible to share your screen from.
- [ ] Pre-load the Student Lesson and Worksheet for this lesson so you can screen-share the worked example.
- [ ] Test that Canva templates for "featured project" thumbnails (if you use one) are shared to the class Canva team/folder.
- [ ] Know which students in your section are under 16 (portfolio-first path) vs. 16+ (LinkedIn path) so you can pair the right demo/instructions to each breakout.

---

### Teaching Sequence

| Time | Segment | Instructor Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:05 | Welcome + framing | State the goal plainly: "Today you turn your best Course 16 project into something a stranger can find and understand in 30 seconds." |
| 0:05–0:12 | Mini-lesson: Curation over completeness | Deliver the "best work prominently, not everything" talking point (below). Show a bad example (10 tiny screenshots, no context) vs. a good example (2 strong entries, each with a title, outcome, and link). |
| 0:12–0:20 | Anatomy of a showcase entry | Break down the three parts: title, result-focused description, link. Show 2–3 real-feeling examples. Contrast a "process description" with a "result-focused description." |
| 0:20–0:32 | Live demo: adding a case study to a profile | Screen-share the full add-to-Featured (or add-to-Projects) flow using the fictional student (below). Narrate every click. |
| 0:32–0:34 | Transition to work time | Explain the worksheet: draft 2–3 showcase entries from their own Course 16 work. |
| 0:34–0:48 | Independent/paired work time | Students draft entries on the Worksheet, then add at least one live to their actual profile/page. Instructor circulates (see Troubleshooting). |
| 0:48–0:56 | Portfolio Review Checklist pass | Students open `Portfolio_Review_Checklist.md` and run it against their own profile/page. Instructor walks the group through the checklist section by section, pausing for students to check items live. |
| 0:56–1:00 | Discussion + close | Run 2 discussion questions aloud, assign reflection prompts, state submission instructions, close. |

---

### Talking Points: "Show Your Best Work Prominently, Not Everything"

Use these as spoken script anchors, not a script to read verbatim.

1. **The 30-second test.** "Nobody scrolls through 15 projects to find the good one. Whoever looks at your profile decides in the first few seconds whether to keep looking. Your job is to put your best 2–3 pieces of work where they can't be missed — not to prove you were busy."

2. **Featured ≠ archive.** "The Featured section (or your Projects section) is not a filing cabinet for everything you've ever made. It's closer to a store window. A store doesn't put every item it owns in the window — it puts the items most likely to make someone walk in."

3. **Quality signal, not quantity signal.** "Three strong entries with clear results tell someone 'this person finishes things and can explain them.' Ten weak entries tell someone 'this person didn't know what to leave out' — which is a worse signal, even though it's more work to produce."

4. **Context is the whole point.** "A screenshot with no caption tells a viewer nothing. 'Built a budgeting app that helped 12 beta testers track spending in one week' tells them everything: what you built, who it helped, and what changed. Context is not decoration — it's the actual content."

---

### Live Demo Script: Adding a Case Study to a Fictional Student's Profile

**Fictional student for the demo:** *Amara Osei*, 17, completed a Course 16 case study titled "Track-It: A Study Habit Tracker for Teens," a mobile app mockup with a written case study covering problem, process, and outcome (12 beta testers used it over 2 weeks; 9 reported improved study consistency).

**LinkedIn path (16+):**
1. Open Amara's profile → click "Add profile section" → "Recommended" → "Add featured."
2. Choose "Add a link" (since the case study lives as a Google Doc with view access, or a Canva-exported PDF/link).
3. Paste the shareable link to the case study doc. LinkedIn auto-pulls a preview image and title — pause here and show students this can look wrong or generic, so it needs a fix.
4. Edit the custom title field to: **"Track-It — Study Habit Tracker (App Concept)"**
5. In the description field, add the result-focused description: **"Designed and mocked up a study-habit tracking app; tested with 12 peers over two weeks, with 9 reporting improved study consistency."**
6. Click "Save," then drag to reorder so this entry sits first/most prominent if Amara has more than one featured item.
7. Click "View as [public]" to confirm what a stranger actually sees, and check the link opens correctly in a new tab.

**Portfolio-first path (under 16), Google Docs/Canva-built page:**
1. Open Amara's portfolio page (a Google Doc formatted as a one-pager, or a Canva website/document).
2. Scroll to the "Projects" section.
3. Add a new entry block: Title → Description → "View Project" link (pointing to the shared Google Doc/Canva case study).
4. Same title and description as above.
5. Set sharing permissions on the linked doc to "Anyone with the link can view" and test the link in an incognito/private window to confirm it's actually accessible to someone without edit rights.

**Narrate while demoing:** call out the difference between what you clicked and *why* — e.g., "I'm checking the public view because what I see as the owner is not what a stranger sees. This is the single most skipped step."

---

### Anatomy of a Showcase Entry (for the mini-lesson)

| Part | Purpose | Bad example | Good example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Title | Names the project and its type in a few words | "Project 3" | "Track-It — Study Habit Tracker (App Concept)" |
| Description (1–2 sentences) | States the outcome/result, not just what was done | "Made an app in Canva for my coding class." | "Designed and mocked up a study-habit tracking app; tested with 12 peers over two weeks, with 9 reporting improved study consistency." |
| Link | Sends the viewer to real evidence | No link, or a broken/private link | A tested, publicly viewable link to the case study doc or live project |

---

### Discussion Questions

1. "If you only had room to feature ONE project, which one would you choose from your Course 16 work, and why that one over the others?"
2. "Read your description out loud. Does it tell someone what changed or what result happened — or does it just describe what you did? What's one word you could cut?"

---

### Common Misconceptions

**Misconception 1: "I should show everything I've ever made."**
Reality check: More entries dilute attention rather than adding it. Coach students to rank their Course 16 projects and pick the top 2–3 by strength of outcome, not by how much time they spent. If a student insists on including a weak project, ask: "What does this one add that the other two don't already show?" If they can't answer, it stays out of Featured (they can still keep it in a private working folder).

**Misconception 2: "Showcasing = just posting a screenshot with no context."**
Reality check: A screenshot alone answers "what does this look like" but not "why should I care." Every entry needs the title + result-focused description + link trio. If a student wants to post only an image, have them add the caption fields first — most platforms (LinkedIn Featured, Canva page blocks) support a title/description right alongside the image or link.

---

### Anticipated Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | What it looks like | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Can't decide which project to feature | Student stalls, tries to feature all of them | Ask: "Which one has the clearest number or outcome attached?" Numbers (testers, time saved, users) make the decision concrete. |
| Description reads as a task list, not a result | "I used Canva and Google Docs to make a tracker app for my project." | Ask: "What happened because you made this? Who used it? What changed?" Rewrite together live. |
| Case study link is private/broken | Link opens to a "request access" page | Walk through sharing settings together: Google Docs → Share → "Anyone with the link" → Viewer. Canva → Share → "Anyone with the link can view." |
| LinkedIn auto-preview looks wrong (blank image, wrong title) | Featured entry looks broken or unbranded | Show them the manual title/description override fields — the auto-pull is a starting point, not the final version. |
| Under-16 student unsure their portfolio page is public-facing | Page is Google-Doc-shaped and feels private | Confirm sharing is set to "Anyone with the link – Viewer" and test the link in an incognito window together. |
| Student wants to skip the checklist because they "already did it right" | Rushes past the review pass | Require at least one item from the checklist to be checked live before moving on — most students find at least one fixable gap. |

---

### How to Review Student Work

Use `Shared_Resources/Checklists/Portfolio_Review_Checklist.md` as the review instrument for this lesson — do not write a separate rubric. During the 0:48–0:56 block, walk the checklist section by section as a group, then during independent grading/spot-checks, confirm for each student:

- At least one Course 16 project is added as a showcase entry (LinkedIn Featured or portfolio Projects section).
- The entry has a title, a result-focused (not task-focused) description of 1–2 sentences, and a working, publicly viewable link.
- The student ran the Portfolio Review Checklist against their own profile/page and can name at least two specific edits they made as a result — vague answers like "it looked fine" mean the checklist wasn't actually applied and should be redone with you watching.

---

### Lesson Close

Recap in one sentence: "You just turned a project you already finished into proof that a stranger can find and understand." Confirm submission instructions (see Student Lesson) and preview Lesson 4's focus if applicable (expanding reach/network based on this presence). Thank the group and end.

lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Lesson 4: Share What You Know

**Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building**

## What This Lesson Is About

Today you're writing the first of five short pieces of content you'll create this course — your **Content Piece #1**. This isn't a resume, and it isn't a big formal essay. It's a short, honest post or note where you teach one small, specific thing you actually learned — a tip, a lesson from a project, or a mini-tutorial.

Depending on your track, this will eventually become:
- A **LinkedIn post** (if you're 16+ and using LinkedIn), or
- A **Notes/Blog entry** on your portfolio site from Course 16, or
- A **shared Google Doc** you can send to a teacher, mentor, or program you're applying to.

Today, you're just focused on writing it — formatting for your specific platform comes later.

## Why This Matters

Here's the one rule to remember for all five content pieces:

> **Teach something small and specific — don't try to sound like an expert on everything.**

Nobody trusts "I'm skilled in Python and problem-solving." Almost everybody trusts "I kept getting an error when someone typed a city name with a space in it, and here's the one-line fix that solved it." Specific, honest content is more convincing, more useful to readers, and — good news — much easier to write, because you already have the details. You just have to report them.

## The Content Formula

Every content piece you write, all five, can follow this same three-part formula:

1. **What I was doing** — the task, project, or situation. One or two sentences.
2. **What I learned or noticed** — the specific tip, insight, or mistake-turned-lesson. Two or three sentences. This is the heart of the piece — be concrete.
3. **Why it might help someone else** — one sentence connecting your experience outward to a reader who might face the same thing.

That's it. Three parts. If all three are there, you have a complete content piece.

## Worked Example: Jordan R.

Here's a fictional example from a student named Jordan, who just finished a small project building a to-do list app.

> **Testing your app's "empty state" actually matters**
>
> This week I built a simple to-do list app where you can add and check off tasks. It worked great — until I deleted every task and the app crashed with a blank error screen.
>
> I learned that I had only tested my app with tasks already in the list, so I never noticed that my code assumed there would always be at least one item. The fix was one `if` statement checking whether the list was empty before trying to display it.
>
> If you're building anything with a list — tasks, messages, search results — try emptying it out completely before you call it done. The "nothing here" case is easy to forget and easy to break.

Notice what this example does:
- **Hook**: the bolded opening line pulls the reader in with a specific, useful claim, not a generic one.
- **What I was doing**: one sentence, plain language, no jargon.
- **What I learned**: the specific detail (an empty list crashing the app, the one-line fix) — not "I learned a lot about coding."
- **Why it helps others**: a direct, actionable sentence any reader could apply.
- **Takeaway**: the closing line lands the point in one sentence anyone could remember.
- **Honesty**: Jordan doesn't claim to be an "expert in error handling." Jordan describes one true thing that happened.

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Content piece** | One complete short post, article, or note — the unit you're building 5 of this course. |
| **Hook** | The opening line or title that makes a reader want to keep reading — usually the most specific, concrete part of the piece stated up front. |
| **Takeaway** | The closing line that sums up the one useful point you want the reader to remember or act on. |

## Step-by-Step Activity: Draft Content Piece #1

1. **Pick your material.** Choose one real project, class exercise, or coding attempt from the last few weeks — big or small. It's fine if it's small.
2. **Fill in the three formula parts** using the Worksheet (What I was doing / What I learned / Why it might help someone else).
3. **Write a hook.** One sentence or short title that states your specific lesson up front.
4. **Write a takeaway.** One closing sentence that sums up the point.
5. **Assemble the draft.** Put hook → what I was doing → what I learned → why it helps → takeaway into one short piece, about 100–250 words.
6. **Run the self-check** (see Worksheet): does it sound honest and specific, or does it sound exaggerated or vague anywhere? Revise anything that doesn't pass.
7. **Save your draft** in your content-planning doc/sheet, ready for platform formatting in a later step.

## Knowledge Checks

1. What are the three parts of the content formula, in order?
2. True or False: A content piece should try to make you sound like an expert in as many skills as possible.
3. Which is a stronger opening line: "I am proficient in debugging methodologies" or "My app crashed every time a user typed an extra space — here's the one-line fix"? Why?
4. Why is a small, specific mistake-and-fix often *more* convincing content than a broad claim of skill?
5. Name the two "bookend" parts of a content piece that go at the very beginning and the very end.

## Reflection Prompts

1. What is one real, specific moment from your own coding work in the last few weeks that could become a content piece?
2. Think of a claim you were tempted to exaggerate in your draft. Why did you want to inflate it, and what happened when you scaled it back to the honest version?
3. Now that you've written content piece #1, what do you expect to be easier or harder about writing pieces 2–5?

## Submission Instructions

- Complete the Worksheet's "Content Piece #1 Draft" template in full.
- Save your draft in your content-planning doc/sheet (the same tool you'll use to track all 5 pieces).
- Do **not** publish it publicly yet — your instructor will review the draft first.
- Bring or share your completed Worksheet, including the tracker table for all 5 planned pieces, by the deadline your instructor gives in class.

# Instructor Guide

## Lesson Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path |
| Course | Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building |
| Lesson | Lesson 4: Share What You Know |
| Age Range | 15–18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led |
| Duration | 60 minutes |
| Tools | LinkedIn (16+) OR portfolio "Notes"/Blog section (Course 16 site) OR Google Docs; Canva; a content-planning doc/sheet |
| Prerequisite | Course 16 personal site or portfolio exists; Course 18 Lessons 1–3 completed (professional presence basics, profile/bio, goal-setting for opportunities) |
| Deliverable link | This lesson produces **Content Piece #1 of 5** required for the course's "5 pieces of professional content" milestone |

## Overview

Students write and prepare to publish the first of five short pieces of original content: a tip, a lesson learned from a project, or a mini-tutorial. The lesson centers on one repeatable formula so students never face a blank page, and on one core value: **teach something small and specific, honestly, rather than trying to sound like an expert on everything.** By the end, every student has a complete draft ready for final formatting and posting (LinkedIn post, portfolio Notes/Blog entry, or shared Google Doc, depending on their track).

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Explain why narrow, honest, specific content performs better and feels more authentic than broad, impressive-sounding claims.
2. Apply a three-part content formula (What I was doing → What I learned/noticed → Why it might help someone else) to a real experience of their own.
3. Draft a complete, honest, non-exaggerated content piece (100–250 words) ready for platform-specific formatting.
4. Identify red flags of exaggeration or vagueness in their own writing and revise them out.

## Prep Checklist (Before Class)

- [ ] Confirm each student's publishing track: LinkedIn post vs. portfolio Notes/Blog vs. Google Doc.
- [ ] Have the fictional "worked example" (Jordan R., see Student Lesson) ready to project or share.
- [ ] Open a blank doc/slide for the live demo — do not pre-write the demo draft; you will build it live in front of students.
- [ ] Have each student bring one recent project, class exercise, or personal coding attempt to draw content from (remind them a day ahead if possible).
- [ ] Have the Worksheet ready to share (digital or printable).
- [ ] Test screen-share/demo tool for Canva and Google Docs.

## Materials

- Student_Lesson.md (student-facing)
- Worksheet.md (Content Piece #1 Draft + tracker)
- A shared or projected copy of the Jordan R. example
- Access to Canva, Google Docs, LinkedIn, or portfolio Notes/Blog section per student track

---

## Teaching Sequence

### 1. Hook & Frame (5 min)
Open with a direct question: *"Has anyone ever explained something to a friend — a game trick, a recipe, a homework shortcut — and they said 'oh that's actually really helpful'?"* Take 2–3 answers. Point out: that is exactly what professional content is. Not a TED talk. Not a resume. One small useful thing, explained clearly.

State the lesson's core rule out loud and keep it visible the whole class:

> **Teach something small and specific. Don't try to sound like an expert on everything.**

### 2. Why This Matters (5 min)
Talking points:
- People (including future teachers, mentors, internship reviewers, or college admissions readers) trust specific stories over broad claims. "I debugged a loop that kept off-by-one errors and learned to test edge cases first" is more convincing than "I am skilled in Python and problem-solving."
- Specific content is also *easier to write* — you already have the details, you just have to report them.
- This piece is #1 of 5 for the course milestone. Getting a repeatable formula now saves time on pieces 2–5.

### 3. Introduce the Content Formula (5 min)
Write/display the three-part formula:

1. **What I was doing** — the task, project, or situation (1–2 sentences).
2. **What I learned or noticed** — the specific tip, insight, or mistake-turned-lesson (2–3 sentences).
3. **Why it might help someone else** — one sentence connecting it outward to a reader.

Emphasize: this is a formula, not a rulebook. Order can flex slightly, but all three parts should be present.

### 4. Live Demo: Drafting a Fictional Student's First Content Piece (15 min)
Do this live, out loud, showing your thinking — do not just present a finished piece.

- Invent (or use) a fictional student, e.g., "Marcus," who just finished a small project: a simple weather-lookup app in Course 15/16 that kept crashing when the user typed a city name with a space in it.
- Narrate your drafting process step by step:
  - "What was Marcus doing? Let's write that first, plainly." → *"I was building a small weather app that looks up a city and shows the forecast."*
  - "What did he learn?" Push for specificity: not "I learned about errors" but *"I learned that user input needs to be cleaned before it's used — I didn't expect someone to type 'New York' with a space and it broke my lookup until I added a simple `.strip()` and reformatted the string."*
  - "Why would this help someone else?" → *"If you're building anything that takes user text input, test it with spaces, weird capitalization, and typos before you assume it works."*
- Assemble the three parts into a short paragraph (100–150 words) live, reading it back and trimming filler.
- Add a **hook** (opening line) and a **takeaway** (closing line) — see Key Terms in Student Lesson — and show how they bookend the piece.
- Deliberately show one bad first draft that oversells ("I mastered debugging and became an expert in error handling") and revise it down to something honest and specific, so students see the correction happen, not just the end result.

### 5. Discussion Questions (5 min)
Ask and take answers from several students:
- "What's a small, specific thing you learned this month that you could explain in three sentences?"
- "What's the difference between 'I'm skilled in coding' and a specific story? Which would you trust more from a stranger?"
- "Why might a short, honest post actually be *more* impressive than a long, impressive-sounding one?"

### 6. Address Common Misconceptions (5 min)
Name these directly and correct them:

- **"I have nothing worth sharing."** Response: Everyone who has done any exercise, project, or even a tricky homework problem has something. The bar is not "invent something impressive" — it's "report one true, specific thing." Remind them of the demo: Marcus's content came from one bug.
- **"It needs to sound impressive or formal."** Response: Formal, stiff language usually makes content *less* trustworthy and harder to read. Plain, honest, conversational language explaining one real thing beats jargon every time. No inflated titles ("I engineered a robust solution") for small tasks.
- **"I need to wait until I've done something bigger."** Response: This is content piece 1 of 5 — the goal is to build the habit now with what they have today, not to wait for a impressive future project that may never feel "big enough."

### 7. Independent Work Time: Draft Content Piece #1 (15 min)
Students work through the Worksheet's fill-in template individually. Instructor circulates. See "Common Student Difficulties" and "Troubleshooting" below for what to watch for.

### 8. Self-Check & Peer Share (Optional, 3 min if time allows)
Students run their own draft through the Worksheet's "does this sound honest and specific?" self-check. If time allows, pair students to read one line of their draft aloud to each other.

### 9. Lesson Close (2 min)
- Recap the formula and the core rule once more.
- Remind students: this draft is not yet the final formatted post — formatting/publishing (Canva graphics if used, platform-specific posting) is covered in the next step of the course.
- Preview: "Next, you'll do this four more times — but now you have the formula, so it gets faster."
- Confirm submission instructions (see Student Lesson) and due date/time.

---

## Common Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | What it looks like | Instructor response |
|---|---|---|
| Blank page / "nothing to write about" | Student stares at worksheet, says they haven't done anything worth mentioning | Ask 3 quick questions: "What's something you built or fixed in the last 2 weeks in this course? What went wrong the first time? What did you change?" Almost always surfaces material. |
| Over-claiming / inflated language | Draft says "I'm now an expert in..." or "I mastered..." for a small task | Point to the core rule on the board. Ask: "Would you be comfortable if your instructor asked you three follow-up questions about this claim?" If not, scale the claim down to match the actual experience. |
| Too vague | "I learned a lot about coding" with no specifics | Ask: "What's the ONE specific line, error, or moment? Name it." Push for a concrete detail (a function name, an error message, a specific fix). |
| Sounds like a resume bullet, not a story | "Proficient in debugging methodologies" | Ask them to say it out loud to a friend first, then write down what they just said. Spoken language is usually more honest and readable than written "professional" language. |
| Missing the "why it helps others" line | Draft stops after describing what happened, with no outward connection | Prompt: "If a younger student read this, what would you want them to do differently because of it?" |
| Anxious about publishing publicly | Worried about being judged, especially on LinkedIn | Remind them: content piece is reviewed before anything is posted publicly (see below), and portfolio-first/Google Doc options exist if they're not comfortable with LinkedIn yet. |
| Confusing platforms | Unsure whether to write for LinkedIn tone vs. blog tone | Clarify: for this lesson, focus on the content itself (the three-part formula). Platform-specific formatting is a later step; today's draft works for any of the three tracks. |

## How to Review Student Drafts

When circulating or reviewing submitted drafts, check for:
1. **All three formula parts present** — task, learning, outward value.
2. **Specificity** — is there at least one concrete detail (a real tool, error, number, or decision)? Vague drafts get sent back with the "name the specific detail" prompt.
3. **Honesty check** — no claims of expertise/mastery disproportionate to the described experience. Flag words like "expert," "mastered," "guru" attached to small tasks.
4. **Length** — roughly 100–250 words. Too short usually means missing a formula part; too long usually means unnecessary padding or resume-style language creeping in.
5. **Hook and takeaway present** — opening line draws a reader in, closing line lands the point.
6. **Track-appropriate readiness** — LinkedIn-track drafts should read as a complete post; portfolio/Google Doc drafts should read as a complete short blog entry or note.

Do **not** require polish or perfect formatting at this stage — that is out of scope for this lesson. The bar is: complete, honest, specific, three-part draft.

## Lesson Close Script (Suggested)

"Today you wrote the first of five pieces of content — and you did it without needing a huge accomplishment to talk about. You used something real, kept it honest, and made it specific enough that someone else could actually use it. That's the whole skill. Next time, you'll do this again, faster, because you already know the formula."
