lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Lesson 5: Build a Professional Presence Beyond LinkedIn

## What This Lesson Is About

LinkedIn has an age minimum, and even if you're old enough, you might not have it set up yet — and that's completely fine. A real professional presence doesn't depend on one platform. It depends on whether the people who matter (teachers, mentors, competition judges, internship coordinators, scholarship reviewers, future employers) can find real, credible proof of what you can do.

**This lesson's core idea: a strong portfolio-first presence — built on your Course 16 site plus a few other channels — is not a smaller or "junior" version of a professional presence. It is equally credible.** A live project someone can actually see and try tells an evaluator more than a network profile ever could.

## Why This Matters

Adults who evaluate teenagers are not expecting a polished LinkedIn network. They're expecting to see specific, real, checkable evidence: a project you built, a competition you entered, a showcase you were part of, growth they can trace over time. Every student can build that, starting today, regardless of age or platform access.

## Presence Channels Beyond LinkedIn

| Channel | What it is | Why it builds credibility |
|---|---|---|
| **Portfolio site** (your Course 16 site) | A site you fully control, showing your projects, skills, and how to reach you | Direct evidence of real work — the single most important channel you own |
| **Content/notes section** | A simple, ongoing log on your portfolio site — short updates about what you're building and learning | Shows growth over time and recent activity, not a one-time snapshot |
| **School-sanctioned showcases & competitions** | Science fairs, hackathons, robotics leagues, app challenges, art/writing contests, class exhibitions | Third-party recognition — someone outside you vouched for the work |
| **Community project boards** | Places built for sharing specific kinds of work: GitHub for code, Behance for design, a class-wide showcase page or Padlet | Discoverability within a community of people who understand the work |
| **Referral networks** | Teacher recommendations, school mentorship programs, alumni-to-student introduction systems | Personal vouching from someone with credibility of their own |

You don't need every channel. You need a **primary channel** (usually your portfolio site) plus **one or two supporting channels** that reinforce it.

## Worked Example: Alex T., age 15

Alex is building a presence around web development, without LinkedIn.

- **Portfolio site:** `alext.lumexa.dev` — home page with a one-line bio, a projects page with two real sites Alex built (a chess-timer app and a local animal shelter's volunteer sign-up page), each with a short write-up of the problem solved and tools used.
- **Content/notes section:** Every two weeks, a short entry like *"Sept 1: Rebuilt the shelter sign-up form so it works on phones. Took a while to figure out why the layout broke on small screens — turned out to be a missing CSS unit."*
- **School showcase:** The shelter sign-up project was entered in Alex's school's community-impact tech fair and won "Most Useful Project."
- **Community project board:** Both projects are uploaded to Alex's class GitHub organization, where classmates and teachers can browse them.

Nowhere in this presence does Alex need LinkedIn. An evaluator looking at this sees real projects, visible growth, and outside recognition — everything a strong presence requires.

## Step-by-Step Activity

1. **Open your Course 16 portfolio site.** Check that it has: a bio, at least one real project with a description, and a way to contact you.
2. **Add or update your content/notes section.** Write two short entries (2–4 sentences each) about work you've actually done. Use this starter if you're stuck: *"This week I worked on ___. The hardest part was ___. Next I want to try ___."*
3. **Pick two channels beyond your primary one.** Look at the Presence Channels Map above. Choose one channel to strengthen this month (for example: submit a project to a school showcase, upload a project to a community board, or ask a teacher about a referral/mentorship program).
4. **Write one concrete next action for each channel you picked**, with a realistic date (this week or this month — not "eventually").
5. **Bring your updated site and your two next actions to class** for discussion and instructor review.

## Key Terms

- **Channel:** Any specific place or way that people can discover your work and skills — a website, a showcase, a competition, a community board.
- **Credibility:** How trustworthy your presence is to someone evaluating it — built through real evidence, specificity, and outside recognition, not through how many platforms you're on.
- **Discoverability:** How easy it is for the right person to actually find your work — a clear link, a searchable name, a listed project — regardless of which platform hosts it.

## Knowledge Checks

1. True or False: A professional presence is not real or complete unless it includes a LinkedIn profile.
2. Give one reason a live, working project on a portfolio site can be *more* convincing to an evaluator than a LinkedIn profile alone.
3. Name two presence channels, other than a portfolio site, that are open to students of any age.
4. What is the purpose of a content/notes section on a portfolio site?
5. Why does third-party recognition (like a competition placement or school showcase) strengthen credibility more than a self-written claim alone?

## Reflection Prompts

1. Which of your current presence channels feels strongest right now, and why?
2. If an internship coordinator or college admissions reader looked only at your portfolio site today, what would they learn about you — and what's missing?
3. What is one specific, dated action you're committing to this week to strengthen a presence channel beyond your portfolio site?

## Submission Instructions

Submit the following to your instructor by the start of the next lesson:
- The link to your updated portfolio site (with at least 2 content/notes entries added).
- Your completed Worksheet ("Presence Beyond LinkedIn"), including your channel-selection table and reflection.
- Come prepared to briefly share (1–2 sentences) the one channel you're strengthening this month.

# Instructor Guide — Lesson 5: Build a Professional Presence Beyond LinkedIn

## Metadata

- **Path:** Digital Independence Path → Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building
- **Lesson:** 5 of course — "Build a Professional Presence Beyond LinkedIn"
- **Age range:** 15–18
- **Format:** Live, instructor-led (video conferencing classroom)
- **Duration:** 60 minutes
- **Tools used:** Canva, Google Docs, a content-planning tool (Notion, Trello, or a simple spreadsheet — instructor's choice), the student's Course 16 portfolio site
- **Prerequisite:** Course 16 (Portfolio Building) completed — every student has a live portfolio site. Lessons 1–4 of Course 18 (resume basics, LinkedIn for eligible students, elevator pitch, networking etiquette).
- **Key constraint this lesson exists to solve:** LinkedIn requires users to be 16+ in most regions, and even eligible students may not have parental sign-off. This lesson gives every student — regardless of LinkedIn access — a complete, credible professional presence built on channels open to all ages.

## Lesson Overview

Many students will leave Lesson 4 (LinkedIn) believing that a real professional presence *requires* LinkedIn, and that anything else is a workaround for kids who "aren't old enough yet." This lesson directly corrects that. Students learn that a **portfolio-first presence** — a live site showing real, working projects, reinforced by school showcases, competitions, and community project boards — is not a substitute for LinkedIn. It is a different, equally credible way of being discoverable and trustworthy to the people who matter: teachers, mentors, competition judges, scholarship committees, internship coordinators, and future employers who will Google a name long before they check a professional network.

By the end of this lesson, every student — LinkedIn-eligible or not — will have:
1. A clear map of presence channels beyond LinkedIn and what each one is *for*.
2. A strengthened version of their Course 16 portfolio site, including a simple content/notes section.
3. A concrete plan to add at least one school-sanctioned showcase or community channel to their presence.

## Instructor Prep (before class)

- [ ] Confirm every student's Course 16 portfolio URL is reachable. Spot-check 3–4 in advance; note any broken links or stale content to reference (anonymously) during the demo.
- [ ] Have the fictional example ("Priya's presence") open in a browser tab, built in Canva/Google Docs beforehand — see Live Demo section below for full content.
- [ ] Prepare a shared Google Doc or slide with the "Presence Channels Map" (table in Student Lesson) ready to screen-share.
- [ ] Have a content-planning tool open (Notion/Trello/spreadsheet) to demonstrate planning a content/notes section live.
- [ ] Look up 2–3 real, age-appropriate examples relevant to your region/school to mention as "other professional communities appropriate for teens": school or district STEM/arts showcases, competitions (science fairs, hackathons for teens, robotics leagues, Congressional App Challenge, Scholastic Art & Writing Awards, local youth entrepreneurship pitch nights), community project boards (GitHub for code projects, Behance for design, a class-wide showcase page), and school-run alumni/referral networks or teacher recommendation systems. Do not require LinkedIn substitutes that also carry age minimums — verify each option's terms before recommending it.
- [ ] Review each student's roster note (if available) for LinkedIn-eligibility status, so you can privately tailor encouragement without singling anyone out publicly.

## Teaching Sequence (60 minutes)

### 1. Open + Reframe (8 min)
Start with a direct question to the group: "If you Googled your own name right now, what would show up?" Take 2–3 verbal answers. Pivot: "Today isn't about LinkedIn. It's about everything else that makes you discoverable and credible — and the truth is, for most of you, these other channels will matter *more* than LinkedIn does for years." State the lesson's thesis plainly: **a strong portfolio-first presence is not a fallback. It's a legitimate, complete professional presence on its own.**

### 2. Talking Points: Why Portfolio-First Is Equally Credible (10 min)
Deliver these points, inviting brief reactions after each:

- **A live, working project speaks louder than a network profile.** A LinkedIn headline says "aspiring developer." A portfolio site with a working app, the code behind it, and a short write-up of what was hard and what was learned *proves* it. Anyone reviewing candidates — a judge, a recruiter, an admissions reader — trusts evidence over description.
- **Discoverability doesn't require one specific platform.** What matters is that the work is *findable* and *presentable* — a clean URL that can go on a resume, a QR code on a poster, a link in a competition submission. A portfolio site does this as well as, or better than, a social network profile, because it's fully under the student's own control.
- **Credibility comes from specificity, not size of network.** A student with 12 LinkedIn connections is not more credible than a student with zero LinkedIn connections and three well-documented projects, a competition placement, and a showcase feature. Adults evaluating teenagers know this — they are not expecting a professional network; they are expecting to see real effort and real thinking.
- **School-sanctioned showcases and competitions carry independent institutional credibility.** A science fair placement, a hackathon finish, or being featured in a school showcase is verifiable and often more impressive to an evaluator than an unverified social profile, precisely because a third party (the school, the competition) vouched for it.
- **This approach also ages well.** The habits built now — documenting projects, writing clearly about your own work, keeping a content/notes section current — are the same habits that make a LinkedIn profile strong later. Nothing here is wasted once a student turns 16 or 18.

### 3. Live Demo: A Strong Portfolio-First Presence (15 min)
Screen-share the fictional example below. Walk through each section, narrating *why* it works.

> **Fictional student: Priya Nandakumar, age 15, aspiring game developer**
>
> **Portfolio site (from Course 16), lumexa-hosted at `priyan.lumexa.dev`:**
> - **Home page:** One-line bio ("15-year-old game developer building small, weird, playable things"), a photo or avatar, links to her top 3 projects.
> - **Projects page:** Three projects, each with a 1-paragraph description, the problem it solved, tools used (Unity, C#), a screenshot or short gameplay clip, and a link to the code repository.
> - **New: Notes/Content section** — a simple running log, updated every 2–3 weeks: short posts like *"Week of Sept 8: Finished the enemy AI for Comet Chase. Here's what I got wrong the first time and how I fixed the pathfinding bug."* This is not a blog in the adult-influencer sense — it's a lightweight, low-pressure devlog that shows growth over time and gives evaluators something fresh to find.
> - **About/Contact page:** Grade level, school (if the student is comfortable sharing), a school-appropriate contact method (a monitored email, or a contact form), and a note: "I'm looking for summer coding programs and game jam teams."
>
> **Beyond the site:**
> - Placed 2nd in her school's regional Congressional App Challenge with Comet Chase — mentioned on the site's home page and projects page, with a link to the challenge's public results page as third-party proof.
> - Project uploaded to her school's community project board (a shared class showcase site) where teachers and other students can see it.
> - Entered in her school's spring STEM showcase; the showcase program (a printed/digital event booklet) lists her name and project — she added a photo of the booklet page to her site.

Ask: "What makes this credible, even with zero LinkedIn?" Draw out: verifiable outside recognition (the competition, the showcase), visible growth over time (the notes section), and specific, checkable claims instead of vague ones.

### 4. Guided Practice: Strengthen Your Own Presence (18 min)
Students open their own Course 16 portfolio sites plus a content-planning tool.
1. **Audit (5 min):** Each student checks their site against a 4-item checklist (displayed on screen): Does it have (a) at least one real project with a description, (b) a way to contact you, (c) any third-party proof of skill (competition, showcase, class recognition), (d) any sign of recent activity?
2. **Add a content/notes section (7 min):** Using Google Docs or directly in their site editor, students draft their first 2 notes/log entries about a project they've already done. Instructor circulates to help students who freeze on "what counts as worth posting" — anything specific and true counts.
3. **Pick two channels to strengthen (6 min):** Using the Presence Channels Map (from the Student Lesson), each student identifies one primary channel beyond their portfolio (a school showcase, competition, or community board) and one action they'll take this week (e.g., "submit my robotics project to the district showcase by Friday").

### 5. Discussion Questions (5 min)
Pose 2–3 of these to the full group:
- "Which channel on the map feels most realistic for you to use in the next month, and why?"
- "If a college admissions reader or an internship coordinator only had your portfolio site to go on — no LinkedIn, no social media — would it tell them who you are? What's missing?"
- "Why might a competition placement or school showcase feature actually be *more* convincing to an adult evaluator than a LinkedIn profile with a lot of connections?"

### 6. Lesson Close (4 min)
Restate the thesis: "You do not need LinkedIn to have a real professional presence. What you need is evidence — real projects, documented growth, and outside recognition — and every one of you can build that starting today." Preview next lesson (typically: pulling all presence channels together into a simple personal "opportunity radar" for ongoing discovery of programs, competitions, and mentors). Assign the take-home activity from the Student Lesson.

## Common Misconceptions to Address Directly

- **"Without LinkedIn, I don't have a real presence."** Correct this explicitly and early. A real presence is defined by *evidence of real work being discoverable*, not by which specific platform hosts it. LinkedIn is one tool for this; it is not the definition of it.
- **"Portfolio-first is just for younger students who aren't old enough for LinkedIn yet."** Correct this directly: portfolio-first is not a junior version of a "real" presence — it is the foundation every strong professional presence is built on, LinkedIn or not. Many working professionals with fully active LinkedIn profiles still lead with a portfolio site because it's where the actual proof lives. Point back to the Priya example: nothing about her presence is "less than" — it's simply built on different, equally strong channels.
- **"A school showcase or class project board doesn't count as 'professional.'** Reframe: professional means credible and discoverable to someone evaluating you, not "adult-only." A juried school showcase or a public competition result is exactly as verifiable as a corporate reference.

## Anticipated Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | What it looks like | Instructor response |
|---|---|---|
| "I don't have any competitions or showcases at my school." | Student feels stuck with no institutional channel. | Redirect to community project boards (GitHub, a class Padlet/showcase site, a subject-specific student competition run online, national contests open to individual entry regardless of school). Not every channel requires school sponsorship. |
| Blank content/notes section — "I don't know what to write." | Freeze on tone or perceived need for polish. | Model that entries can be short, plain, and imperfect — a devlog, not a press release. Give a sentence starter: "This week I worked on ___. The hardest part was ___. Next I want to try ___." |
| Portfolio site is stale or was never finished from Course 16. | Broken links, empty sections, no projects. | Have the student fix the single most visible issue today (home page bio + one real project) rather than trying to perfect the whole site in one session; assign the rest as follow-up. |
| Overreliance on one strong channel, ignoring others. | Student has a great portfolio but no plan to add a second channel. | Use the guided practice's "pick two channels" step to require diversification — one deep channel plus one broadening channel. |
| Comparing themselves to peers with LinkedIn access. | Discouragement, "mine feels less official." | Reaffirm the lesson thesis one-on-one; point to the credibility talking points (verifiable evidence > network size). |

## How to Review Student Work

For each student, check:
1. **Content/notes section exists and has at least 2 entries** that are specific (mention a real project, a real problem, or a real result) — not generic filler like "worked on stuff this week."
2. **At least one channel beyond the portfolio site is identified**, with a concrete, dated next action (not "look into it sometime").
3. **The student can articulate, in their own words, why their presence is credible** without LinkedIn — listen for mention of evidence, third-party recognition, or documented growth during discussion or in their reflection prompts.
4. Flag (privately, supportively) any student whose portfolio site still has no real project attached — this is the one item to prioritize before the next lesson.

## Lesson Close (recap for instructor pacing)
End on the reframed thesis and the concrete next step every student is taking this week. Confirm the worksheet is either completed in class or assigned with a clear due date before Lesson 6.

# Lesson 6: Networking and Professional Communication

**Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building — Digital Independence Path**

## What Is Networking, Really?

Forget the awkward image of "networking" you might have in your head — messaging strangers, forcing small talk, asking people you don't know for favors. That's not what this lesson is about, and it's not good networking anyway.

**Real networking, at your age, means staying in touch with people who already know you** — in a way that's clear, respectful, and genuine. It's your former teacher, a coach, a family friend who works in a field you're curious about, or an instructor from a program you took. You already have a network. This lesson is about using it well.

## Why It Matters

People are far more likely to help, advise, or remember someone they already have a real connection to than a stranger who messaged them out of nowhere. A short, thoughtful message to someone who knows you will almost always get a warmer response than a generic message blasted to fifty strangers. **Quality beats quantity, every time.**

## Networking Is NOT

- Messaging strangers you found online because they have a job you want.
- Copy-pasting the same message to dozens of people.
- Asking someone you just met for a big favor right away.
- Something you do without a trusted adult knowing.

## Safety Norms (Know These Before You Send Anything)

1. **A trusted adult (parent, guardian, or your instructor) should know about any outreach message before or as you send it.** This isn't about "asking permission" like you're a little kid — it's a normal professional practice: even adults loop in a mentor before an important email.
2. **You never meet someone from an online or written introduction in person alone.** If a conversation ever leads toward meeting up, that only happens with a trusted adult involved in the plan.
3. **LinkedIn requires you to be 16 or older.** If you're under 16, or you or your family prefer not to use it, you'll build the exact same skills using a personal portfolio page or a one-page PDF resume plus email — that path is just as legitimate.
4. **Never share your address, school schedule, passwords, or financial information** in an outreach message, no matter who it's to.
5. **If a reply ever feels strange, pushy, or makes you uncomfortable — stop responding and tell a trusted adult right away.** That is always the right move, never something to feel embarrassed about.

## The Introduction Message Formula

A good outreach message is short — usually 80-150 words — and follows this shape:

1. **Greeting + who you are + shared context** (how do they know you?)
2. **Genuine reason for reaching out** (why them, why now?)
3. **A small, specific, low-pressure ask** (or no ask at all — just reconnecting counts)
4. **Gracious close + your full name**

That's it. No hard sell, no long life story, no big ask on the first message.

## Worked Example

**Scenario:** Jordan R., 17, wants to reconnect with Ms. Alvarez, who taught Jordan's sophomore-year Intro to Coding elective, to ask a quick question about a summer program.

**Jordan's message:**

> Subject: Question from a former student — Jordan R.
>
> Hi Ms. Alvarez,
>
> I hope your school year is off to a good start! This is Jordan Reyes — I was in your Intro to Coding elective sophomore year (I sat near the front, and did the maze-solving robot project).
>
> I'm applying to a summer coding program this year and remembered how much I enjoyed your class. Would you be open to answering one or two quick questions about how you got started in tech, whenever you have a few minutes? No pressure at all if you're busy — I completely understand.
>
> Thank you for considering it, and I hope you're doing well!
>
> Best,
> Jordan Reyes

**Ms. Alvarez's reply (a few days later):**

> Hi Jordan,
>
> So good to hear from you — I remember that robot project well! Happy to help. Feel free to send your questions over whenever, or we could do a quick 15-minute call if that's easier. Good luck with the application!
>
> Ms. Alvarez

**Jordan's follow-up (same day):**

> Hi Ms. Alvarez,
>
> Thank you so much for getting back to me! A quick call would be great if you have time — I'll let my mom know so she can help me find a time that works, and I'll send a couple options over email.
>
> Thanks again,
> Jordan

Notice: Jordan mentions a trusted adult naturally as part of arranging a call — not as an afterthought. That's normal, professional, and safe, all at once.

## Activity: Draft Your Own Introduction Message

1. **List 3-5 real people already in your network** — a teacher, coach, family friend, relative, or past instructor. (Use the Worksheet to help brainstorm.)
2. **Pick one person** you'd genuinely like to reconnect with or ask a small question.
3. **Draft one real message to them** using the formula above, in a Google Doc.
4. **Decide how you'll loop in a trusted adult** — before you send it, share the draft with a parent/guardian or your instructor for a quick look.
5. Do **not** send the message during class. Take it home, get it reviewed, and send it with a trusted adult's awareness.

## Key Terms

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Networking** | Building and maintaining genuine professional relationships with people you know or are warmly introduced to — not mass-messaging strangers. |
| **Warm introduction** | Being connected to a new person through someone you already know and trust, rather than reaching out cold. |
| **Professional etiquette** | The expected norms of polite, clear, respectful communication in a professional context — tone, timing, gratitude, and follow-up. |

## Knowledge Check

1. What is the main difference between networking and mass cold-messaging?
2. List the four parts of the introduction message formula in order.
3. True or False: You should ask for a big favor (like a job or internship) in your very first message to someone. Explain your answer.
4. Why should a trusted adult know about your outreach messages before you send them?
5. If you don't hear back from someone after a message, what should you do?

## Reflection Prompts

1. Who are 1-2 people already in your life who could be part of your professional network, and why did you pick them?
2. Think about a message you've received (from a friend, a group chat, an ad) that felt too pushy or impersonal. What made it feel that way, and how will you avoid that in your own outreach?
3. Why do you think "quality over quantity" is true for networking, even though it might feel slower or less impressive than reaching out to lots of people?

## Submission Instructions

Share your Google Doc containing:
- Your list of 3-5 real network contacts (from the Worksheet)
- Your one drafted introduction message
- A one-sentence note on who your trusted adult is and how/when you'll share the draft with them

Submit the shared Google Doc link through your Lumexa dashboard for this lesson. Remember: **do not send your message before a trusted adult has seen it.**

# Instructor Guide

## Lesson Metadata

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Path | Digital Independence Path |
| Course | Course 18: Professional Presence & Opportunity Building |
| Lesson | Lesson 6: Networking and Professional Communication |
| Age range | 15-18 |
| Format | Live, instructor-led (video conference), 60 minutes |
| Tools used | LinkedIn (16+ only; portfolio site/PDF resume as alternative for under-16 or those who opt out), Google Docs, Email |
| Prerequisites | Lesson 1-5 of Course 18 (student has a draft resume/portfolio and understands online safety basics from the Digital Independence Path's earlier privacy lessons) |
| Group size | Best with 6-16 students to allow discussion and message review |
| Materials students need | A laptop/device, an existing email account, access to Google Docs, list of 3-5 real people they already know (teacher, family friend, coach, past instructor, relative) |

## Lesson Overview

This lesson reframes "networking" for teenagers away from the anxiety-inducing, transactional image many of them have absorbed (cold LinkedIn messages, "hustle culture" content, mass outreach). Instead, students learn that professional networking at this age is about **nurturing real relationships they already have** — teachers, coaches, family friends, alumni of their school, instructors from Lumexa or other programs — and communicating with them respectfully and clearly.

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

1. Explain the difference between networking and cold/mass messaging strangers.
2. Identify 3-5 real, existing contacts appropriate for professional outreach.
3. Write a polite, well-structured introduction or outreach message using a repeatable formula.
4. Apply professional communication etiquette (tone, timing, follow-up, gratitude) across email, Google Docs comments, and LinkedIn.
5. State the lesson's safety norms from memory and apply them to their own outreach plan.

## Safety Framing (Non-Negotiable — Read Before Class)

This lesson is about **existing, known, real-world connections** — not meeting or messaging strangers. Instructors must not let the lesson drift into "add strangers on LinkedIn to grow your network" territory. Reinforce constantly:

- Every outreach message a student plans to send should be **known to a trusted adult** (parent, guardian, or the instructor) before or as it is sent.
- Students **never** arrange to meet anyone from online outreach in person alone. If an outreach contact suggests meeting, a trusted adult is involved in planning it (and in practice, at this age, almost all "networking" contact stays in writing/video, not in-person solo meetings).
- LinkedIn has a **16+ minimum age**. Under 16, or any student/family who prefers not to use LinkedIn, uses the portfolio-first alternative (a personal portfolio site or PDF one-pager + email) instead. Do not pressure any student to create a LinkedIn account.
- Students should never share home address, school schedule/location details, financial information, or passwords in any outreach message.
- If any contact's reply ever feels off, pushy, overly personal, or makes a student uncomfortable, the instruction is simple: **stop responding and tell a trusted adult immediately.** This is not a failure on the student's part — it is the correct, expected action.

## Prep Before Class

- Review each student's Course 18 portfolio/resume draft from prior lessons so you can reference it during the demo.
- Have the fictional demo exchange (below) open and ready to screen-share.
- Confirm which students have parental permission for LinkedIn (16+) vs. who will use the portfolio-first path — do not assume.
- Open a blank Google Doc to model live message-drafting.

## Teaching Sequence

### 1. Warm-Open & Reframe (5 min)
Ask: "When you hear the word 'networking,' what comes to mind?" Expect answers like "awkward," "asking strangers for jobs," "LinkedIn spam," "used-car-salesman energy." Validate that this reaction is common and reasonable — because most of what teens see modeled online *is* that.

Reframe: "Real networking, especially at your age, is just **staying in touch with people who already know you, in a way that's clear and respectful.** It's not messaging 500 strangers. It's writing one thoughtful message to your old robotics coach."

### 2. Networking vs. Mass Cold-Messaging (8 min)
Present the contrast directly (write on shared screen or slide):

| Networking (what we do) | Mass cold-messaging (what we don't do) |
|---|---|
| Reaching out to someone who already knows you or is one warm introduction away | Messaging strangers you have no connection to, hoping one responds |
| One thoughtful, specific message | Copy-pasting the same generic message to dozens of people |
| A real reason tied to a shared context ("you taught my Intro to Python class") | No context, just "let's connect" |
| No immediate ask, or a small, specific, low-pressure ask | Asking a stranger for a job/favor immediately |
| Trusted adult is aware | No one else knows the outreach is happening |

Talking point: "Quality over quantity isn't just etiquette — it's what actually works. One genuine message to your former teacher who remembers you will get a warmer, more useful reply than fifty generic messages to strangers who don't know you and have no reason to respond."

### 3. Live Demo: A Polite Introduction Message (12 min)
Screen-share a Google Doc. Build the message live, narrating each choice, using the fictional example below (also in the Student Lesson).

**Scenario:** Jordan R., 17, wants to reach back out to Ms. Alvarez, who taught Jordan's sophomore-year intro coding elective, to ask a small, specific question about a summer program.

**Demo message (write it live, line by line, narrating why):**

> Subject: Question from a former student — Jordan R.
>
> Hi Ms. Alvarez,
>
> I hope your school year is off to a good start! This is Jordan Reyes — I was in your Intro to Coding elective sophomore year (I sat near the front, and did the maze-solving robot project).
>
> I'm applying to a summer coding program this year and remembered how much I enjoyed your class. Would you be open to answering one or two quick questions about how you got started in tech, whenever you have a few minutes? No pressure at all if you're busy — I completely understand.
>
> Thank you for considering it, and I hope you're doing well!
>
> Best,
> Jordan Reyes

Narrate the structure as you go: **who you are + shared context → genuine reason for reaching out → small, specific, low-pressure ask → gracious close → full name.** Point out what's absent: no attachment of personal documents yet, no request for a job, no urgency/pressure language, no personal contact info beyond what's needed.

Then show a **sample reply** and model a **thank-you follow-up** (see Student Lesson worked example) so students see the full loop, not just the opening message.

### 4. Etiquette Across Tools (8 min)
Briefly cover tool-specific norms:

- **Email:** Clear subject line, greeting, sign-off with full name, check spelling/tone before sending, reply within a few days if you receive a reply.
- **Google Docs (comments/shared drafts):** When commenting on a shared doc (e.g., a mentor reviewing your resume), keep comments specific and gracious ("Thanks for catching that — fixed!"), don't @-mention people repeatedly, resolve comments once addressed.
- **LinkedIn (16+ only):** Always send a connection request with a short personal note (never blank), use real name and a professional-looking photo or none at all, keep the profile portfolio-first (projects, skills) rather than treating it like a general social feed.
- **Portfolio-first alternative (under 16 / opt-out):** A one-page site or PDF resume + email is fully equivalent for this lesson's purposes — reassure students this is not a lesser option.

### 5. Guided Activity Launch (15 min)
Students open their own Google Doc (from the Worksheet) and:
1. List 3-5 real people from their existing network.
2. Pick one.
3. Draft one real introduction/outreach message using the formula.
4. Note how/when they'll tell a trusted adult about this outreach (before sending, ideally).

Circulate (or use breakout rooms if virtual) to review drafts one-on-one. Do **not** let students send the message during class — the message should go home for trusted-adult review first, unless a parent/guardian is present and reviewing live.

### 6. Discussion Questions (Weave in during activity or close, ~7 min total)
- "Why might a short, specific message get a better response than a long, vague one?"
- "What's the difference between asking someone to 'grab coffee and pick their brain' and asking one clear question?"
- "If someone you reached out to never replies, what should you do? What should you *not* do?" (Answer: it's fine, people are busy; don't send repeated follow-ups or take it personally; one polite follow-up after 1-2 weeks is the max.)
- "Why does a trusted adult need to know about this kind of outreach, even though it feels like 'just an email'?"

### 7. Lesson Close (5 min)
Recap the three big ideas: (1) networking = nurturing real, existing relationships, not mass-messaging strangers; (2) a good message is short, specific, and low-pressure; (3) a trusted adult is always in the loop on outreach. Preview that Lesson 7 will build on this by covering how to follow up and keep in touch over time.

## Common Misconceptions to Correct

- **"Networking means messaging as many people as possible."** Correct: one genuine message beats dozens of generic ones; quality and relevance matter far more than volume.
- **"I need to ask for something big right away (a job, an internship, a recommendation)."** Correct: the first message should have a small, low-pressure ask, or no ask at all beyond reconnecting — trust and relationships are built over multiple respectful interactions, not one transactional request.
- **"If I don't have a 'real' professional connection, I have no one to reach out to."** Correct: teachers, coaches, relatives' colleagues, past instructors, and school alumni all count as real network contacts at this age.
- **"Not hearing back means I did something wrong."** Correct: busy adults often don't reply immediately or at all; it is not personal and does not require an apology-toned follow-up.

## Anticipated Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | Instructor Response |
|---|---|
| Student can't think of anyone to list | Prompt with categories: teachers/coaches, family friends in any job, relatives, past camp/program instructors, school alumni they've met. Everyone has at least 2-3. |
| Message drafts are too long/rambling | Point back to the formula; ask "what's the one sentence version of your context, and the one sentence version of your ask?" |
| Student wants to ask for something big (e.g., a job) right away | Redirect gently: "Let's make the first message just about reconnecting or one small question — bigger asks come later, after there's a relationship again." |
| Student is anxious about "bothering" someone | Normalize: most adults are flattered when a former student reaches out respectfully; a polite, brief message is never a bother. |
| Student wants to add a stranger found online because they "seem successful" | Firmly redirect: this lesson is only about real, existing connections; cold-adding strangers is explicitly out of scope and discouraged. |
| Under-16 student feels excluded by LinkedIn examples | Reaffirm the portfolio-first path is equal in value; use their existing portfolio/PDF resume for the same exercise. |

## How to Review Student Work

Check each drafted message for:
- [ ] Names a real, specific person the student actually knows (not a stranger or invented person).
- [ ] States shared context clearly in the first 1-2 sentences.
- [ ] Has a genuine, low-pressure reason for the message.
- [ ] Ask (if any) is small and specific, not vague or large.
- [ ] Tone is warm, respectful, and appropriately brief (roughly 80-150 words).
- [ ] No personal safety information included (address, schedule, passwords, financial info).
- [ ] Student has identified a trusted adult and a plan to loop them in before sending.

Give feedback as a comment directly on the student's Google Doc so they practice receiving professional-style feedback in the same tool they'll use for real mentor review later in the course.

## Assessment Tie-In

This lesson's knowledge checks and worksheet feed the Course 18 portfolio project rubric criterion "Professional Communication," which is scored in the course capstone in Lesson 10.

# Lesson 7: Build Your 90-Day Opportunity Plan

## What You're Doing Today

You've spent six lessons building real things: a professional presence, content pieces, a presence on more channels, and your first networking contacts. Today you turn all of that into one plan — a 90-day calendar with three monthly blocks that tells you exactly what to do and when, so it actually happens instead of staying scattered.

## Why This Matters

Here's the truth about most plans people never follow: they're either too big ("I'm going to post every day and message 20 people this week") or too vague ("I'll keep working on my stuff"). Both fail. The first burns you out in a week. The second never turns into anything you can point to.

A good plan is **paced and specific**. Small, consistent actions beat sporadic bursts almost every time. One piece of content every 2–3 weeks for three months gives you 5 finished pieces. One weekend where you try to make 5 pieces at once usually gives you 2 finished pieces and then nothing for two months, because you burned out.

And a plan doesn't mean nothing can change. It's a **default**, not a cage. If something better comes along in Month 2, you can take it. The plan just means you're not starting from zero every week trying to figure out what to do next.

## Breaking 90 Days Into 3 Monthly Blocks

Your plan has three sections, each covering about 30 days:

- **Month 1 (Days 1–30):** Get moving on what's already in progress. Finish something you started. Make your first networking touchpoint of the plan.
- **Month 2 (Days 31–60):** Build momentum. Publish new content. Reach out to new contacts. Take action on a concrete opportunity (apply, submit, register).
- **Month 3 (Days 61–90):** Finish strong. Wrap up your content total. Follow up with contacts. Complete or submit your opportunity goal.

Each block needs three kinds of goals:

1. **Content goals** — what you'll finish or publish, roughly one piece every 2–3 weeks (aim for 5 total across 90 days).
2. **Networking goals** — at least one touchpoint per month (a message, reply, or introduction — not necessarily a big ask).
3. **Opportunity goal(s)** — one or two specific, checkable things you're working toward (a competition entry, an application, a submission).

Every goal also needs a **"how I'll know"** — a real piece of evidence that proves you did it: a published link, a sent message you can point to, a confirmation email.

## Worked Example: Jordan's Plan

Jordan is a junior who wants to break into game development. Going into this lesson, Jordan has: a portfolio site, one finished blog post and one half-finished project writeup, a presence on a game-dev forum and a Discord server, and one cold email sent to an indie developer with no reply yet.

**Month 1:** Finish the half-finished writeup and publish it (Week 2). Start drafting a new short piece (done by Week 4). Follow up with the indie developer if no reply by Day 10. Introduce self in the Discord server. Find one game jam or student competition with a deadline in the next 90 days.

**Month 2:** Publish the piece drafted in Month 1. Start a third piece. Message 2 new contacts (a teacher, a meetup organizer, someone active in the Discord) — spaced out, not both the same day. Submit an entry to the competition found in Month 1, or get halfway through the jam project.

**Month 3:** Finish and publish piece 3 (and piece 4 or 5 if the pace allows — 5 pieces total is the target). Follow up with the 2 contacts from Month 2, and send one more new message. Finish and submit the competition entry if not already done. Write a short reflection on what came of the outreach.

Notice: nothing here is vague. Every action has a rough date and something checkable.

## Key Terms

- **Cadence** — how often you produce or publish something on a repeating schedule (e.g., "one piece every 2–3 weeks").
- **Milestone** — a specific, dated checkpoint inside your plan that marks real progress (e.g., "piece #3 published by Day 70").
- **Opportunity goal** — a concrete, checkable target tied to a real chance to grow (an application, a competition, a submission, a specific ask) — not a vague hope like "get better" or "get noticed."

## Step-by-Step Activity

1. Open your Worksheet (Google Doc or your planning tool).
2. List what you already have from Lessons 1–6: your presence, your content pieces (finished and in progress), your channels, and your networking contacts so far.
3. Fill in Month 1: what will you finish or start, who will you reach out to, what opportunity will you identify.
4. Fill in Month 2: what new content publishes, who are your new contacts, what action do you take on your opportunity goal.
5. Fill in Month 3: how do you finish your content total (aim for 5 pieces across 90 days), follow up with contacts, and complete your opportunity goal.
6. For every goal, write down how you'll know you did it — a link, a log, a confirmation.
7. Read your whole plan back. If any month has more than 2–3 actions, move something to a later month.

## Knowledge Checks

1. Roughly how often should you aim to publish a content piece over the 90 days? What's the total target?
2. Why does a plan that's "too much at once" usually fail, even for a motivated person?
3. Give an example of a networking touchpoint that is NOT a big, formal ask.
4. What's the difference between a content goal and an opportunity goal? Give one example of each.
5. Why does every goal in your plan need a "how I'll know" statement?

## Reflection Prompts

1. Which month of your plan feels the most realistic for your actual schedule, and which one worries you? Why?
2. Is there an opportunity (competition, program, application) you already know about that you could put into your plan right now?
3. If something unplanned but exciting came up in Month 2, how would you decide whether to adjust your plan around it?

## Submission Instructions

Submit your completed Worksheet (Google Doc or your planning tool export) with all three monthly blocks filled in: content goals, networking goals, opportunity goal(s), and a "how I'll know" statement for each. Make sure at least one opportunity goal names something specific and real, not a general hope.

Remember: this plan is a default, not a lock. If a real opportunity shows up that isn't on this sheet, you can still take it — just update the plan afterward so it stays useful.
lessons.teacherNotes:
# Instructor Guide — Lesson 7: Build Your 90-Day Opportunity Plan

## Metadata

- **Path:** Digital Independence Path
- **Course:** Course 18 — Professional Presence & Opportunity Building
- **Lesson:** 7 of 8 — Build Your 90-Day Opportunity Plan
- **Age range:** 15–18
- **Format:** Live, instructor-led (video classroom)
- **Duration:** 60 minutes
- **Tools needed:** Google Docs (plan document), content-planning tool already used in L4/L5 (e.g., a simple content calendar — spreadsheet or planner app)
- **Prerequisite state:** Student has an established professional presence (L1–3), at least one content piece drafted or published with more in progress (L4), presence extended across broader channels (L5), and outreach/networking activity started — at least one message sent or contact made (L6)
- **Lesson position in course arc:** This is the synthesis lesson. Everything built in L1–6 gets converted into a forward-looking, dated plan. L8 will likely be a review/showcase, so this is the last lesson where new planning work happens.

## Overview

Students have spent six lessons building pieces: a presence, content, channels, and early networking contacts. Those pieces are real but scattered in time — a profile here, a draft there, one message sent last week. This lesson has students convert that scattered work into a single **90-day plan** broken into three monthly blocks, each with a content cadence, networking touchpoints, and one or two concrete opportunity goals. The plan is realistic on purpose: paced for a teenager's actual weekly schedule (school, homework, other activities), not an idealized burst of activity.

The instructional bet here is pacing over ambition. Most students at this age either want to do everything in week one and burn out, or treat "make a plan" as a one-time abstract exercise disconnected from real dates. This lesson corrects both by making the plan concrete, dated, and checkable.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

1. Break a 90-day goal into three monthly blocks with specific, dated actions.
2. Set a realistic content cadence (roughly one piece every 2–3 weeks, five pieces total) instead of an unsustainable burst.
3. Define networking touchpoints as a repeatable monthly habit, not a one-off task.
4. Write one or two opportunity goals that are concrete and checkable ("apply to X by date," "publish 2 more pieces"), not vague ("get better at coding" or "become successful").
5. Identify a way to know whether each goal was actually completed.

## Prep Checklist (before class)

- Open a blank Google Doc titled "90-Day Opportunity Plan — Demo" for the live build.
- Have the Worksheet.md template ready to share/screen-share.
- Review each student's L4–L6 artifacts if accessible (content drafts, channel list, outreach log) so you can reference their real work during the plan-building activity — this lesson lands much better when tied to what a student already did, not hypothetical work.
- Prepare the fictional student example ("Jordan R.") talking points below so the live demo is fluent, not read verbatim.
- Have today's actual date on screen so month blocks can be dated live (e.g., "Month 1 = Sept 12–Oct 12").

## Teaching Sequence (60 minutes)

### 1. Opening + Framing (5 min)
Ask: "What's one piece of content or one networking thing you did in the last two weeks?" Take 2–3 quick answers. Frame the lesson: "Today we're not creating anything new — we're taking everything from the last six lessons and putting it on a calendar so it actually keeps happening."

### 2. Talking Points: Why Pacing Matters (8 min)
Deliver these points directly, not as a slide dump — talk through them:

- **Small and consistent beats big and sporadic.** One piece of content every 2–3 weeks for three months is five real, finished pieces. One "content sprint weekend" that burns you out produces two pieces and then nothing for two months.
- **A 90-day plan is not a cage.** Having a plan doesn't mean nothing can change — it means you have a default so you're not starting from zero every week deciding what to do. If an opportunity comes up that isn't on the plan, you can still take it. The plan is a floor, not a ceiling.
- **Networking touchpoints are a habit, not an event.** One outreach message a month, every month, for three months, builds a small real network. Reaching out to 15 people in one week and then never following up builds nothing — most of those contacts go cold.
- **Realistic means it fits around school.** A plan that assumes 2 hours a day of free time is not a plan a 16-year-old with homework, sports, and a life will follow. Ask what a student can actually do in a normal week, not their best week.

### 3. Live Demo: Building Jordan's 90-Day Plan (20 min)
Build this live in the Google Doc, narrating decisions out loud. Use a fictional student, "Jordan R.," a rising junior who wants to break into game development and has: a portfolio site (L1–3), one finished blog post and one half-finished project writeup (L4), a presence on a game-dev forum and a Discord server (L5), and one cold email sent to an indie developer with no reply yet (L6).

**Month 1 (Days 1–30):**
- Content goal: Finish and publish the half-finished project writeup (Week 2). Start a new short piece — "what I learned building X" (draft by Week 4).
- Networking goal: Reply-follow-up to the indie developer if no response by Day 10; introduce self in the Discord server's intro channel (Week 1); reply meaningfully to 2 threads on the forum (ongoing).
- Opportunity goal: Identify one game jam or student competition with a deadline in the next 90 days and register/bookmark it by end of month.
- How Jordan will know: writeup is live at a URL; one new Discord/forum interaction logged each week; competition name and deadline written down.

**Month 2 (Days 31–60):**
- Content goal: Publish the short piece drafted in Month 1 (Week 5–6). Start piece #3 — a short devlog about jam progress if entered, or a tutorial if not.
- Networking goal: Reach out to 2 new contacts (a teacher, a local dev meetup organizer, or someone active in the Discord) — one message each, spaced out, not both in one day.
- Opportunity goal: Submit an entry or application for the competition identified in Month 1, OR complete 50% of the jam project.
- How Jordan will know: piece #2 published; 2 new outreach messages sent and logged with dates; submission confirmation email or draft entry saved.

**Month 3 (Days 61–90):**
- Content goal: Finish and publish piece #3 (Week 9–10). Publish piece #4/#5 if pace allows — total of 5 pieces across the 90 days is the target, not 3.
- Networking goal: Follow up with the 2 new contacts from Month 2; one more new outreach message.
- Opportunity goal: Complete and submit the competition/jam entry if not already done in Month 2; reflect in writing on what came of the outreach (replies, no replies, next steps).
- How Jordan will know: final piece count reaches 5; outreach log shows 3+ new contacts total across 90 days; competition entry submitted with confirmation.

While building this, stop twice to ask the class: "Is this too much for one month? Too little?" and adjust live — this models that the plan is a draft, not a contract.

### 4. Discussion Questions (5 min)
- "Jordan's content cadence was one piece every 2–3 weeks. Is that realistic for you, or does your schedule need something slower or faster?"
- "What's one networking touchpoint you could actually repeat every month without it feeling exhausting?"
- "What's one opportunity — a competition, program, internship, or job — that has a real deadline in the next 90 days?"

### 5. Guided Activity: Students Build Their Own Plan (18 min)
Students open the Worksheet.md (as a Google Doc or their planning tool) and fill in their own 3-month table using their real L1–6 work as the starting point. Circulate to check in 1:1 or in breakout pairs. Prompt students who freeze on "opportunity goal" with: "What's one specific thing — an application, a submission, a competition, a request — you could point to on day 90 and say 'I did that'?"

### 6. Close (4 min)
Have 2–3 students share one goal from their plan out loud. Remind them: the plan gets checked in on (suggest a monthly self-check date), and it's fine to revise it — the point is having a default, not being locked in.

## Common Misconceptions (address explicitly during talking points or activity)

- **"I need to do everything at once."** Correct with the small-and-consistent point above. If a student's Month 1 has 4 content pieces and 5 outreach messages, that's a sign to redistribute across the 90 days, not to admire their ambition.
- **"A plan means nothing can change."** Correct with the "floor, not ceiling" framing. A plan is a default so you're not starting from scratch, not a contract that forbids new opportunities.
- **"Networking touchpoint" means a big ask.** Some students think every networking action has to be a formal request. Reinforce that a touchpoint can be small — a comment, a reply, a short check-in message.
- **"Opportunity goal" is the same as "keep doing content."** Students sometimes just restate their content goal as the opportunity goal. Push for something distinct and checkable — an application, submission, competition entry, or specific ask.

## Student Difficulties & Troubleshooting

| Difficulty | What it looks like | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Overloads Month 1 | Plans 5+ actions crammed into the first 30 days | Ask "what happens in a normal school week with homework?" and move items to Month 2/3 |
| Vague opportunity goal | Writes "get noticed" or "improve skills" | Ask "what's the specific thing — a form, a deadline, a person — that this points to?" |
| No real opportunity identified | Can't name a competition/program/internship | Give 2–3 generic examples appropriate to their interest area (school science fair, open-source contribution, student hackathon, local business asking for help, a relevant online competition) and let them adapt |
| Can't state "how I'll know" | Leaves that column blank or restates the goal | Ask "if I looked at your evidence 90 days from now, what would I actually see — a link, a screenshot, an email?" |
| Treats plan as rigid | Says "but what if I get a better idea in month 2?" | Reassure: revise it then — the written plan is today's best guess, not a lock |

## How to Review Student Work

Check each submitted plan for:
1. Three distinct monthly blocks, each with dated or week-numbered actions.
2. A content cadence that totals roughly 5 pieces across 90 days (not fewer than 3, not an unrealistic 10+).
3. At least one networking touchpoint per month, phrased as a repeatable or specific action (not "network more").
4. One or two opportunity goals that are concrete and named (a specific competition, application, or submission) with a rough target date.
5. A "how I'll know" statement for each goal that names actual evidence (a link, a log entry, a confirmation).

Plans missing item 4 or 5 are the most common gap — give feedback there first.

## Lesson Close / Transition to Next Lesson

End by telling students their plan is now their default calendar for the next 3 months, and that Lesson 8 will look back at what they've built across the whole course. Encourage them to put a recurring monthly reminder (phone, calendar) to check the plan against what actually happened.

lessons.title: Course 18, Lesson 8: Measure, Reflect, and Improve
lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Course 18, Lesson 8: Measure, Reflect, and Improve

**This is it — the final lesson of your entire Digital Independence Path.** Twenty-four lessons across three courses have led here. This lesson isn't about learning a new skill. It's about honestly checking your work, understanding what actually changed in you, and taking full ownership of what happens next.

## What & Why

Over this path you built real things: your identity and values (Course 16), your services and a practiced client relationship (Course 17), and a public presence with real content and real outreach (Course 18). That's a lot of work. Before you move on, you need to do two things well:

1. **Measure honestly.** Not "how many likes did I get," but "did I actually do the things I said I'd do?"
2. **Reflect on the whole journey**, so what you learned actually sticks and travels with you into whatever comes next — a job, an internship, college applications, your own projects.

Skipping this step is like finishing a workout and never checking whether your form was right — you'd repeat the same mistakes next time. Reflection is what turns "things I did" into "things I learned."

## Honest Progress Measures vs. Vanity Metrics

A **vanity metric** is a number that feels good but doesn't tell you whether you're actually building skill or momentum. Likes, followers, views, shares — these are shaped by algorithms, timing, and luck as much as by your effort. A **meaningful metric** is something only you control: did you finish the thing, did you follow through, did you learn something you can name.

| Vanity metric | Meaningful metric |
|---|---|
| "40 people liked my post" | "I published all 5 content pieces I planned" |
| "I have 200 followers" | "My portfolio is live and I can send someone the link right now" |
| "My video did really well" | "I completed the full client simulation, start to finish" |
| "A stranger commented something nice" | "I sent every outreach message in my networking plan" |
| "My profile looks impressive" | "I can explain what I do, clearly, in under a minute" |

Here's the key idea: **vanity metrics measure how other people reacted. Meaningful metrics measure what you actually did.** You have almost zero control over the first kind — the algorithm decides who sees your post, and luck decides who happens to be scrolling at that moment. You have complete control over the second kind. Right now, early in building a professional presence, the habit that matters most is following through — not going viral.

This doesn't mean an audience never matters. Later on, reach and engagement genuinely help you find opportunities. But building the *habit* of honest follow-through now is worth more than a lucky viral moment, because the habit is what you can repeat for the rest of your career.

## Whole-Path Reflection: Course 16 → 17 → 18

Before today, take a minute to actually think back — not just skim your memory. Answer these for yourself (you'll discuss some with the class):

**Course 16 (Identity):**
- What's one thing you believed about your strengths or interests back then that you'd describe differently now?
- What part of your personal narrative feels most true to you today?

**Course 17 (Services & Client Work):**
- What was the hardest moment in your client simulation? What did it teach you about working with real people?
- Did building your pricing worksheet change how you think about the value of your own time and skill?

**Course 18 (Presence & Opportunity Building):**
- What's one piece of content or one outreach message you're genuinely proud of, and why?
- What surprised you about putting yourself out there publicly?

**Whole path:**
- If a friend outside this course asked "what did you actually learn?" — what would you tell them in two sentences?
- What's different about how you think about "being a professional" now compared to 24 lessons ago?

## Worked Example: A Student's Honest Self-Review

Here's a fictional example — Priya, age 16 — reviewing her own path honestly.

> **Checklist review:** "My portfolio is live — I can send the link right now. I published 5 pieces, though honestly 2 of them were shorter than I wanted. My client simulation is fully done. My 90-day plan is written but I've only completed the first two weeks of actions so far, since the course isn't over yet."
>
> **Vanity vs. meaningful check:** "My most-liked post only got 12 likes, which used to bother me. But that post was actually the one I learned the most from writing, because I had to explain a technical idea simply. I'm choosing to count that as a win even though the like count is small."
>
> **Whole-path reflection:** "In Course 16 I thought my strength was 'being good at coding.' Now I'd say my strength is explaining coding to people who don't code yet — that came out of building content in Course 18. The client simulation in Course 17 was hard because my fake client kept changing their mind, and I learned to ask clarifying questions before I started building instead of after. I don't think I saw myself as someone who could offer a real service before this path. Now I have a pricing worksheet, a portfolio, and a plan — I actually believe I could do freelance work, even small jobs, starting now."
>
> **Next action:** "By next Friday, I'm sending three more outreach messages from my networking plan. I told my older sister to ask me about it so I actually do it."

Notice what Priya did: she was honest about what wasn't finished, she reframed a low like-count as a real win because of what she *learned*, and she connected all three courses into one story about herself.

## Step-by-Step Activity

1. **Get your materials ready:** your L7 90-day plan, and access to your portfolio/profile/content.
2. **Open the Worksheet** ("Path Completion & Reflection") and complete Part 1, the full deliverables checklist — mark each item honestly as Done, In Progress, or Not Started. No one is grading this. A "not started" is useful information, not a failure.
3. **Complete Part 2**, the "most proud of / would improve" reflection.
4. **Answer the whole-path reflection questions** above, in writing, in the worksheet or your own notes.
5. **Open your 90-day plan.** Identify: what's the very next action, what date is it due, and who will you tell about it so you stay accountable without a class checking in on you?
6. **Write and sign your commitment statement** (Part 3 of the worksheet).
7. **Bring your checklist and reflection to class** for the whole-group discussion.

## Key Terms

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Vanity metric** | A number that feels good or impressive but doesn't reliably indicate real progress or skill, because it's shaped mostly by factors outside your control (algorithm, luck, timing) — e.g., likes, followers, views. |
| **Meaningful metric** | A measure of progress that reflects something you actually did and fully control — e.g., did I publish it, did I finish it, did I send it. |
| **Reflection** | The deliberate act of looking back at what you did and asking what it taught you, so the experience turns into a lesson you can carry forward — not just a memory of an event. |

## Knowledge Checks

1. Which of these is a vanity metric, and which is a meaningful metric: "My portfolio is live" vs. "My latest post got 80 likes"? Explain your reasoning in one sentence.
2. Why is a meaningful metric something you have more control over than a vanity metric?
3. Name one thing from Course 16 (identity) that directly helped you in Course 17 or Course 18. Be specific.
4. True or false: once this course ends, your 90-day plan is finished too. Explain your answer.
5. Give one example of a "not yet done" item that would be completely reasonable to have on your checklist today, and explain why it's not a failure.

## Reflection Prompts

1. What is the one deliverable from this entire path that you're most proud of, and what does it prove you can do?
2. What is one honest gap on your checklist, and what's your plan to close it in the next 30 days?
3. Looking back at all 24 lessons, what's the biggest shift in how you see yourself professionally — compared to who you were before Course 16?

## Submission Instructions

Submit the following to your instructor by the end of this lesson (or within 24 hours, if your program allows async submission):

- Your completed **Worksheet.md** (all three parts: checklist, reflection, commitment statement).
- Your written answers to the five knowledge checks and three reflection prompts above.
- A link to your live portfolio/profile, so your instructor can see your presence work is real and accessible.

## Closing Note

You just completed the Digital Independence Path — 24 lessons, three courses, and a lot of real, verifiable work: an identity you can articulate, services you can actually offer, a presence that's live on the internet, and a plan with your name on it for what comes next. Whatever your checklist looks like today, fully checked or not, you are measurably further along than when you started, and — unlike most people your age — you have a specific, dated plan for continuing to build. That's not the end of the story. It's the part where you take the plan and run with it. Congratulations.

# Worksheet: Path Completion & Reflection

**Digital Independence Path — Final Worksheet (Course 18, Lesson 8)**

Name: _______________________  Date: _______________________

There's no passing or failing score on this worksheet. Its only job is to tell you the truth about where you are, so your next 90 days are built on facts instead of guesses. Mark each item honestly.

---

## Part 1: Full-Path Deliverables Checklist

For each item, mark **Done**, **In Progress**, or **Not Started**. Add a one-line note where useful (a link, a date, or what's missing).

### Course 16 — Identity Foundations

| Item | Status | Note |
